items.title: Ten pandemic-era dining sheds that show "wildly different tastes" of New Yorkers
items.summary:
From hastily installed sheds and tents to more intricate structures with signage and considered design, author Penny Hardy highlights the absurdity, delight and ingenuity of dining sheds installed in New York during the Covid-19 pandemic. Collected in Hardy's recently announced book, Pandemic Architecture: NYC Dining Sheds 2020-2024, the sheds represent a very specific time in […] 
 The post  Ten pandemic-era dining sheds that show "wildly different tastes" of New Yorkers  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Ben Dreith US editor 11 October 2026 From hastily installed sheds and tents to more intricate structures with signage and considered design, author Penny Hardy highlights the absurdity, delight and ingenuity of dining sheds installed in New York during the Covid-19 pandemic . Collected in Hardy’s recently announced book, Pandemic Architecture: NYC Dining Sheds 2020-2024 , the sheds represent a very specific time in the landscape of the city, when restaurants tried to operate during indoor dining restrictions. Many have since been deconstructed, as the city tries to implement a standardised shed programme to keep the seating while maintaining safety and sanitation standards. New York mayor Zohran Mamdani recently cleared the legal way for year-round installation . Hardy took photos of the sheds in Downtown Manhattan on walks during the height of the pandemic and afterwards, as many remained up for years after the 2020 to 2021 lockdowns. Though many of the restaurants have since closed or moved, Hardy believes that it’s clear that the impact of the structures has changed the way we view the streetscape. Penny Hardy’s new book looks at the range of impromptu dining sheds installed in New York during the Covid-19 pandemic “These structures created a new typology for building in public space and have forever changed the way we use the street,” she told Dezeen. “Before this new typology, the street was aggressively preserved as a place of transit by the city. Now, in addition to transit, it offers a place for people to connect and socialise.” She added that the recent city legislation opens up room for a return to the creativity that has been limited by the high costs of storage and assembly of the structures during the winter months. “The restaurant owners’ resourcefulness, humour, and wildly different tastes made the streets more varied and alive,” said Hardy. “The structures were raw, inventive, funny, and as varied as New York itself. They brought an old-school punk, DIY spirit back into an increasingly polished city.” The book contains dozens of examples taken by Hardy, as well as essays by New York writers such as Michael Bullock and Fred Bernstein . Read on for a selection of images from the book and Hardy’s commentary. “Suburban design via Home Depot” in Greenwich Village “‘We need to get something up quick. Go to Home Depot. Improvise’. I imagine this was the directive given to an employee or self-imposed by the owner. “Ubiquitous ‘colonial moulded interior door’ with handle and lock, surrounded by vibrant magenta plastic panelling, taped heart detailing and painted soft pink plywood. Why didn’t they paint the door?” “Less is enough” in West Village “Use structures that already exist. They provide privacy, protection, and shelter from the weather. Why make things more complicated? “The neighbourhood institution, Julius, kept it simple. Perhaps the owner was a camper – bring in a tent from the country, order a few more, and they were done.” “Learning from Las Vegas” in Little Italy “If only Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown had been able to see these sheds: one a decorated shed, the other architecture becoming the sign itself. “Baby John created a dining structure fit for his namesake. A curved vinyl banquette pulled from deep storage, a monumental crown, and signage visible from blocks away combined to create a VIP experience that drew long lines and gave the place instant cachet. Venturi and Scott Brown would surely have joined the queue.” “An imposing mash-up of classical architecture” in Little Italy “Down the street, a fellow, longtime restaurateur created an imposing mash-up of classical architecture and gothic detailing. “Its sense of grandeur, in direct contrast to the temporality of the sheds, creates a playful contradiction. Venturi and Brown would have appreciated the ‘complexity and contradiction’.” “The wild west” in Chinatown “Almost overnight, the street became a space of radical improvisation, where rigid building restrictions of the city were tossed aside, as restaurants fought for survival. “Exposed electrical wires brought air conditioners and fans into the sheds. Practical and terrifying at the same time.” “Take me away” in SoHo “Perhaps we can transport them somewhere tropical, offering a brief respite from the city. If they can’t get on an aeroplane, maybe the dining shed can take them there. “A thatched roof, white curtains tied with rope tassels, and tropical plants conjure a beachfront cabana.” “Co-existing” in West Village “The interweaving of street signs and structures with the dining sheds created humorous juxtapositions. “Why extend the structure to enclose the postal relay box? Rather than stopping short of it, the shed carefully absorbs it into the design, even carving out space for the neighbouring tree. Existing street infrastructure becomes part of the architecture.” “Living in the street” in NoHo “Owners looked for ways to make street dining feel comfortable, creating environments that helped diners forget they were sitting in a place never meant for a meal. “The dark-stained wood panelling and curated selection of framed paintings evoke the atmosphere of farm life, creating the feeling of dining in the countryside.” “Architecture, design and construction professionals enter the fray” in Flatiron “Whether these were designed by an architect, interior designer or contractor, they all had the visible sign of a professional being involved. Material choices, lighting, and built-in seating suggest a level of planning beyond improvisation. “A classic gable roof, clapboard siding, and exposed stud framing suggest the work of a general contractor with spare materials from their last project?” “Even the heaters have been carefully considered” in Nolita “The minimal, modular design suggests the involvement of an architect. “Even the heaters have been carefully considered, integrated beneath the seating.” Read more Books USA Pavilions Restaurants Roundups D

items.title: Formant Studio reinterprets the classic tavern at contemporary Mexico City restaurant
items.summary:
Local practice Formant Studio created custom furniture and fixtures while designing Mexico City restaurant Nota Tavern, taking references from classic Chicago taverns in the fit-out of a former residence. Located in the city's Escandón I neighbourhood, Nota Tavern is a two-storey Italian-American restaurant. It sits on a site that once held a hacienda-style residence that […] 
 The post  Formant Studio reinterprets the classic tavern at contemporary Mexico City restaurant  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Ben Dreith US editor 9 October 2026 Local practice Formant Studio created custom furniture and fixtures while designing Mexico City restaurant Nota Tavern, taking references from classic Chicago taverns in the fit-out of a former residence. Located in the city’s Escandón I neighbourhood, Nota Tavern is a two-storey Italian-American restaurant. It sits on a site that once held a hacienda-style residence that was converted into an apartment building, with the owner preserving half of the original house. The restaurant sits in this portion. Formant Studio designed the interiors and most of the furniture at Nota Tavern in Mexico City Formant Studio was tasked with translating the design of classic Chicago taverns into a contemporary mode. “The main request was to create a faithful interpretation of the neighbourhood taverns of Chicago – the kind of places built less around spectacle and more around familiarity,” Formant Studio co-founder Alejandro Valencia told Dezeen. “The design translates the character of a classic tavern into a contemporary architectural language.” The two-storey restaurant serves Italian-American cuisine Valencia also said the studio took other cues from Chicago and integrated the clean minimalism of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and the warmer modernism of Frank Lloyd Wright , both architects known for their work in the US city. Also in the tradition of the 20th-century modern architects, Formant Studio designed most of the furniture, from the black-stained oak tables to the steel bar stools and sleek metal sconces. The space was once a hacienda-style residence and its original columns were preserved and restored The majority of the dining room was clad in Mexican rosewood panels, which also form the custom banquettes upholstered in black Kvadrat textiles. Formant Studio said that the previous space defined how it organised the restaurant. Mexican rosewood covers the walls and forms banquette seating The current space still has ornate stone pillars that once framed an entrance portico. The team removed the paint from the pillars, turning them into a centrepiece of the main dining space. An entrance vestibule holds a host stand and a door leads to a metal spiral staircase painted in a rich brown. This staircase leads to a private dining room upstairs. Past the host stand, the main dining room opens up. Visitors walk into a front area with a large banquette and a seating bar that looks out of an operable window onto the street. The design was drawn from classic Chicago taverns “The shape of the existing space largely determined the furniture layout,” said Valencia. “We used the longer walls to accommodate the built-in booths, establishing a clear spatial rhythm while keeping the central area flexible and allowing the dining room to adapt to different group sizes and configurations.” Past the columns, the room has an array of tables arranged under the double-height ceiling. The rafters of the former space were painted white and a mezzanine from the private dining space juts out over a row of banquette seating. This mezzanine has a high boundary that provides privacy from below. At the back of the space is the bar, with a mirror backsplash and rosewood millwork above. Steel contrasts with wood and minimalist decor A sound system by Paxwave was installed in the space. The tablescapes were styled with sheer white cloths, which contrast with the stained-black chairs and the polished grey terrazzo flooring. The kitchen space sits under the private dining room and is hidden from the main space. More mirrors line the wall that divides the kitchen, while the windows opposite have metal grating. Street-facing windows bring light into the space, where mirrors were used to further diffuse the light Art and antiques were curated by Galería Córdoba . Formant Studio also designed its own studio in Mexico City , which it shares with photographer Fabián Martinez . Dezeen included Formant Studio in a list of notable Mexico designers earlier this year. The photography is by Fabián Martinez. Read more Wood Mexico City Restaurants Mexico Interiors Exclusives

items.title: Spirit of Iberian taverns informs wood-heavy Parisian restaurant
items.summary:
Emerging Marseille firm Bétyle Studio has designed the interiors for Arcane 17, a Basque and Catalan restaurant in Paris featuring patinated timber and distinctive marquetry. Located in the city's Le Marais neighbourhood in the 4th arrondissement, Arcane 17 is a petite eatery that sits within a centuries-old building. Bétyle Studio founders Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave […] 
 The post  Spirit of Iberian taverns informs wood-heavy Parisian restaurant  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Jane Englefield Design and interiors reporter 6 October 2026 Emerging Marseille firm Bétyle Studio has designed the interiors for Arcane 17, a Basque and Catalan restaurant in Paris featuring patinated timber and distinctive marquetry . Located in the city’s Le Marais neighbourhood in the 4th arrondissement, Arcane 17 is a petite eatery that sits within a centuries-old building. Arcane 17 is a Basque and Catalan restaurant Bétyle Studio founders Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche wanted to honour the owners’ Catalan roots through their restaurant design. “Rather than reproducing the codes of a traditional Spanish restaurant, we wanted to reinterpret the idea of the Iberian tavern through a more contemporary and refined language,” studio founders Carla Romano and Nicolas Cazenave de la Roche told Dezeen. Bétyle Studio designed the interiors for the space In this spirit, the designers clad the open space in an abundance of wood. The dining area is characterised by ebonised panelling, while the tubular stainless steel bar is topped with delicate slabs of marquetry detailing playful motifs, from shooting stars to a cartoonish lobster. Classic bentwood chairs make up the dining space “We drew inspiration from the energy of rural churches, dark woods and the movement of traditional fans,” explained Romano and Cazenave de la Roche. “We did not want these references to be literal, but rather to emerge through materials, textures and forms.” Classic, bentwood chairs feature alongside uniform timber tables. In one corner, a red-clad banquette subtly nods to traditional Parisian bistros. All of the space’s joinery was conceived bespoke for the restaurant by a Marseille-based carpenter and frequent collaborator of Bétyle Studio. “We worked with different species of wood and experimented with various techniques to stain, ebonise and patinate the timber,” said Romano and Cazenave de la Roche. “The idea was to give depth to the surfaces and create elements that feel as though they could have belonged to the space for a long time.” Playful marquetry was created specifically for the project Local studio Côme Clérino designed a selection of chunky plaster sconces specifically for the restaurant that loosely resemble elongated seashells. Founded in January 2025, Bétyle Studio works across interior architecture and furniture design. Last year, the studio transformed an old farm building in Marseille into a compact, wood-lined home. Elsewhere in Paris, architect Cyrus Ardalan recently renovated a corner apartment with a timber-heavy interior, complete with porthole-style openings designed to feel nautical. items.text: Francesca Tesler 6 October 2026 Cocktail bar and restaurant Bar Shrimp combines red velvet interiors with bespoke acoustic panels from Autex Acoustics to balance music and conversation, shown in this video produced by Dezeen. Located in Manchester , Bar Shrimp has a custom sound system and a dark interior with floor-to-ceiling red velvet curtains and plush banquettes, reminiscent of vintage New York bars and music lounges. The design was informed by the founders’ experience of bars around the world, where co-founder Richard Cossins said they were struck by ones with particularly good sound. “When we first saw the space, we wanted to create a relaxed and comfortable environment, where guests could spend numerous hours within the space,” Cossins told Dezeen. Bar Shrimp’s interior draws on mid-century bar decor The existing space had a concrete floor and glass walls, prompting the team to introduce softer materials to improve the acoustics. Autex Acoustics worked with the team from an early stage, supplying a bespoke Frontier Axis ceiling system and Mirage wall panels to reduce reverberation and echo. The acoustic treatment was designed to complement the interior rather than disappear into it, with laser-etched patterns giving the Mirage panels a textured finish inspired by natural materials. DJs provide a curated music programme throughout the day “We’re looking at it from a technical perspective, but also from an aesthetic perspective,” said Autex Acoustics UK, EU and the Middle East director Daniel Senior. “We laser etch a pattern into a panel,” he continued. “That allows us to create some really intricate designs, to create real depth and texture to a panel, all taking inspiration from natural materials.” Bar Shrimp also features a custom MasterSounds Clarity M-1215 Audio system – a large-format modular speaker system designed to provide high-quality sound throughout the space. The panels were chosen to blend with the rest of the restaurant’s interior. Cossins said the acoustic treatment was intended to make the bar comfortable even when music is playing at a high volume. “It’s an aspect of the guest experience that doesn’t necessarily get noticed, but when you walk into a space and you don’t have to shout and you can hear your guests and your dining companions with real clarity, I think it goes a long way,” he said. The project continues a six-year-long collaboration between Cossins and Autex Acoustics, who also worked together to design the interiors of Higher Ground, Bar Shrimp’s sister restaurant located next door. Founded in 1967, Autex Acoustics produces sound-dampening products for offices and mixed-use interiors. In 2025, the brand created a forest-like installation using its signature acoustic material at LA Design Festival in downtown Los Angeles. items.title: Rockwell Group eschews 90-degree angles for Skywalker Grill at Lucas Museum
items.summary:
Here's a closer look inside the newly opened Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, where design studio Rockwell Group has outfitted a restaurant and bar that "responds to the museum's distinctive biomorphic architecture". Rockwell Group's Los Angeles office designed the Skywalker Grill without a single 90-degree angle, continuing the sweeping curves of the building by MAD […] 
 The post  Rockwell Group eschews 90-degree angles for Skywalker Grill at Lucas Museum  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Dan Howarth 26 September 2026 Here’s a closer look inside the newly opened Lucas Museum of Narrative Art , where design studio Rockwell Group has outfitted a restaurant and bar that “responds to the museum’s distinctive biomorphic architecture”. Rockwell Group ‘s Los Angeles office designed the Skywalker Grill without a single 90-degree angle, continuing the sweeping curves of the building by MAD Architects . The Skywalker Grill features no 90-degree angles to echo the Lucas Museum’s biomorphic architecture The eatery also references the warm cherry wood interiors of Skywalker Ranch, a 4,700-acre filmmaker’s retreat and workspace owned by Star Wars director George Lucas in Marin County, California. Overlooking the Los Angeles skyline, the fifth-floor restaurant and bar is named after the sci-fi media franchise’s principal character. It is open to both museum visitors and the general public for lunch and dinner. Entry to the fifth-floor space is via a corridor wrapped with cherry wood panels “Responding to the museum’s distinctive biomorphic architecture, the restaurant features no 90-degree angles,” said the Skywalker Grill team. “Curved walls are wrapped in individually crafted cherry wood panels, with no two panels alike, while finger-raked cherrywood columns echo the tambour banquettes lining the perimeter of the room.” Shimmering tiles cover the front of the snaking bar, while the back bar is clad in illuminated Corian Guests arrive via elevator to a corridor that leads to the host stand, lined on one side with cherry panelling that folds up and over the ceiling. Booths are formed with swooping partitions that organically rise and fall in height, and curve to create intimate pockets for conversation. The cherry used throughout the restaurant is a nod to the wood found at George Lucas’s Skywalker Ranch in Marin County A central island is ringed by a green crushed velvet banquette that matches the booth upholstery, and surrounded by circular tables and freestanding dining chairs in soft grey. Tamboured cherry-wrapped columns rise at slight angles and branch like tree trunks to meet the ceiling, which opens in the middle to reveal a beige plaster surface illuminated by cove lighting. A large ovoid window opens onto a terrace with panoramic views The snaking, glossy white bar counter is fronted by shimmering fluted tiles covered in crystal silver leaf, while illuminated Corian forms the back bar. A large ovoid window features operable glass panels that provide access to the outdoor terrace, where further seating enjoys views over the University of Southern California campus towards Downtown LA. “The design incorporates elements of cinematic storytelling, including framing, light, scale and atmosphere, while pairing high-tech materials with handcrafted details,” said the team. The restaurant’s American-style menu features California-grown ingredients, including Wagyu beef and honey ricotta sourced from Skywalker Ranch. Curved, undulating partitions form intimate dining booths Set in a 13-acre landscaped site near Los Angeles’ Exposition Park, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is dedicated to storytelling and features a variety of galleries, theatres and educational spaces. MAD and Stantec wrapped the building in over 1,200 curved panels, creating an extraterrestrial form that wouldn’t look out of place in one of Lucas’s beloved movies. The terrace enjoys panoramic views over Los Angeles Rockwell Group is known for its theatrical hospitality projects that immerse diners in atmospheric spaces. Other recent examples include an art deco-influenced Manhattan steakhouse , a revolving restaurant above Times Square and a “cathedral of fried chicken” . The photography is by Tom McGovern . items.title: Surrane Design uses "stages of the rice plant" to tone Thai restaurant in New York
items.summary:

Hommali is located at the edges of New York's West Village neighbourhood and was founded by Bangkok natives […] 
 The post  Surrane Design uses "stages of the rice plant" to tone Thai restaurant in New York  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Ellen Eberhardt US reporter 4 September 2026 New York studio Surrane Design has outfitted Thai restaurant Hommali in New York with a terracotta floor, a central “courtyard” space and personal items of the founders to create a space that resembles a traditional Thai house. Hommali is located at the edges of New York’s West Village neighbourhood and was founded by Bangkok natives chef Chattchakorn “Benz” Khajornchaisan, general manager Kritayanee “Air” Promsarin and operations lead Pichalak “Picha” Srigungvarl after they moved to New York City and met in the hospitality scene. Surrane Design has completed a Thai restaurant in the West Village The restaurant contains an eight-seat bar, a 20-seat dining den, a semi-private mezzanine and auxiliary spaces such as a wine room and dry-age room where ducks and other ferments are on display. Surrane Design layered the space with a rich assortment of textures and patterns, such as dark wood millwork, a marbled bar top and artwork sourced from Bangkok’s Chatuchak Weekend Market. It brings together a rich assortment of textures and colours informed by Thailand According to the team, its palette of browns and greens was informed by the life cycle of a rice plant. “The color palette is inspired by the stages of the rice plant: fresh green for young leaves, golden yellow for mature stalks, earthy brown for paddy soil, soft beige for rice husks, and warm cream white for polished rice,” said the team. Personal items from the ownership team line a partition It was designed to resemble a traditional Thai house, where the central dining den and mezzanine above recall a courtyard, and the terracotta floor also calls to the vernacular architecture of the country. Visitors are greeted with a rice plant light installation at the doorway and enter by the bar, which is clad in a sandy fluted tile with seats upholstered in leather and velvet. Stairs lead to a mezzanine with additional seating Two booths sit in front of the main dining space, which is tucked beneath the mezzanine. Curtains and open shelving separate the two spaces. Personal items from the ownership team, such as vintage Thai cookbooks from the late 1960s and early 1970s and other objects “one would expect to find in a living room” line the shelves. Small bamboo sculptures by Thai artist Korakot Aromdee are also peppered throughout the space. Wood-lined stairs lead to the mezzanine above, which contains additional seating concealed behind a frosted glass railing. A large skylight hangs above the space and sits over a large dining table. Banquets and an off-white white wallpaper embossed with 3D-printed plants also line the space. Like below, a curtain can be drawn across the length of the space to provide additional separation. A large skylight hangs above the space Hommali will serve contemporary takes on traditional Thai dishes created under Benz, such as a seafood cocktail with razor clams imbued with the hot and sour notes of tom yum and the Tomato, “a michelada-meets-spritz with a Singaporean rice wine base accompanied by a Thai chile tincture.” Surrane Design is an independent design studio based in Brooklyn by partners Bud Nitaya and Yoon Her. Other recently opened spaces in the West Village include Love Thy Neighbour next to The Stonewall Inn and The Cherry Lane Theatre The photography is by Hommali Read more USA Restaurants New York City West Village Interiors Exclusives

items.title: Montreal restaurant Minnibar by Ivy Studio "embraces its raw shell"
items.summary:
Japanese minimalism has informed the interiors of this light-filled Italian restaurant in Montreal, designed by locally based Ivy Studio with its first in-house designed chairs. Located on the ground level of a Downtown high-rise residential tower, Minnibar utilises the 20-foot (6-metre) ceilings, corner aspect and almost square floor plan to its advantage. Ivy Studio left […] 
 The post  Montreal restaurant Minnibar by Ivy Studio "embraces its raw shell"  appeared first on  Dezeen .
items.text: Dan Howarth 1 August 2026 Japanese minimalism has informed the interiors of this light-filled Italian restaurant in Montreal , designed by locally based Ivy Studio with its first in-house designed chairs. Located on the ground level of a Downtown high-rise residential tower, Minnibar utilises the 20-foot (6-metre) ceilings, corner aspect and almost square floor plan to its advantage. At the entrance to Minnibar, a pale stone-clad cafe counter drops in height to become an omakase-style ledge Ivy Studio left the building’s structure entirely visible, and only added elements where functionally necessary – using the principles of Japanese minimalism as a guide. “Minnibar embraces its raw shell,” said the studio. “Exposed base-building elements – including the naturally sealed concrete floor, formidable concrete columns, walls, and the ceiling slab – are left untouched.” A slender black ledge along the windows provides space for dining The kitchen, bar and pizza counter are housed within an enclosed central core, allowing the cafe and restaurant spaces to flow openly around the perimeter. Morning patrons have easy access from the entrance to the cafe counter, which is clad in monolithic, cream-colored stone with a leather finish. Triangular shapes can be spotted in the wall-mounted lighting and millwork details As it continues into the space, the counter drops in height and is replaced with an omakase-style ledge crafted from white oak. Opposite, a black shelf runs along the windows to provide additional bar dining space, accompanied by circular white stools. The main dining area is arranged symmetrically around glowing wall-mounted artwork “The design employs a strict monochromatic palette, playing with off-white and grey shades punctuated by sharp black integrations,” said Ivy Studio. “To give the minimalist aesthetic a profound sense of depth, the design introduces subtle, highly tactile finishes: hand-plastered walls, heavily textured stones, opaque stained wood grains, and translucent textiles.” A custom stainless steel DJ booth sits at the apex of sight lines in two directions The main dining space features freestanding black tables for flexibility, which are typically arranged in a symmetrical layout around an adjustable glowing artwork on the back wall. Several custom furnishings, which represent “a study in contrast and craftsmanship,” are installed throughout the restaurant. A largely monochromatic palette evokes a Japanese minimalist aesthetic These include Ivy Studio’s first in-house designed chair, which features softly curved legs and a delicate backrest – all crafted from ash wood and stained soft yellow. The sculptural, stainless steel DJ booth was created in collaboration with local shop Procedures Industries and is equipped with built-in vinyl players. Triangular details recur throughout, including in the stainless steel bar counter footrest, windows into the wine cellar, wall-mounted light fixtures and millwork. Rice-paper screens help to shade the interiors from bright sunlight and also form acoustic buffers across the ceiling. The omakase-style bar and accompanying chairs are crafted from white oak “Minnibar successfully harmonises the gritty, raw shell of downtown Montreal’s urban architecture with the refined, atmospheric principles of Japanese minimalism,” said the studio. “By contrasting heavy, exposed concrete with custom monolithic furniture, dynamic lighting, and an uncompromising dedication to sound and culinary craft, the space transcends the traditional restaurant model to offer a truly immersive, day-to-night destination.” The restaurant features Ivy Studio’s first chair designed in-house Ivy Studio has completed multiple restaurants across Montreal, including the “bold and glamorous” Limousine , the marble-filled Hayat , and Piatti , which was resurrected after a fire. The firm’s portfolio also includes an indoor golf club , an ad agency in a converted bank and a creative hub with a “work in progress” aesthetic . The photography is by Alex Lesage . items.title: A metal-heavy newsletter, from a mirror by a female welder to a Graves-inspired butter dish
items.summary: Plus: Interiors from a bakery, a showhouse, and a tech office.
items.text: 11.07.26 The Weekly A metal-heavy newsletter, from a mirror by a female welder to a Graves-inspired butter dish by Monica Khemsurov Welcome to the new Sight Unseen, a weekly newsletter that delivers the best of the design world — news, trends, shopping advice, interviews, travel recs, and more — straight to your inbox. If you’re not subscribed, follow this link to sign up . Want to partner with us, advertise, or submit your work ( guidelines here )? Email us at hello@sightunseen.com . A Minimalist Conversation Pit and a Maximalist Lounge Were Our Faves at the Brooklyn Heights Showhouse Top and middle left, Llewellyn Chupin’s room at the Brooklyn Heights Designer Showhouse; middle right and bottom, Max Aboody’s. Photos: Tori Sikkema The biennial Brooklyn Heights Designer Showhouse wrapped its latest edition this past weekend, having invited 19 designers to take over a landmarked 1852 mansion on Monroe Place. The results ranged from classic, antique-filled rooms (as we all know, most showhouses skew pretty trad) to a couple of wilder decorative experiments, but two of our favorites happened to occupy opposite ends of the aesthetic spectrum: a serene, almost minimalist gathering space by Llewellyn Chupin and a dark, Space Age–inspired lounge by Max Aboody Interiors. We’ve been following French-born, New York– and Paris-based designer Llewellyn Chupin since naming her to our American Design Hot List last year , with a furniture collection that paired architectural forms with jewelry-like details. For the showhouse, she transformed a small cellar-level room into the equivalent of a chic conversation pit. A continuous, cream-colored banquette wrapped around three sides of the space, facing a low travertine coffee table, while floor-to-ceiling curtains and strategically placed mirrors made the room feel taller and more expansive. In addition to the table, the sofa’s frame and arms acted as pedestals for a smattering of vintage objects. The overall effect evoked an intimate Parisian salon with a Japanese sense of minimalism. Upstairs, Brooklyn designer Max Aboody drenched a room in color and pattern. Aboody — who studied fashion at Parsons and worked in couture before turning to interiors — created a lounge that was almost too rich and layered for its stated inspiration source of “retro space-age design.” Walnut-paneled walls were punctuated by lighted circular openings and perforated shutters, while the rest of the room was swathed in blue carpet and upholstery, offset with a painterly wallpaper from Arte . Perfectly placed objects like a chainmail stool from Mexican studio Panoramma and a vintage tramp art frame from Freaks NY completed the scene. If Chupin’s space invited you to settle in and chat for hours, Aboody’s made you want to pour a drink and put on a record. It’s kind of a bummer that both were only temporary in the end. Of: Enso Fills a New York Office With Vintage Finds and a Painting-Adorned Daybed The new Cosmos offices by Of: Enso include the studio’s own objects as well as vintage ones, but my favorite is a painting hung on the side of a daybed. Photos: Marco Galloway Considering the founder of Cosmos — the visual inspiration platform intended as a Pinterest alternative for high-brow creatives — was also a co-founder of the New York vintage furniture gallery Galerie Was, it tracks that his company’s new headquarters in Tribeca is object-laden and curated to a tee. He invited interiors studio Of: Enso to create a space that feels less like it was furnished all at once than assembled lovingly, piece by piece, over time. We’ve covered more than our fair share of offices that look like living rooms lately, but this one feels particularly appropriate given the client’s obsession with images, objects, and the way people collect and organize them. Occupying the 19th floor of a 1930s building, the office has the kind of architectural bones that don’t need much embellishment: high ceilings, concrete floors, and enormous original windows overlooking the city. Of: Enso used that envelope as a clean backdrop to the furnishing scheme, which mixes vintage finds with their own custom designs like a cherrywood screen with leather-rope detailing, and a mustard-yellow silk pendant with a hand-painted floral motif. Elsewhere, vintage Japanese objects, leather sling-back chairs, and a hanging Indian Kantha quilt give the space texture, in addition to my very favorite part of the scheme: a tiny landscape painting hung on the back arm of a Judd-like daybed, which plays to my ongoing obsession with artworks displayed in unconventional ways . The designers made a point of choosing furniture that could be moved around as the company grows — a practical consideration that thankfully doesn’t seem, in this case, to have come at the expense of aesthetics. Jialun Xiong Explores Her Cozier Side For a New Bakery in L.A. Jialun Xiong’s interiors for the new bakery Dear Guest in L.A.’s Silverlake neighborhood. Photos: Elizabeth Carababas The early work of L.A. designer and Hot List alum Jialun Xiong was almost exclusively monochromatic, angular, and heavy on metal; her 2023 restaurant project, 19 Town , introduced a little more warmth and texture, but still relied on a neutral palette and rigorous architectural forms. We love to see a designer’s practice expand and shape-shift, and Xiong’s newest project — the interiors for a bakery called Dear Guest in L.A.’s Silverlake neighborhood — tests the boundaries of her aesthetic, trading some of that restraint for buttery yellows, reddish-brown wood, polka dots, and a sunnier take on Art Deco in general. The interior combines elements of a vintage hotel lobby with a hint of inspiration from Japanese ryokans; wood trim divides the walls into geometric panels, punctuated by circular mirrors, while overhead, custom lantern-like pendants pair metal frames with silk shades. In addition to those lights, Xiong designed much of the furniture herself, including the upholstere

items.title: Our new, go-to ceramics talent + the best interiors book we’ve read in years
items.summary: Plus: An iconic 1960s lamp gets a long-overdue reissue.
items.text: 10.22.26 The Weekly Our new, go-to ceramics talent + the best interiors book we’ve read in years by Jill Singer Welcome to the new Sight Unseen, a weekly newsletter that delivers the best of the design world — news, trends, shopping advice, interviews, travel recs, and more — straight to your inbox. If you’re not subscribed, follow this link to sign up . Want to partner with us, advertise, or submit your work ( guidelines here )? Email us at hello@sightunseen.com . Su Wu’s Mesoamerican Modern Made Us Rethink the Meaning of Home Casa Amalia, designed by architect Agustín Hernández for his sister, is one of the 16 homes in Mesoamerican Modern by Su Wu. Photos: Luis Garvan Admittedly I’ve only been to Mexico a few times — an Acapulco wedding, a trip to Tulum at the height of its reign, a whirlwind jaunt photographing homes for How to Live With Objects — but I don’t think I’ve ever learned as much about a place from reading an interiors book as I did with Mesoamerican Modern by Su Wu, the California-born curator and artist who moved to Mexico more than a decade ago and began inhaling the country’s customs and culture. Wu has always been a wonderful thinker; it’s what led us to her work all those years ago . Here she’s thought deeply about her adopted home and how its nuances have often been flattened or erased in our post-colonial world, but she’s also exposed how slippery a beast the very concept of home can be. The book is separated into unexpected rubrics — there’s a whole section devoted to “Unsquared Rooms” — but at its heart is a willingness, almost an imperative, to embrace different ways of living. In one section, there’s a circular house sunk into the ground, whose windows look out onto an interior courtyard; in another, there’s a house that remains forever unfinished, as its owner chips away at stone, forming sculptural reliefs. The book encourages painting everything pink, or allowing a tree to grow through the wall, or emptying a house of nearly all its furniture, leaving a bed that can be moved from room to room, depending on the season. One of our favorite projects in the book (featured in the photos above) is Casa Amalia, which the architect Agustín Hernández — widely regarded as the progenitor of contemporary Mesoamerican architecture — built in 1973 for his sister. The house takes its form from the aquiline profile of an indigenous person; “the cranial area… holds the radiating bones of the house, leading up spiral stairs to an eye-shaped window peering out across the valley.” It’s an old pre-Hispanic idea, that a space ought to look towards the cosmos, mixed here with elements of modernism, like Hernández’s use of reinforced concrete. In other words, it’s a perfect encapsulation of the idea of the book itself. An Iconic 1960s Lamp, Notoriously Difficult to Produce, Gets a New Lease on Life The retooled Lotus lamp by Carlo Nason, reissued by Gubi and available through Design Within Reach. Did you know that the iconic Lotus table lamp, by the late Italian designer Carlo Nason, once had a much more technical name? It started life in 1969 as the nominally challenged LT305, and it was only after early collectors — whom I’ll heretofore refer to as “Lotus-heads” — began poetically referring to it by the flower it resembles that the name took hold. Despite its initial popularity, the Lotus lamp soon went out of production and remained so for nearly 50 years — until now. As of this week, the Lotus is available once again through Design Within Reach as a reissue from the Scandinavian furniture company Gubi, who have retooled some of the light’s peskier parts but retained its ineffable beauty. The futuristic light, which nestles four graduated “petals” of mouth-blown glass inside one another, has always been challenging to make. Fabricated by expert artisans in Murano, each layer undergoes a traditional “pulegoso” process, in which hot glass is rolled in fine granules, initiating a reaction that suspends thousands of microscopic air bubbles inside the glass’s clear layers. Each layer is then carefully mouth-blown to ensure the same thickness, clarity, and bubble distribution; even in their uniformity, however, no two layers are alike, making the light an interesting early example of how to produce something on a mass scale yet still retain the hand of the maker. When illuminated, the glass becomes increasingly transparent, bringing the lamp’s lotus-like form into sharper focus, layer by layer. Garrett Morin’s Fledgling Ceramics Practice is Our Favorite New Source for Smalls A few favorite pieces by Garrett Morin, our new go-to for excellent, under-the-radar ceramics. Photos: Joanna McClure Do you know — like really know — what your friends do for a living? Sometimes you think you do and then they pull out a talent you didn’t even see coming. That’s how it was for me with Garrett Morin , who I first met as curator of the excellent design week exhibition The End is Now but know primarily as one-half of the graphic design duo behind the branding of my Substack, Counter Space . In April, Morin started dropping images of his fledgling ceramics line on Instagram and while my first question to him was How many of these can I reasonably buy?, I soon began to wonder, Is the goal to have a fully sustainable art practice? “I’ve had an art practice for a very long time,” says Morin. “Drawing is the foundation: It’s a gestural, stream-of-consciousness approach to mark-making that hints at figuration but is often simply expressive. From there, I’ll often see an opportunity to explore an idea through another medium. When I started working with clay, I quickly realized how close it felt to drawing, with the added benefit of the material having a will of its own, which I often let take over. There’s a kind of energy transfer that makes the work feel intuitive and deeply gratifying.” For now, Morin has been riffing on a few different forms — vases whose long necks erupt and flop open like a cardboard b

items.title: An Edgy London Interior by Max Radford, Three Experimental Design Exhibitions, and More
items.summary: Plus: Two Parisian apartments with really good art.
items.text: 10.19.26 The Weekly An Edgy London Interior by Max Radford, Three Experimental Design Exhibitions, and More by Monica Khemsurov Welcome to the new Sight Unseen, a weekly newsletter that delivers the best of the design world — news, trends, shopping advice, interviews, travel recs, and more — straight to your inbox. If you’re not subscribed, follow this link to sign up . Want to partner with us, advertise, or submit your work ( guidelines here )? Email us at hello@sightunseen.com . A London Couple Asked for “Edgy and Raw.” Max Radford Delivered. We’re gagging over this London townhouse, from the teal-and-steel bathroom to the vintage paintings in the dining room to how Italian classics meld perfectly with works by up-and-comers. Photos: Michael Sinclair In one of the best interior briefs I’ve heard, the clients of this late-Victorian home in London wanted something “edgy, contemporary, and a little bit raw” — the diametric opposite, basically, of the Pinterest aesthetic. They certainly came to the right person: Max Radford , who not only runs an eponymous gallery for new talents working under pretty much the same directives, but also designs interiors as such, often incorporating pieces from his roster. Likeminded clients are every designer’s dream, but the project has me thinking with pride about how far our little world has come. It’s hard to imagine clients with-it enough to hire a decorator this way 15, or even 10, years ago. Or if they did, to give them both carte blanche and a budget (rather than either/or). Working atop an existing renovation by Atomik Architecture, Radford came through in spectacular fashion, but took care not to abuse his mandate; he added in the requisite 20th-century icons like sofas by Pierre Paulin and Alessandro Becchi, lights by the Castiglionis and Mario Botta, and a bed by Carlo Scarpa before wilding out with more directional new British talents — and that scrumptious teal-walled bathroom. The living room features a zigzag steel chair by Grace Prince, the entry hall a custom radiator cover by Radford himself, the bedroom a cabinet by EJR Barnes, and the bathroom a chair by LS Gomma as well as a mirror by Radford and Eddie Olin. The best thing about projects like this one is how they can help make a case for both next-gen furniture design as well as what a contemporary interior can (and should!) look like. As Radford puts it, “you have all these quite hardcore, radical pieces of design. But when they’re set within a beautiful London family house, they’re softened down a lot and become much more liveable.” Preach. A Former Government Chamber Became a Parliament of Experimental Design in Belgium The long desks of Ghent’s former Government House became exhibition plinths during last week’s Cavea exhibition (lamp by Charlotte Jonckheer). Photos: Alexander Popelier Last week in Ghent, Belgium, BRUT Collective and the curatorial platform DesignUnDisciplined took over the historic council chamber of the city’s former Government House for Cavea , an exhibition that imagines the room as a kind of “non-conformist parliament” for people and objects. The name refers to the tiered seating of ancient amphitheaters, which was historically divided according to social class; here, instead, everyone — and everything — gets an equal seat at the table. (In one indicative piece, by Guillaume Slizewicz, a lamp decides whether to turn itself on by holding a democratic vote among five microcontrollers every ten minutes.) It’s a high-minded premise, but the work was weird enough to keep things fun. Théophile Blandet’s Fluid Dynamics lamps are made from rejected components sourced during a residency at a laboratory-instrument factory and controlled using syringes, as though light itself were a liquid. Matthijs De Block puts genetically modified bacteria into a luxury-style box for a project called Gucci, imagining a future in which genes can be designed, patented, and sold. Marie Caye stuck a sculpture made from a Michelin tire inside a volcano for four months until mineral-rich water covered it in crystals, while Studio CoPain made a vase from pâte morte, the unleavened dough traditionally used for decorations in baking competitions. There were more conventionally desirable objects on view, too, including Laurids Gallée’s cedar bar cart carved with symbols of intoxication, Linde Freya Tangelder’s rough-hewn wood furniture and glass sculptures, and a fuzzy-looking aluminum stool by Nicolas Zanoni that starts as handwoven metal wire before being cast in aluminum. In this unexpected location, it all looked not only provocative, but really nice — who knew parliament tables could function so well as exhibition scenography? Two Paris Apartments Mix French Heritage With Contemporary Design Top and middle left: The Voltaire apartment by Diettert Collet, photos: Clément Gérard. Middle right and bottom: The Cherche-Midi apartment by Claves, photos: Alice Mesguich. Considering how many Paris apartments we’ve published lately, you can’t help but start to see a recurring contemporary Parisian interior language — one in which a new generation of French designers feels comfortable drawing on the city’s decorative traditions without producing rooms that feel like pastiche. Two recent projects take very different approaches to that idea (in somewhat similar material/color palettes). For a Haussmannian apartment that hadn’t been renovated since the 1970s, the young firm Diettert Collet kept the colors restrained: cream walls and upholstery, pale stone, warm woods. The living room is anchored by a blocky custom travertine fireplace and matching vintage coffee table, and backdropped by the project’s standout piece: a vintage sculptural wood screen by Cappellini, sourced from House of Barcia , whose three panels are joined by giant zigzagging stitches. Against all those sandy neutrals, black is used almost architecturally: lining a doorway, enveloping the kitchen cabinetry, and reappearing in objects

items.title: An Iconic Midcentury Hotel Reborn, a Belgrade Hi-Fi Listening Bar, and More
items.summary: Plus, a shopping guide for chic fireplace andirons.
items.text: 08.10.26 The Weekly An Iconic Midcentury Hotel Reborn, a Belgrade Hi-Fi Listening Bar, and More by Monica Khemsurov Welcome to the new Sight Unseen, a weekly newsletter that delivers the best of the design world — news, trends, shopping advice, interviews, travel recs, and more — straight to your inbox. If you’re not subscribed, follow this link to sign up. Want to partner with us, advertise, or submit your work ( guidelines here )? Email us at hello@sightunseen.com . A Listening Bar Where Yugoslav Modernism Meets Japanese Hi-Fi Culture Supaform’s interiors for EJE incorporate his furniture and art, plus original London Underground textiles, vintage speaker systems, and more. Photos: Varvara Toplennikova Had you visited Yugoslavia in the 1970s, you would have seen thousands of modular structures dotting the streets, instantly recognizable by their rounded, space-age exteriors and large central picture windows. Expandable to encompass anything from newspaper stands to copy shops to small cafes, these were the iconic K67 kiosks, envisioned by the Slavic architect and industrial designer Saša J. Mächtig in 1966 and now altogether more rare in the country. It was these stands — along with Yugoslav brutalism and futurism in general, plus the aesthetic and sound design of Japanese listening bars, that inspired the interiors of Esthetic Joys Embassy, or EJE , in Belgrade. Comprising a bar, a restaurant, a DJ booth, a vinyl library with listening stations, and a dance floor that’s attached to a hotel, EJE was designed by Supaform , and features not only principal Maxim Scherbakov’s furniture designs but his artworks as well, as seen in the lower right photo above. Other key details include a pair of vintage JBL 4435 studio monitors, an iconic Japanese train station clock called the Dulton Double Face, and archival Mischa Black upholstery fabric — used on the London Tube in the 1970s — that Scherbakov’s team sourced from the original London mill that made it. The idea, he says, was to transform the space into a utopia that inspired both nostalgia and optimism; “a futuristic, autonomous station of aesthetic pleasures.” One of Athens’s Great Midcentury Landmarks Enters a New Era At top, a suite at the newly renovated Conrad Athens the Ilisian; bottom, its original 1963 facade and a shot from its Yabu Pushelberg–designed Onuki restaurant. Back in 2024 we asked the Greek design studio Objects of Common Interest to compile their 10 favorite modernist buildings from around the country . The Hilton in Athens was not one of them, but it easily could have been; Hiltons these days may not be the first thing you think of when you think “design hotel,” but this one was built in 1963 by prominent Greek architects Prokopis Vassiliadis, Emmanouil Vourekas, and Spyros Staikos, who hired artist Yiannis Moralis to adorn its front facade with an iconic, very midcentury-coded display of Greek hospitality-themed engravings. Add to that its landmark 82-foot pool, and the modernist building was long venerated both as a hotel and a piece of cultural history. Now, having undergone a four-year restoration and renovation, it has reopened to much fanfare as Conrad Athens the Ilisian , its 278 guest rooms and public spaces reimagined by AvroKo — with a restaurant by Yabu Pushelberg . While the new interiors definitely have that luxury-corporate-hotel vibe in some areas, there are lots of nice midcentury touches — both original and inspired by the original. The former are concentrated in the hotel lobby , where bronze snail-shaped fountains from the original pool, by Moralis and Bouba Lyberaki, have been repositioned into a long water feature that runs down the center of the space. At one end is a fully restored 1963 ceramic mural that Moralis created for the Hilton’s rooftop Galaxy Bar. The hotel’s suites feature elements like the Praying Mantis lamp that Francois Rispal designed in 1950, plus a newly created wood relief wall mural, pictured above, that clearly pays homage to the era. The art throughout — curated by Mare Studio — was also selected to highlight Greek and Greek midcentury artists, though guests who have stayed at the hotel since its opening in April report that none of it can really compete with the art on display through its oversize windows: sweeping views of Athens itself. This Highly Personalized Art Deco Apartment Takes Cues from Vermeer and Balkan Textiles Some of our favorite details in the Gentleman apartment by YSG include a painting by Laura Jones from Chalk Horse Gallery and a custom polka-dot ceramic planter by Remy Pajaczkowski-Russell (top), plus the most stunning galley kitchen we’ve seen (bottom right) and a dining room anchored by a vintage floor lamp (bottom left). Photos: Anson Smart Sometimes I feel like all I ever do in these newsletters is write about apartment renovations in Art Deco–era buildings (mostly in Paris), all of which look impossibly glamorous and full of sleek metal surfaces and expensive period pieces sourced from high-end dealers. I love all of the ones I’ve featured here, of course, but it’s interesting to see a project that departs from the mold a little bit. This space, a 950 square-foot apartment in a landmarked 1929 building in Sydney, was unburdened of past wayward renovations by the firm YSG in order to return to its Art Deco clarity, but then warmed up to something much more layered, colorful, and unexpected. Two points from the project description caught my interest in particular; first, that the clients, a couple, have a thing for Vermeer, so the designers painted the walls in one of the Dutch painter’s favorite colors, lead white. They also incorporated his muted yellow and ultramarine blue into the upholstery of a piano chair, and into a custom rug with ochre accents. Second, they chose some of the apartment’s other colors, along with many of its textiles and textures, as a way of paying homage to the Bosnian/Croatian heritage of one of the owners. That includes
credits: Anson Smart Sometimes I feel like all I ever do
Varvara Toplennikova Had you visited Yugoslavia

items.title: In the Hollywood Hills, a mirrored sauna hides among the trees
items.summary: Actor Michael B Jordan once lived here
items.text: Photography: courtesy of Acme A mirrored sauna pavilion reflects the surrounding trees at this Hollywood Hills home, recently redesigned by Los Angeles studio OME DEZIN. Set on more than an acre in Upper Nichols Canyon, the property was originally designed by architect Jeffrey Mills in 1997 and is now on sale for $14 million. Photography: courtesy of Acme Photography: courtesy of Acme Photography: courtesy of Acme Photography: courtesy of Acme Photography: courtesy of Acme Photography: courtesy of Acme Photography: courtesy of Acme Photography: courtesy of Acme 1 of 8 The 4,910sqft house combines exposed timber beams, concrete, glass and stone, with large windows looking onto the gardens. Wood-panelled walls, sculptural furnishings and fireplaces lend warmth to the interiors, while the main living space opens directly onto the swimming pool . There are four bedrooms, including a principal suite with a fireplace, corner terrace and a marble bathroom overlooking the treetops. A screening room and library sit alongside a kitchen fitted with a La Cornue range and professional pizza oven. Outside, mature trees and tropical planting surround the pool, with terraces and garden rooms arranged across the grounds. The mirrored sauna reflects the surrounding foliage, while a stepped waterfall, outdoor kitchen and fire-pit seating provide further places to spend time outdoors. Previously owned by actor Michael B Jordan, the property is listed with Acme x Serhant. items.title: At Danielle Frankel's breathtaking new bridal flagship, vows come with wows
items.summary: Interior designer Augusta Hoffman reimagined the grand interiors of a historic Queen Anne building in Tribeca for the modern bride
items.text: (Image credit: Clement Pascal) Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Instagram Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Designer Danielle Frankel Hirsch has a knack for bringing something old and something new into her bridal creations, be it a minimalist trumpet-hem gown trimmed in Lyon lace or satin-wrapped Birkenstocks embellished with pearls. When it came to finding the perfect space for a new downtown New York bridal salon, the designer had a similar approach: ‘We were looking for a gem,’ she tells Wallpaper*. (Image credit: Clement Pascal) She found it in a soaring gallery inside a 19th-century Queen Anne-style building in Manhattan’s Tribeca neighbourhood, complete with 30-foot ceilings, 20-foot windows and 12,000 sq ft of space to transform into her brand’s elegant world. ‘It felt right immediately,’ Frankel Hirsch says. (Image credit: Clement Pascal) While the grand, loft-like space, once the home of the New York Mercantile Exchange, had majestic period features like cast-iron columns and dramatic, Romanesque windows (eagle-eyed design lovers will recognise the space from a 2024 Roman & Williams lighting installation ), it had no heat, HVAC or modern electrics. There was an even bigger logistical nightmare: there was no staircase connecting the main salon floor to an upper level mezzanine. (Image credit: Clement Pascal) So Frankel Hirsch called on a friend and trusted collaborator, New York-based interior designer Augusta Hoffman . The pair met when Hoffman herself was wedding dress shopping (the US400 designer wore a dramatic Daniel Frankel coat to her wedding in 2021). The two hit it off so well that Hoffman went on to design Frankel Hirsch’s Garment District atelier, and, two years later, a Los Angeles showroom. ‘She originally came to me as a bride, so she understands the experience from both sides,’ says Frankel Hirsch. Hoffman was more than game. ‘You rarely have the opportunity to work in a space with 30-foot-high ceilings and a client who wants to keep original details,’ she says, ‘even when they may be crumbling.’ (Image credit: Clement Pascal) Disrepair aside, the biggest hurdle was how to make the imposing historic space feel intimate, with places to display garments and accessories, as well as private spaces for clients and their families. ‘It was so important to create a warm, inviting and timeless space for her brides,’ Hoffman says. ‘You want them to have the same feeling you have at a friend's dinner party you never want to leave.’ (Image credit: Clement Pascal) For inspiration, Hoffman looked to grand private manors across Europe as well as art and antiques from the era. Her design team stripped back decades of paint from the original cast iron columns, and leaned into their raw drama. Out went the all-white palette and harsh overhead lighting. In came rich walnut paneling, an Art Deco-style staircase, antique furnishings, and opulent gold rugs. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: Clement Pascal) The main level contains lounge spaces furnished in vintage seating reupholstered in soft down; vitrines that display jewellery and objets; custom niches crafted from ceruse oak and lined in Japanese Washi paper to display bridal slippers; and leather-and-steel racks that showcase Danielle Frankel’s ethereal collection of gowns. Once betrothed choose their favoured frocks, they can float up the new staircase with their entourage to private changing rooms. (Image credit: Clement Pascal) Every element was considered and made to feel special, from leaf-shaped cast-bronze hardware that pins back sheer curtains, to the customer’s experience of the rooms. ‘We meticulously worked through the scale of every detail – from doorway thresholds to the dressing room mirrors. They each needed to feel proportionally appropriate to the space and also the clients,’ Hoffman says. (Image credit: Clement Pascal) Frankel Hirsch even brought her bridal design sensibilities to some elements. The stair, for instance, is flanked by monumental églomisé glass panels, a decorative technique in which metal leaf is applied to glass to create a mirrored finish, designed in collaboration with artist Miriam Ellner. ‘I approached it much as I would the placement of lace on a gown,’ Frankel Hirsch says. ‘There is something very satisfying about bringing that same way of looking at detail into an entirely different material and scale.’ (Image credit: Clement Pascal) Hoffman compares the interior design process to Frankel Hirsch’s meticulous approach to dressmaking. ‘This is something that begins with her own designs and is a throughline in all of our interiors,’ she says. ‘Selecting your wedding gown should be a joyful process of discovery that unfolds in just as thoughtful of a setting.’ Danielle Frankel is located at 6 Harrison Street, New York, NY 10013, USA TOPICS Anna Fixsen U.S. Editor Anna Fixsen is a Brooklyn-based editor and journalist with 13 years of experience reporting on architecture, design, and the way we live. Before joining the Wallpaper* team as the US Editor, she was the Deputy Digital Editor of ELLE DECOR, where she oversaw all aspects of the magazine’s digital footprint.

items.title: Goldenbird cocktails are made like your favourite perfume
items.summary: The new ready-to-drink cocktails are elegant, premium, and bring mixology mastery to your home bar
items.text: Goldenbird cocktails (Image credit: Courtesy of Goldenbird) Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Instagram Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter ‘I believe cocktails could be so much more interesting than the overly sweet, one-dimensional drinks you often come across. We appreciate complexity in food and fragrance, so why not cocktails?’ says model Jarrod Scott. ‘I’ve always been fascinated by how a perfume evolves, with different notes revealing themselves over time. I wanted to bring that same approach to cocktails, creating something layered and unexpected, where you discover different flavours with every sip.’ This is where Goldenbird comes in: Scott’s award-winning ready-to-drink bottled cocktail maison – launched in partnership with his co-founder and life partner, Brioney Prier, alongside Comte de Grasse, a distillery in Grasse (maker of 44N Gin) – embraces this layered, sensorial approach. After its official launch in Europe in January 2026, Goldenbird is now available in the UK . Discover Goldenbird Goldenbird The Way You Look at Me | Gin Cocktail - 200ml The mixes are designed for customers to enjoy a quality cocktail from the comfort of their own home or hotel room. For the core range, they wanted two cocktails to be twists on the classics, in this case a Negroni and a martini, and two to be something a little more surprising. Goldenbird’s sun-kissed cocktails include: ‘The Way You Look At Me’, a citrus gin cocktail; ‘Late Night Phone Call’, a Martini mix; and ‘Romance Apocalypse’, a floral vodka cocktail. Goldenbird Room 302 | Negroni Cocktail - 200ml ‘Room 302’ is a sour cherry and fig Negroni, and there is a story behind its name, as Scott explains: ‘Over the past 15 years, I’ve travelled constantly for work, staying in hundreds of hotels around the world. Strangely enough, I kept finding myself in room 302. It happened so often that I started to wonder if there was something more to it than coincidence. Goldenbird Late Night Phone Call | Martini Cocktail - 200ml ‘I’ve always loved science fiction and the idea of things having a hidden meaning, so I started writing a story around Room 302 while developing the cocktail itself. The two sort of evolved together. I like that the name has this personal history, but also leaves a little mystery for everyone else to interpret. Each cocktail has a very detailed backstory behind the inspiration, and the names really reflect that inspiration rather than just naming the ingredients inside.’ Goldenbird Romance Apocalypse | Vodka Cocktail - 200ml To establish the cocktails, Scott trialled hundreds of different recipes, which were then narrowed down to 12 flavours. ‘We had a lot of friends tasting them, which was a pretty fun part of the process’, says Scott. ‘Six [cocktails] kept coming up as the favourites, so I decided to enter them into the Global Spirits Masters competition. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. (Image credit: Courtesy of Goldenbird) A few months later, we got a call asking who we were because we’d won five gold medals and a silver. We barely had a website at that point, so I think they were quite surprised that this new brand had come out of nowhere and done so well.’ (Image credit: Courtesy of Goldenbird) Ready-to-drink cocktails are notorious for tasting below par and are often packaged in cans/garish bottles. Goldenbird has stepped away from this. ‘You could go to one of the world's best bars and have an incredible cocktail, so why couldn't you have that same level of quality at home? We also felt the packaging had become quite predictable. Every other industry seemed to be pushing boundaries with design, but five years ago, the ready-to-drink category was still dominated by the same cans and bottles,’ explains Scott. (Image credit: Courtesy of Goldenbird) ‘I wanted Goldenbird to feel like something you'd be proud to have sitting on your bar at home, almost like an object you'd want to keep. I designed the bottle shape taking inspiration from perfume flacons and emerald-cut diamonds, then we chose a black mineral finish for the cap to give it a slightly sportier, more contemporary edge. It was important that the design felt as considered as the cocktail inside.’ Goldenbird is classy, inside and out, and is quickly redefining the industry one mix at a time. You don’t have to be a master bartender to shake up a quick fix. goldenbirdcocktails.com Tianna Williams Staff Writer Tianna Williams is Wallpaper’s staff writer. When she isn’t writing extensively across varying content pillars, ranging from design and architecture to travel and art, she also helps put together the daily newsletter. She enjoys speaking to emerging artists, designers and architects, writing about gorgeously designed houses and restaurants, and day-dreaming about her next travel destination.

items.title: Discover the ‘Klismos’ chair and dive into a Greek-evocative design odyssey
items.summary: We put contemporary reinterpretations of ancient classical designs on a pedestal for a Wallpaper* interiors shoot, an odyssey of Greek-evocative glory led by TH Robsjohn-Gibbings' ‘Klismos’ chair
items.text: ‘Model no.11’ Klismos chaise longue, by TH Robsjohn-Gibbings, for Saridis of Athens. Untitled (1961/2026), by Archivio Corrado Cagli and Marmonil, from Brun Fine Art. Testa di putto (18th century), from Brun Fine Art (Image credit: Photography Alecio Ferrari. Creative Direction Nick Vinson) Share {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent hover:[&_svg]:filter-none w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Instagram Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter TH Robsjohn-Gibbings (1903-1976) was a British-born, American-based designer who later in life moved to Athens . He is best known for creating the ‘Klismos’ collection in 1961, inspired by drawings of stools found on a lekythos vessel (from the middle of the 5th Century BC) and a red-figured Kylix (circa: 465-460 BC), discovered in Spina. Through his furniture work, he ‘distilled ancient Greek principles into modern forms’ in Greek walnut and bull-leather thong. Sixty or so years on, Saridis of Athens still produces his original designs. ‘Model no.3’ Klismos chair, by TH Robsjohn-Gibbings, for Saridis of Athens. Dionysus (2024), by Sergio Roger. ‘Athene’ plinth in white suede, by Giobagnara. Panels covered in ‘Charles’ fabric in Tabacco, by Rubelli (Image credit: Photography Alecio Ferrari. Creative Direction Nick Vinson) In the 1990s, Michael Gabellini conceived the Jil Sander stores and showrooms on Avenue Montaigne in Paris , evoking an 1890 French Beaux-Arts home, and the designer’s own headquarters and showroom in Hamburg as a mid-19th-century villa on the shores of Lake Alster. Both interiors were skilfully reduced down to the minimum, and both featured the ‘Klismos’ stools and benches in walnut. This was the most considered and perfect bridge between classicism and modernity, and the starting point for this Greek-themed photoshoot, featured in the December 2026 issue of Wallpaper* . ‘Coppe della Filosofia Mistica’ (maquette) (2008-2009), by Michele De Lucchi and Philippe Nigro, for Sèvres. ‘Athene’ plinth in white suede, by Giobagnara. ‘Cleide’ chair in brushed light oak and bull leather (1993/2023), by Antonio Citterio, for Maxalto. Panels covered in ‘Charles’ fabric in Ortensia and Tabacco, by Rubelli (Image credit: Photography Alecio Ferrari. Creative Direction Nick Vinson) I found some nods to the same idea of classicism in chairs from Antonio Citterio, the 1993 ‘Modus’ collection for Maxalto (later updated in 2023 as ‘Cleide’), as well as in Tobia Scarpa’s recent ‘Ule’ chair from Bottega Ghianda , and in ‘Irene’, from Promemoria . ‘Pippa’ writing desk and stool, by Peter Coles and Rena Dumas; ‘Ulysses’ calfskin notebooks in blue and gold, all by Hermès. Untitled (1961/2026), by Archivio Corrado Cagli and Marmonil, from Brun Fine Art. Panels covered in ‘Charles’ fabric in Tabacco and Lichene, by Rubelli (Image credit: Photography Alecio Ferrari. Creative Direction Nick Vinson) Rena Dumas, the Greek-born Paris-based architect and founder of RDAI , named her 1985/1987 travelling furniture collection for Hermès ‘Pippa’, after her friend and the folding furniture’s co-creator Peter Coles. The collection included a desk , a high console and a folding armchair . According to the Cooper Hewitt Museum , Dumas believed the essence of Greek architecture was functionality, which is reflected in the simple nature of her interiors and furniture. ‘Ule’ chairs in mahogany, by Tobia Scarpa, for Bottega Ghianda. Sensitive Centaur (2025), by Francis Upritchard (Kate MacGarry). ‘Assoluto’ plinth in white suede, by Francesco Balzano, for Giobagnara. Panels covered in ‘Charles’ fabric in Tabacco and Lichene, by Rubelli (Image credit: Photography Alecio Ferrari. Creative Direction Nick Vinson) Every trip I make to Athens includes a visit to one of its many fine museums, so the art selected needed to be evocative of a classical source. Sergio Roger’s plant-dyed antique linen head is aptly called Dionysus ; it sits on a white suede ‘Athene’ plinth, made by Giobagnara; Francis Upritchard’s balata rubber work is titled Sensitive Centaur ; and, Jaime Hayon, speaking of his symbolic ‘ Etruscado ’ vessel, says, ‘its form evokes ancient histories and civilizations, carrying a sense of time, memory, and permanence’. Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. Shelley Jaisalmer Head (2026), by Emily Young. Panel covered in ‘Charles’ fabric in Ortensia, by Rubelli (Image credit: Photography Alecio Ferrari. Creative Direction Nick Vinson) Two pieces from Michele de Lucchi are likewise reduced in form, being based on classical silhouettes, and Emily Young’s majestic Shelley Head in Jaisalmer sandstone, standing tall on its plinth, shares the same strong nose shown in the ‘Profilo’ rug by Fornasetti for CC Tapis . The charming 18th-century Testa di Putto from Brun Fine Art stands atop the ‘Aphaia’ marble column by Claesson Koivisto Rune for Kreoo , taking its name and shape from the Greek Doric temple of Aphaia in Aegina, Greece . ‘Profilo’ Rug, from €3,711, By Archivio Fornasetti, For cc-Tapis. ‘Assoluto’ Plinth In White Suede, price on Request, by Francesco Balzano, for Giobagnara. ‘Basequadra’ Vase (1997), €628, by Michele De Lucchi, Mario Rossi Scola and Alberto Nason, from Produzione Privata. ‘Irene’ Chair, price on request, by Romeo Sozzi, for Promemoria.
