items.title: 11 Best Aspen Hotels and Homes for Your Next Winter Getaway (2026)
items.summary: Five-star lodges and backcountry cabins to après-ski in style
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story When it comes to mountain towns, there’s good, there’s great, and then there’s Aspen—so needless to say, Aspen’s hotels are the height of luxury. Among one of the world’s finest ski towns (with a whopping four mountains on one lift ticket), this winter wonderland is rife with dazzling accommodations. The best hotels in Aspen offer everything: luxury spa experiences; fine dining; ski-in, ski-out access; and all the après-ski cocktails you can get your hands on. If resort life isn’t quite your speed, fear not—there are plenty of picture-perfect rentals you can snag on Airbnb or Vrbo . Expect a robust selection of spacious condominiums, luxury mountain chalets, and backcountry cabins, most of which are within walking distance from one of Snowmass or Aspen Mountain’s peak-reaching gondolas and ski resorts . Don’t love the snow? Good thing Aspen is a top-tier year-round destination. Ideal for climbers, equestrians, cyclists, and other adventure-seekers, the Rocky Mountains provide a backdrop for just about any summertime alpine experience you can dream up. The town’s famed Food & Wine Classic in June is also a can’t miss. Each luxury hotel and off-the-beaten-path rental we found offers access to some of the best adventures in the West, whether you visit in January, July, or anytime in between. Consider this your cue to scroll below and book your stay while date availability lasts. Browse by Category AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Hotels Private Homes Best Hotels in Aspen Courtesy of Marriot Bonvoy The St. Regis Aspen Resort Perks: Daily champagne sabering, full-service spa, heated outdoor pool, multiple on-site restaurants, pet-friendly, valet parking For the ultimate choice in old-school luxury, check in to the St. Regis. The grand, chalet-style property sits at the foot of Aspen Mountain—just a five-minute walk from the Silver Queen Gondola—and pairs classic Rocky Mountain charm with five-star hospitality. Inside, rooms are outfitted with buttery leather headboards, fine linens, marble bathrooms, and mountain views framed by mahogany trim, while the hotel’s on-call butler service can handle tasks like unpacking luggage and drawing a post-ski bath. The RAKxa Wellness Spa remains one of the best in town, offering oxygen facials, a heated outdoor pool (perfect for a post-slopes soak), and many more wellness-minded amenities. Still, this grande dame doesn’t take itself too seriously. Since 2023, it’s been home to The Snow Lodge, a winter spinoff of Montauk’s famed Surf Lodge. The après scene here has become the hottest ticket in Aspen—Diplo, Rampa, and Bob Moses have all spun sets in the open-air courtyard—while the group’s new supper club and nightlife concept brings coastal-cool energy to the Rockies with candlelit dinners, Champagne towers, and late-night dancing under the stars. It’s a rare blend of heritage and hedonism—the kind of place where you can trade ski boots for stilettos without missing a beat. From $649 per night. CHECK AVAILABILITY Photo: Noe DeWitt Hotel Jerome Perks: Fitness center, multiple restaurants and bars, in-town transport, heated pool and hot tubs, pet-friendly If you know the Auberge Resorts name, you know to expect the best of the best when it comes to amenities and design. Set in a stately redbrick building on East Main Street, the Hotel Jerome has been an Aspen icon since 1889—long before the town became synonymous with jet-set ski culture. The interiors preserve the Western charm (think rich leather furnishing, vintage photographs, and taxidermy) that is the Jerome’s birthright while providing luxury touches and see-and-be-seen nightlife options like the Michelin-recommended on-site restaurant, Prospect, or the live music at the sultry, subterranean Bad Harriet cocktail bar. Also within their walls is the storied J-Bar, which is said to have been a favorite of regular Hunter S. Thompson. Between soirees, guests can take advantage of the hotel’s complimentary shuttle to Ajax, Buttermilk, Snowmass, and Highlands, or sign up for exclusive Auberge-curated outdoor excursions like backcountry snowmobiling, starlit snowshoe treks, or romantic horse-drawn sleigh rides through the valley. From $694 per night. CHECK AVAILABILITY Courtesy of The Little Nell The Little Nell Perks: Ski-in/ski-out, heated outdoor pool, spa and fitness center, airport transfers, concierge desk, complimentary mini bar snacks and soft drinks The only AAA Five Diamond–rated hotel in Aspen, the Little Nell blends the best of the West with the cosmopolitan luxuries you’d expect from a five-star hotel. Every detail is dialed in. Guests can unwind at the heated outdoor pool and hot tub, book a treatment at the Little Nell Spa, or rely on the property’s Les Clefs d’Or–certified concierge team, who have a reputation for making the impossible happen (heli-skiing trip to Telluride, anyone?). Food and wine take center stage here, too—the hotel’s Chefs & Somms dinners pair Michelin-caliber cuisine with rare vintages from a 20,000-bottle cellar, one of the most impressive in the Rockies. But it’s on the mountain where The Little Nell truly shines. The Ski Concierge team can arrange first tracks before the lifts open, snowcat powder tours, or private gear fittings in your room, ensuring you’re perfectly prepped with your helmet and bindings. From $800 per night. CHECK AVAILABILITY Courtesy of Mollie Aspen Mollie Aspen Perks: Rooftop hot tub, lobby bar and restaurant, pet-friendly, EV charging For a quieter boutique experience, you’ll want to stay at Mollie Aspen. Opened in late 2023, the hotel blends Japanese and Scandinavian design, creating an atmosphere that feels immediately restorative. items.title: In the Berkshires, an Intensely Yellow Kitchen Is Anything but Mellow in This Lakeside Cottage
items.summary: With free license from open-minded clients, Jess Cooney Interiors brought their unchecked and layered vision to a cozy lakeside retreat
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story “I personally would not want this yellow in my kitchen,” says Jess Cooney. It’s a cheeky comment about the beaming hue she herself chose for clients in the Berkshires —a color that defines their entire lakeside home, one she calls the diva of the whole project, requiring (no, demanding ) decisions in every square foot to balance out its intensity. Cooney’s clients didn’t blink at the bold idea. Unusually carefree for a couple with high-powered jobs, they gave the AD PRO Directory designer free license to create. The bungalow was purchased as a weekend retreat from life in New York, but even before paint swatches were discussed, the kitchen was a sticking point. “The kitchen was crazy—it was this tiny little makeshift kitchen,” says Cooney. Cooney’s clients weren’t initially convinced by reclaimed brick flooring in the entryway, but Cooney’s team proved convincing—they believed the space needed a worn palette to counterbalance the intensely yellow kitchen. Much to their clients’ delight, it worked beautifully. A Croft House Morro Credenza with leather-front doors anchors the space, topped with a vintage lamp from Millerton Antiques Center and set beneath an unknown artwork from Brimfield Flea Market. Cooney opted to stain wood-paneled walls in custom blue and brown stains from Rubio Monocoat, allowing rustic grains to shine through. Atop a Jaipur Hazan rug, an upholstered George Smith Emma Ottoman anchors the room and is accompanied by a set of armchairs and a velvet mordoré sofa from Lawson-Fenning. A 20th-century oil painting by Paul Berg hangs above the reworked fireplace, while in the corner, above a Charles Dudouyt side table, hangs a vintage painting sourced from The Little Store in Massachusetts. “We just decided to kind of lean into it and go almost in a maximalist way,” says Cooney of the dining room’s focal point, a painting by K.G. Narendra Babu that inspired the home’s many colors. For the inside of a Four Hands Camila Sideboard, they commissioned artisan Joel Haynes to hand-paint a leafy pattern. A Hubbardton Forge Disq fixture hangs above a custom Bossi dining table surrounded with Tribute Modern Dining Chairs from Craft Associates. The husband, an English lawyer, craved a small cabin in the woods , while the wife, an Italian who loves cooking, wanted a home large enough to host intimate gatherings. “This house was a happy compromise,” says the husband. But while the home spans three levels and around 4,500 square feet, the main floor measured just about 1,000. The kitchen, in a cramped corner, didn’t cut it Cooney’s team reconfigured a few walls. They collapsed oversized closets in the entryway, shrinking the space to a slimmer mudroom while letting the entire layout exhale, expanding the footprint of the semi-open cooking area. The room is now the proper heart of the home, and its bright yellow cabinets aren’t shy about it. Cabinets with glass windows were fabricated by Westek Architectural Woodworking and feature an array of white porcelain that punctuates and calms the intensely painted millwork; the pieces were all sourced from shops in the Berkshires, including Millerton Antiques, All that Jazz, and Montage Antiques. “It’s the diva of the project,” says Cooney of the yellow Benjamin Moore paint used throughout the kitchen, a choice that influenced nearly all palettes throughout the home. Ceilings, walls, and upper cabinets were painted in Farrow & Ball’s New White. The kitchen island is topped with a wooden counter and is paired with Amber Interiors Cade Counter Stools in walnut. A set of Matthew Fairbank Allegro Pendants hang above the island. The saturated hue, Benjamin Moore’s Glen Ridge Gold, wasn’t a choice made on a whim. Like many colors peppering the home, it was inspired by a painting by Chennai-based artist K.G. Narendra Babu that now hangs in the couple’s dining room. The artwork was given to the couple by a family member who worked in India, and it features an array of folk and musical motifs. “The whole point of the project is that it’s bright and energetic and deeply relaxing at the same time,” says Cooney. “That was the trust that they put in us—to believe that both could happen.” The architecture itself lacked a definitive style. Light traces of Arts & Crafts style gave Cooney a point of view to reinvent existing character. A fireplace in the living room is now reimagined with glazed brick Clé tiles, their dappled surface cladding the surround with clean lines and a crafted look; a custom stain allowed wood-paneled walls to bear rustic grains but in modern blue-green tones. To expand the kitchen’s footprint, Cooney reclaimed space from unnecessarily large closets in the entryway. Her team moved the wall to install smaller, but equally useful, cabinets that turn the space into a mudroom. The custom millwork, crafted by Westek Architectural Woodworking and painted in Farrow & Ball’s Blue Gray, complements a vintage rug and a built-in bench. A custom walnut vanity injects warmth as an alternative to a colder stone. Cooney’s team used a boat sealer to coat and protect the walnut, giving the material a high-gloss finish. A fabric shade made with Eric Kuster’s Micha 002 textile occupies the space that might traditionally feature a mirror. “You can kind of break a rule and have it be playful and fun, especially in a powder bath,” says Cooney, noting that a mirror hangs on the side wall instead. The wallcovering is Pierre Frey’s Uberon print. Cooney describes an almost cottagey feel in the primary, thanks to a walnut Flora Bed by Jacob May, which was locally made and turned by hand, layered with cozy and textural textiles like Parachute Home’s Hand Stitched Cotton Quilt . Gentle patterns add to the mix through a Scandinavian kilim with geometric design from Rug & Kilim, and light drapes made with a Best Buds textile by Kerry Joyce. Making the most of existing features, light touches to the bathroom reimagine
designers: Paul Berg hangs above the reworked fireplace

items.title: 45 AD-Approved International Interior Photographers to Know for Your Next Project Abroad
items.summary: London flats, Mediterranean villas, hotels in Morocco, ranches in New Zealand—the pros below have captured habitats around the globe in all their glory
items.text: Comment Loader Save Story Save this story Comment Loader Save Story Save this story They jet around the globe, camera in hand, capturing expansive views from clifftop villas and intimate reading nooks in private homes. The international interior photographers on these pages don’t just record living spaces; they tell stories and create moods, turning their eyes to details such as the light streaming through a red curtain or a marble statue waiting to welcome guests into a villa’s entryway. Each image is infused with a sense of place and the spirit of the people who pass through it. Read on to discover top talents working in Europe, Asia, Oceania, North Africa, South America, and Canada. Interior by Marie-Anne Derville. Matthew Avignone Matthew Avignone , Paris Born in South Korea, raised in Chicago, and currently living and working in Paris, Matthew Avignone brings a truly international perspective to his photography. His images often center around the collected objects that make a space personal and give it life. A bathroom in Cap Martin along the French Riviera, designed by Studio Humbert & Poyet. Photo: Ludovic Balay Ludovic Balay , Paris With Harry Nuriev , Festen , and Bernard Dubois among his collaborators, Ludovic Balay is no stranger to interiors with a point of view. The Paris photographer’s roster also includes Halleroed, adding another distinctive design voice to the picture. The drawing room of a Notting Hill home designed by Olivia Williams . Photo: Henry Bourne Henry Bourne , United Kingdom Henry Bourne’s photographs open a window into creative people’s private worlds. The UK photographer’s interiors and portrait work includes subjects such as John Pawson, Faye Toogood, Luca Guadagnino, and Rose Uniacke . A London townhouse designed by AD100 designer Leonora Hamill Photo: Helen Cathcart Helen Cathcart , London Helen Cathcart brings a painterly, atmospheric quality to her work, which has resonated with some of the world’s hottest brands, designers, and publications. Cathcart’s photos of interiors, in particular, proffer serenity and calm through their tonality. A home gym by Lecoadic Scot. Photo: François Coquerel François Coquerel , Paris The Row, Lemaire, and a host of AD interiors: François Coquerel’s portfolio is in very good company. The Paris photographer moves between fashion and design, with Massimo Adario and Oitoemponto among his architectural collaborators. Designer Luca Cipelletti delivers architectural precision and material opulence to an art collector’s Porta Nuova apartment . Photo: DePasquale+Maffini DePasquale+Maffini , Paris and Milan Partners in life and work, Michael Depasquale and Martina Maffini count industry names like Dimore Studio , Nilufar Gallery , and JW Anderson among their clients. The duo splits their time between Paris and Milan and injects dynamism into each shoot that becomes evident in the final, glossy-ready results. A villa in New Zealand by Patterson Associates. Photo: Simon Devitt Photographer Simon Devitt , Wellington, New Zealand Simon Devitt doesn’t stop at photographing architecture: fine art photo books, exhibitions, and workshops also fill his calendar. Based in Wellington, he has worked with Fearon Hay, Shigeru Ban , and Olson Kundig , documenting buildings across New Zealand and beyond. Joseph Dirand’s Paris apartment. Also based in Paris, Adrien contributed photography to the book Joseph Dirand Interior . A creative family, to say the least. Inside the Paris headquarters of ACNE studios Photo: Felix Dol Maillot Felix Dol Maillot , Paris Having started his career in fashion, Dol Maillot is as beloved for his street style shots and travel photography as he is for his interiors. Born in the South of France, the globetrotting artist now lives in Paris. A duplex in Thames City. Photo: Veerle Evens Veerle Evens , London A Kelly Behun apartment at London’s Whiteley hotel is just one reason to linger over Veerle Evens’s portfolio. The London photographer moves between interiors, food, and travel, with HBA Residential, Owl Design, and Christian Bense among her collaborators. A color-drenched home in the Canary Islands. Photo: Miguel Flores-Vianna Miguel Flores-Vianna , London and New York Some interiors tell you as much about their owners as a portrait might. Miguel Flores-Vianna seeks out those personal worlds, bringing his curiosity not just to interiors but also to his books, including Haute Bohemians and Haute Bohemians Greece. Armchair travelers, settle in. Get AD -Approved Join the AD PRO Directory, AD’s professional network that gives you access to exclusive events and exposure to the future clients. Photo: Jérôme Galland Jérôme Galland , Paris Among international interior photographers, Jérôme Galland ups the ante with his photos through a combination of striking contrasts, dramatic angles, and an appreciation of scale. French châteaus, Italian palazzos, and Greek villas all appear at their most grand through his lens. A villa in Morocco. Photo: Kasia Gatkowska Photography Kasia Gatkowska , Amsterdam Venetian interiors and Moroccan retreats make tempting subjects: Kasia Gatkowska’s portfolio travels well. The Amsterdam-based photographer has worked with Vincenzo De Cotiis , Vincent Van Duysen , Axel Vervoordt , and Massimo Adario, among others. The home of the ABC Concept founders in Karuizawa, Japan. A dining room in Greenwich, Connecticut, designed by Alison Hammatt Home. items.title: 10 Best Coffee Table Books to Buy in 2026, According to AD

items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Whether placed on a shelf or the coffee table in your living room, coffee table books can easily serve as pieces of decor. “I feel that books complete any room,” says global editorial director Amy Astley . “They are a record of your life and passions—I am profoundly connected to all of my printed matter!” We’ve picked the best coffee table books from this year’s batch, and we’re thrilled to hole up with them until warmer days make their appearance. Here are our favorites from 2026’s bountiful assortment of debuts—many of them featuring AD -approved talents—all packed with invaluable design insights and gorgeous interiors past and present. Browse by Category The Best Coffee Table Books of 2026 The AD Coffee Table Book Gift Guide The Best Coffee Table Books of 2026 Save to wishlist Save to wishlist “AD at Home: Architectural Digest” Edited by Amy Astley $100 Shop $100 $62 (38% off) Amazon There are over 400 pages of inspiration-packed interiors to peruse in Amy Astley ’s second coffee table book, AD at Home . Throughout the book you’ll find dreamy pictures and thoughtful essays pulled straight from our pages, including anecdotes from former cover stars like Marc Jacobs, Dakota Johnson, Gwyneth Paltrow, and more. “Even in a world of oversharing on social media, there is still such a frisson of entree in glimpsing the private world of a public figure, and AD will eternally share the fantasy,” Astley says in her editor’s letter. With the holidays approaching, we think AD at Home also makes a perfect gift for the collector, the design enthusiast, and anyone who’s just a little bit nosy about what’s going on behind a celebrity’s closed doors. Save to wishlist Save to wishlist La Bibliothèque de l’Amateur Catalogue €20 Editions Delamateur Created by AD France’s former editor-in-chief, Marie Kalt, La Bibliothèque de l’Amateur is a collection of compact, accessible monographs devoted to the great names of 20th-century design. The contents explore the work of acclaimed designers, including Alvar Aalto, Charlotte Perriand, Ettore Sottsass, while including emerging talents in the conversation as well. Each $30 volume pairs a brief introduction with about 60 images and detailed captions, offering an engaging visual primer on a designer’s life and work. The volume takes you inside the homes of 20 leading designers across the country—including Andre Mellone, Kelly Wearstler, and Robin Standefer and Stephen Alesch of Roman and Williams—each reflecting its creator’s distinctive taste and personal passions. “As my dear friend Markham Roberts—one of the designers featured in the book—says, ‘If stuff makes you happy, you want it around,’ and this book makes me very happy,” says global interiors and garden director Alison Levasseur . Like its namesake, Upton’s book is an expert guide, specifically to a world of extraordinary interiors and visual pleasures. “Some of my favorite stories ever to appear in the pages of AD were photographed by Upton,” says Levasseur. “Many are gathered here, including those featuring Adwoa Aboah, Dakota Johnson, and Sienna Miller.” Save to wishlist Save to wishlist "On Artistry: Architecture and Interiors" by Joan Craig $65 Shop $65 Rizzoli Bookstore This beautiful debut monograph not only showcases Chicago architect Joan Craig's elegant classical architecture, but it also spotlights the artistry behind it. “I love that Craig shares the spotlight with the often-unsung craftspeople who bring her interiors to life, including Brittany’s masters of straw marquetry and Bologna’s terrazzo artisans,” says senior digital editor Catherine Hong . “It's a tribute to design excellence and also the art of collaboration." items.title: ELLE Decor Checks In: The Cooper, Charleston
items.summary: The South Carolina city’s first waterfront hotel features nautical-inspired interiors by Meyer Davis and Champalimaud Design.
items.text: Founded as a seaport more than 350 years ago, Charleston evolved into one of the most important trade hubs in colonial America. As the South Carolina city’s wealth grew, handsome estates began filling up its coastline. But throughout Charleston’s rich, colorful, and complicated history, the city never had a high-end hotel that took full advantage of its waterfront setting—until this year, with the debut of The Cooper. Located on the site of the former State Ports Authority headquarters (which was demolished in 2019), the 191-key property sits on Charleston’s historic peninsula and overlooks the Cooper River. Interiors by Champalimaud Design pay homage to the city’s maritime heritage, referencing the “Lowcountry” culture that took root in the surrounding region. Matthew Kappas The Cooper hotel in Charleston, South Carolina. “We wanted The Cooper to feel like a natural extension of the city, balancing the ease of a waterfront home with the refinement of a luxury hotel,” says Jun Chun, principal at Champalimaud Design. “The overall inspiration was Charleston itself, particularly its coastal heritage, architectural history, and gracious, unhurried way of life.” The six-story property, which is operated by Beemok Hospitality Collection, has a relaxed feel infused with a subtle Southern flavor. The experience starts before guests even step inside thanks to an entryway lined with an allée of crepe myrtle trees—a Charleston staple with tumbles of showy, hot-pink blooms. Matthew Kappas Conceived by Champalimaud Design, the lobby features a marble flooring with a basketweave pattern that references the local art of braiding sweetgrass. Inside, the lobby sports creamy marble flooring with a basketweave pattern that nods to the local art of braiding sweetgrass. Meanwhile, a mural inspired by changing tides lines the spiral staircase, leading to the public areas upstairs. Matthew Kappas The lobby seating area. The hotel’s Mediterranean-style signature restaurant, The Crossing, helmed by chef Nick Dugan, was designed by multidisciplinary studio Meyer Davis . (There are three additional, smaller dining venues on site.) For the restaurant’s meandering floor plan, the design team created a series of distinct indoor and outdoor spaces, hewing to a marshland palette of soothing neutrals and calming blues as well as strategic doses of lacquer, teak, and honey onyx. Matthew Kappas The Crossing, the Mediterranean-style restaurant at The Cooper. References to the local culture continue in the guest rooms, which feature bespoke headboards, wardrobes, and credenzas adorned with woven details, once again tying back to vernacular craft. “We approached the guest rooms as elegant waterfront homes rather than traditional hotel rooms,” says Chun. “Wide-plank oak floors, painted shiplap walls, woven textures, and residential-style Roman shades establish a sense of warmth and familiarity.” Matthew Kappas The Cooper features 191 guest rooms. Among the amenities are a 7,000-square-foot spa as well as a heated saltwater infinity-edge pool on the fourth-floor terrace. The pool deck, which has its own bar, overlooks not just the harbor but even more perks: a new waterfront park by Rees Roberts + Partners plus a private marina, where guests can charter one of the property’s cruising vessels, such as a Hinckley motor yacht. Matthew Kappas Guests can charter the property’s Hinkley for private harbor cruises. For the design team, bringing The Cooper to life was a careful balance of respecting tradition while also looking forward. “Charleston has an extraordinary architectural heritage and a strong tradition of craftsmanship, and we wanted to acknowledge those qualities without simply reproducing the past,” explains Chun. “Ultimately, we wanted The Cooper to feel as though it belongs in Charleston today and will continue to feel relevant for years to come.” Jovani Demetrie/Courtesy of the Cooper The pool deck overlooks the harbor. Geoffrey Montes Geoffrey Montes is an associate editor at ELLE Decor with a serious love for all things real estate and design. Before that, he worked at Architectural Digest , Galerie, and Preservation magazines, covering everything from jaw-dropping listings to world-famous architects and design events like Salone del Mobile and Homo Faber. items.title: This St. Bart’s House Was Designed to Look Nothing Like Its Neighbors
items.summary: Built for maximum family time, a converted boutique hotel puts the emphasis on entertaining, hanging out, and blending into the surroundings.
items.text: Few clients ask their designer to make the bedrooms in their vacation home smaller and simpler, but that was just the edit the homeowners made to plans for their house in St. Bart’s, says designer David Ries. “They didn’t want these humongous bedrooms with huge floating beds and massive bathrooms.” Instead, the couple wanted to be able to host as many people as possible, a request that didn’t surprise Ries, who’d already worked with the family on homes in Manhattan, Long Island, and Telluride. “It’s what this client has always asked for. They can’t have enough bedrooms.” Situated on a steep hillside above one of St. Bart’s famously pristine white sand beaches, the house had initially been a boutique hotel. The plan was to turn it into a retreat for themselves and their adult children and grandchildren. The family are longtime visitors to the island—“the daughter told me it was her ‘happy place,’” says Ries, lead designer of the New York-based interior design firm Ries Hayes —and knew exactly what they wanted. Not the white box look popular with luxury new builds on the island, but instead something reminiscent of the “old St. Bart’s,” says East Hampton-based landscape designer Edwina von Gal , who, like Ries, has collaborated with the clients on other projects. Matt Kisiday The second level houses bedrooms with outdoor areas that unfold to the view of the water. A Caribbean island is a challenging place to work under any circumstances. Everything has to be brought in from far away, including all the plants, which came by barge from Miami. St. Bart’s in particular requires anyone building to work with a local architect and engineer. In their initial proposal, this French team defaulted to that “slick and modernist” look, as von Gal describes it, with the oversized bedrooms and white color scheme that dominates much of the island’s luxury housing stock. The design team pushed back—asking for a lot of bedrooms (eight) and generous living spaces. They also had strong opinions on the building materials. Given the island’s climate, the humid, salt-soaked air can be hard on everything. “If we did white paint, which is prominent throughout St. Bart's, it’s constant maintenance, constant painting,” says Ries. The design team insisted on cladding the buildings in Ipe, the durable tropical hardwood, which wears well. It mystified the local architects and set the complex apart from its neighbors. It also makes the buildings disappear into the greenery of the hillside. Matt Kisiday The living room features Serena & Lily’s Sundial sofa and Arpa armchairs by Bonacina covered in Fabricut’s Capri fabric. But the architects quickly caught on to the new plans, and von Gal is eager to praise their technical accomplishments. Regulations require properties to conserve rainwater, so there are cisterns beneath the buildings, plus technology infrastructure and laundry facilities. “Working on the hill is so complex,” she says. “It's such a tight little package of technology and function. What they did was amazing.” The team decided to reconfigure the property as a series of pavilions that face the view of the ocean and surrounding hills. The main entry is at the top of the steep hill, along with parking. The next level down is for family bedrooms; below that is a primary suite and study; and finally the fourth level is the main living space, including a playroom. “We made sure this playroom was front and center,” says Ries. “My client loves her grandkids.” Matt Kisiday “Our client loves blue,” says Ries. “In any pop of color that we can bring in is welcome as long as the overall feel is blue.” The playroom and study have built-in daybeds that can be used as spare guest rooms in a pinch. But the clients did get their eight bedrooms. “We know how to make compact bedrooms and make them very efficient, make them very livable, which allows us to fit in a lot of space for a lot of guests, and then that puts a lot of emphasis on having main entertaining spaces that are big and gracious,” says Ries. “The idea is that everybody hangs out together.” Everything is united by generous outdoor spaces, which wind between the bedrooms. “Every room has an amazing view,” says Ries. “It feels almost like your own little treehouse in a way.” The bottom living area opens out to a pool and an expansive deck where the family eats most of their meals. Matt Kisiday In the playroom, vintage Aalto stools from 1st Dibs pull up to a custom banquette covered in Sister Parish Mahalo fabric. The house has an elevator, but stairs are the primary way the family moves between levels and finally down to the beach. “We hung on for a really great, gracious, fun set of stairs,” says von Gal. “They really introduce you to how amazing the different levels are and all the wonderful secret places.” Durable fabrics and materials were chosen throughout and Ries made sure everything could be easily moved around and reconfigured. Outside on the main deck, three long dining tables from Sutherland were outfitted with casters so they could be maneuvered into a single long table or several smaller ones; 26 lightweight dining chairs can be pulled from different parts of the deck. If the infamous “Christmas winds” bring a downpour, the tables can even be moved indoors so a dinner party can proceed in inclement weather. Outdoor seating can be arranged as a 15-foot sofa or several love seats. Matt Kisiday An antique bed in one of the bedrooms. “It's so flexible,” says Ries. “We know this from working with a client that their needs for entertaining change every day, or sometimes a couple times a day.” The kitchen is also efficient, designed to produce easy, clean meals. The family would rather spend time in the pool than over a stove. And no part of the living room is oriented around a TV. “They're readers,” says Ries. “There’s always stacks of new books when you go to their homes. items.title: What’s Your Vacation Vibe?
items.summary: Whether brand new or reimagined, these four hotels offer distinctive stays. The only question is, which style to choose?
items.text: To be a discerning traveler is to have, in equal measure, preference and knowledge of the endlessly evolving hotel landscape. But even the greatest of globetrotters need a guide to what’s new every once in a while. Below, find four recently opened (or reopened) hotels, organized by travel preference: Looking for something in the city? We’ve got you. Country? We have that too. A place to hot air balloon? No worries. The toughest part will just be figuring out where to go first. CHILL / CITY Hassler Roma, Rome Jonathan Maloney / What The Fox Studio A suite at the Hassler Roma. Time and Place: Perched atop the Spanish Steps, this 133-year-old mainstay is Old World luxe translated with fresh verve following a lavish update with revamped public spaces by ELLE Decor A-List designer Jacques Garcia. Design Vibes: Delving into the archives for the Palm Court Garden redo, Garcia collaborated with Italian firm Colleoni Roberto & C. on a green-and-white-striped upholstery and with a Roman blacksmith on vintage-style lanterns. Hide Out In… One of the damask-covered suites or at the renovated Michelin-starred Imàgo restaurant. CITY / PLAY The Public, West Hollywood Ian Schraeger Company A private screening area in a room at the Public. Time and Place: Some will recognize this property as the former home of the Standard, sans human fish tank at the check-in desk. Actually, sans any check-in desk. There’s also no room service, but there is a rooftop park with a gym, a neon blue pool, and 360° views. Design Vibes: Legendary hotelier Ian Schrager, with his “luxury for all” philosophy, teamed up with minimalist maestro John Pawson on the architecture. Rooms feature custom-made plush seating, pale woods, and custom lighting systems for shifting moods. Hide Out In… Your own private cineplex. Each room has a projector and 66-inch screen. Or disappear on the dance floor of the Studio, a speakeasy-style nightclub clad in marble and velvet. CHILL / COUNTRY The Seminary, Vermont Place in Mind A reading nook in a guestroom at the Seminary. Time and Place: Occupying a colonial-style former school in Old Bennington dating from 1829, this intimate inn was brought to life by Rafe Churchill, co-founder of the Elle Decor A-List firm Hendricks Churchill, and Casey Sunderland, Churchill’s partner in the new hospitality firm Place in Mind. Design Vibes: The hotel leans into its links to a family of writers and to nearby Bennington College with an inviting library stocked with books by alums. Each of the eight unique guestrooms is cozily layered, mixing rich jewel tones and florals with antiques and art that ranges from the Hudson River School to Keith Haring. Hide Out In… The gardens. Landscape designer Grace Fuller Marroquin lent her wild, cinematic touch to the grounds, which feature an array of native plants as well as a fruit orchard. PLAY / COUNTRY Le Graal, Cortina d’Ampezzo Giulio Ghiardi The Dolomites make for dramatic views at Le Graal. Time and Place: Steps from slopes that hosted ski events for two Olympics (1956 and 2026), the hotel occupies a former palazzo from the 1920s. Design Vibes: Eschewing the traditional Alpine look, designer Achille Salvagni tailored the guestrooms with bespoke references to the local landscape and culture, like plaster bas-reliefs of mountains, ceiling motifs based on traditional clothing embroidery, and hardware in the shape of native wildlife. Hide Out In… A hot air balloon. The hotel arranges private tours in the off season for unparalleled mountain views. Or, more down to earth, the spa includes a cryo chamber and a plunge pool. This story originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of ELLE Decor . items.title: Are Zen Hotels Now Putting Us to Sleep?
items.summary: Rich, layered maximalism is the latest form of escapism—historically inspired decor spiked with creative contemporary flair. Get ready to Instagram every nook.
items.text: Above: One of the cottages at Little Saint in Healdsburg, CA. On the top floor of a Gilded Age McKim, Mead & White mansion in New York, now reincarnated as the Fifth Avenue Hotel, Martin Brudnizki recently put the finishing touches on a two-bedroom suite dubbed the Flâneur Penthouse. With his hallmark exuberance, the Elle Decor A-List designer arrayed the space with distinctive flourishes: a spirited Scalamandré wallcovering trimmed in grosgrain ribbon, bespoke furnishings mixed with French Art Deco pieces, India-inspired inlaid nightstands, Japanese-style lamps, and Murano glass ceiling lights. Each element connects to an imagined narrative that shaped Brudnizki’s vision for the hotel: “this cinematic idea of the home of a flâneur who has traveled the world, has seen and acquired a lot, and put it together here,” the designer says. “It’s a multicultural journey.” Douglas Friedman Designer Martin Brudnizki used a Scalamandré wallcovering in the entry vestibule of the Flâneur Penthouse at the Fifth Avenue Hotel in New York. Brudnizki is among a cadre of prominent designers whose approach contrasts markedly, and quite intentionally, with the school of quiet hotel luxury that has become ubiquitous over the past few decades, defined by natural woods, pale stone, organic fibers, and warm minimalist palettes. It’s a style that has a universal appeal—as practiced by Aman, say—when executed in more mundane, cookie-cutter fashion it can feel just, well, beige . “There’s a homogeneity that passes as mass luxury where you could be anywhere,” says Elle Decor A-List designer Ken Fulk, who is currently reimagining the Beverly Hills Hotel’s public spaces. “I think we all crave spaces that avoid this sameness, to feel deeply connected with a place.” Simon Brown A sitting room by Kit Kemp at New York’s Warren Street Hotel. Hotels in this vein tend to be -owner-operated properties looking to carve out a niche. One could trace a baroque family tree that links mold-breaking 1980s boutique hotels like Ian Schrager and Philippe Starck’s Royalton in New York to Jacques Garcia’s interiors for the Hôtel Costes and L’Hotel in Paris to Ilse Crawford’s Ett Hem in Stockholm to Kelly Wearstler’s Proper Hotel in Austin. “It’s Studio 54 meets your grandmother’s Soho townhouse, a disco granny kind of thing.” —Martin Brudnizki Fulk’s hospitality design, like Brudnizki’s, embraces spaces inspired by history and storytelling, with an emphasis on artistry, material richness, and character. Both men’s work is rooted in tradition, with idiosyncratic twists that feel fresh. And they have plenty of kindred spirits working in a diversity of styles, including such designers as Lorenzo Castillo, Kit Kemp, and Laura Gonzalez. While far from a coherent movement, the sumptuous, high-impact aesthetics practiced by these designers just might be today’s most zeitgeisty current. Oskar Proctor A lounge area at the Broadwick Soho in London by Martin Brudnizki. Take Fulk’s Cottages at Little Saint in Healdsburg, California, each one an elevated boho mashup of influences. “Sixties and ’70s rock and roll, and a sort of Laurel Canyon meets Northern California spirit,” explains the designer. “The cottages feel utterly like nowhere else.” And that, of course, is the point. For his part, Brudnizki doesn’t care much for maximalism as a label. In the case of his glamorously moody interiors for the Broadwick Soho in London—shimmering surfaces, lavishly upholstered furnishings, a riot of pattern—everything began with an idea he describes as “Studio 54 meets your grandmother’s Soho townhouse, a disco granny kind of thing.” Jérôme Galland A bar Laura Gonzalez designed for the Casa Monti hotel in Rome. Then there are the roughly dozen memorable properties created by Kit and Tim Kemp under their Firmdale Hotels group. The most recent is the Warren Street Hotel in New York, with the forthcoming Bedford Place Hotel slated to open next year in London next to the British Museum. “It’s about personality, a sense of arrival, and fun,” says Kit Kemp, who outfits each of her hotels with a more-is-more mix of her ebullient textiles and wallpapers in splashy colors, animated by art and craft. Kimberley Cohen, the creative director behind Maisons Pariente, says her family’s small portfolio of hôtels de charme are about creating a residential-feeling experience that is also “something you have never seen, that you would not do in your own home.” She has worked with Brudnizki on Le Grand Mazarin in Paris, with Charles Zana on two hotels in the South of France, and with Pierre Yovanovitch on a Méribel chalet. Her latest project, opening this winter, is a Courchevel retreat named Saint Roch, with interiors by Friedmann & Versace that channel the chic romanticism of traditional dachas. Next up for Brudnizki, meanwhile, is the Knox Hotel, set to open soon in Dallas, new territory for him. As for what one should expect of the decor, he sums it up as “100 percent unapologetic glamour. It won’t be boring.” This story originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of ELLE Decor . SUBSCRIBE Stephen Wallis ELLE Decor features director Stephen Wallis has spent three decades covering art, design, and culture. He was previously the consulting features editor for Galerie and held top positions at Architectural Digest and Departures. His writing has appeared in numerous publications, including The New York Times, T magazine, WSJ magazine, Esquire, Town & Country, Veranda, and Cultured . He is the author of Fontainebleau, a history of the iconic Miami Beach hotel, and Jim Thompson: Beyond Silk, Beyond Thailand . items.title: The Kitchen Trends Designers Expect to See Everywhere in 2027
items.summary: The National Kitchen & Bath Association’s 2027 forecast has arrived.
items.text: 2 min read Above: the kitchen of an Athens home designed by Nashmita Rajiah. Partial walls, hidden appliances, and pantries with room for prep are among the kitchen features expected to gain ground next year, according to the National Kitchen & Bath Association’s 2027 Kitchen Trends Report . Based on a survey of 830 kitchen-industry professionals—including designers, manufacturers, remodelers, and architects—the report looks at the layouts, materials, lighting, and technology they expect to be popular over the next three years. Here are the main takeaways. Defined Layouts Gieves Anderson In a David Netto-designed apartment , linen curtains with Samuel & Sons trim divide the space between the kitchen and dining area. NKBA reports growing interest in partial walls, movable partitions, and separate kitchen zones—a shift from last year’s forecast, when open layouts were still gaining ground. Dedicated prep spaces and back kitchens are also emerging features, cited by nearly half of designers. Kitchens are still expected to get bigger, with 52 percent of designers anticipating growth. The kitchen’s surrounding rooms are growing, too. NKBA reports that mudrooms and laundry spaces are increasingly being integrated into kitchen plans. The vast majority of designers expect attached mudrooms to be popular over the next three years, with 45 percent anticipating mudrooms getting larger and 43 percent expecting laundry spaces to grow. Hidden Appliances and Enclosed Storage Appliances are increasingly being incorporated into cabinetry rather than left on display. Eighty-five percent of designers agree cabinets are being designed to hide appliances and other functional elements, and roughly two-thirds say open shelving is on its way out in favor of enclosed storage. Pantries are taking on more work, too. Nearly 90 percent agree they are becoming multifunctional extensions of the kitchen, and three-quarters expect dedicated small-appliance stations to be popular. Separate beverage areas continue to gain support, with 90 percent anticipating their popularity, up from 85 percent in the 2026 report. Martin Morrell An English Victorian manor designed by Linda Boronkay features an enclosed pantry with bespoke oak joinery. Wood Cabinets and Neutral Colors Neutrals remain the leading color of choice, followed by greens and blues. For cabinetry, light and medium tones draw equal interest, and white oak is the preferred wood for roughly half of designers. Islands don’t necessarily have to match: a little more than half expect them to feature a different color from the surrounding cabinets. Quartzite and quartz lead countertop preferences, with nearly half of designers favoring honed or matte finishes. Layers of Lighting The lighting forecast includes under-cabinet lights, illuminated cabinet interiors, nighttime path lighting, sconces, and pendants. Eighty-four percent of designers agree kitchens will incorporate multiple layers of light, and 78 percent say lighting is increasingly being used as a design feature rather than just a functional necessity. Under-cabinet lighting leads the forecast at 87 percent, followed by interior-cabinet lighting at 76 percent. Ventilation, Water Filtration, and Leak Protection NKBA identifies ventilation, water filtration, touchless faucets, and sound-absorbing materials among the report’s wellness features. Designers are also discussing ways to make kitchens more resilient: 65 percent cite leak-detection systems and automatic shut-off valves, 62 percent cite backup power, and a little over half point to ventilation and air filtration. Julia Cancilla Social Media & News Editor Julia Cancilla is the social media & news editor at ELLE Decor, where she oversees the brand's socials and covers design, pop culture, and emerging trends. She also authors the monthly ELLE Decoroscope column. Her work has appeared in Inked magazine, House Beautiful, Marie Claire, and more. items.title: 7 Gilded Age Homes Where You Can Live Like the Astors
items.summary: In honor of   The Gilded Age  ’s fourth season, here are the period mansions-turned-hotels you can stay in right now.
items.text: Erin McGinn Above, Castle Hill Inn in Newport, Rhode Island. Gilded Age barons of industry constructed extravagant homes—year-round mansions and summer “cottages”—that were more palaces to their wealth than practical residences. Notable families like the Vanderbilts, Carnegies, and Astors once had houses dotted across New York City and throughout fashionable summer retreats like Newport, Rhode Island. Many of these elaborate structures have since fallen to the ravages of time, with the staggering costs of upkeep rendering their use as private residences all but obsolete. Yet, though some of these private homes have disappeared, our curiosity about them has only increased. Since HBO’s hit show The Gilded Age debuted, interest in visiting the era’s architectural marvels has surged, and in Newport, which is home to one of the country’s largest concentrations of Gilded Age mansions, there’s been a steady rise in visitors touring the town’s mansions specifically because of the show. Visiting the opulent, and often wildly impractical, mansions that inspired the fictional lives of The Gilded Age ’s characters has its charms, but rather than just taking a tour, why not spend the night? Up and down the East Coast, a handful of Gilded Age mansions are preserved not as museums, but as hotels—inviting curious travelers to do more than just visit and admire the history, but to sleep within the jewel boxes of their walls. Courtesy of Castle Hill Inn Castle Hill Inn Newport, Rhode Island Castle Hill Inn is a different kind of Gilded Age mansion, one that turns to timber and antiquities over marble and gilding. The home’s original owner, Alexander Agassiz, was a Harvard professor of natural sciences who made his fortune in copper mining. With his newfound wealth, Agassiz built his summer home—Castle Hill—on a relatively isolated parcel of forty acres, a fifteen minute drive away from the pomp and pageantry of the Vanderbilt’s side of town. He used the home as a summer research lab, hosting students in its many rooms and running the lab in what is today the parlor, while also entertaining a who’s who of literary luminaries, including Edith Wharton and Mark Twain. Today, Castle Hill Inn is one of the most famous places to stay in Newport, not only for its luxurious rooms, afternoon tea, and award-winning restaurant, but also for its sweeping ocean-front lawn and seaside views. Thorton Wilder lived in the turret suite—Agassiz’s former observatory and today the hotel’s most beautiful room—while writing his last book, and Grace Kelly lived in one of the beach cottages during the 1955 filming of “High Society.” Stopping by Castle Hill Inn for a drink and taking a short walk to its still in-use lighthouse remains a summer essential in Newport, but there is nothing quite like staying the night. Courtesy The Chanler at Cliff Walk Hotel Chanler Newport, Rhode Island Hotel Chanler is, unlike Castle Hill, right in the thick of Newport’s Gilded Age neighborhood, and it’s clear from its location that it was built (to use a period expression) to keep up with the Joneses. The opulent mansion was constructed in 1873 as the summer “cottage” of New York Congressman John Winthrop Chanler and his wife Margaret Astor Ward. Chanler hosted an elaborate range of guests at his summer home, including President Theodore Roosevelt and poet Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. The home, which Chanler called “Cliff Lawn,” was the very first mansion to be built on the Cliff Walk, now a public walkway with views of these historic homes. Over the years, the mansion went from being a private residence to a museum and later a girl’s school. It wasn’t until 2003 that it opened as the twenty-room Chanler Hotel. Today, it’s ornately decorated in various period-specific styles such as Regency, Louis XVI, Renaissance, and English Tudor. Last spring, The Chanler opened a more pared down restaurant, Remy’s Loose. Remy’s feels fit for Mr. Chanler and his guests, who we can imagine sprawling out across the chenille, fringed edged slipper chairs, and enjoying the just fussy-enough French menu. Advertisement - Continue Reading Below Courtesy of The Fifth Avenue Hotel The Fifth Avenue Hotel New York, New York The Fifth Avenue Hotel, which opened its doors in late 2023, has a multi-layered history rooted in the Gilded Age. In 1856, legendary hostess and doyenne of New York society, Charlotte Goodridge, commissioned the construction of a lavish private home and carriage house at the coveted corner of Fifth Avenue and 28th Street. Goodridge filled her mansion with treasures from around the globe and entertained lavishly. But following her death, Goodridge’s home met the same fate as much of the neighborhood and was torn down. However, rather than being replaced by a skyscraper like much of the surrounding area, Goodridge’s mansion was reborn in 1907 as a striking five story neo-Renaissance palazzo design by McKim, Mead & White, the architects behind many of the New York’s most famous early 20th century buildings including The Morgan Library and Museum, the Bowery Savings Bank, and the Metropolitan Club. More recently, a decades-long renovation overseen by Flâneur Hospitality, Martin Brudnizki Design Studio, and architect Perkins Eastman transformed the building into a 153-room hotel, with a restored limestone and brick façade, an added-in glass tower, a ballroom fit for a Goodridge party, and a European inspired restaurant, Café Carmellini. The hotel now has a Gilded Age-inspired look, complete with polished marble floors, grand arched windows, rich color palettes, and art and curiosities from around the world. Michael Worthington Hotel Bardo Savannah, Georgia Hotel Bardo may have opened in 2024, but its history extends much further back. It was built in 1888 as a private home for Lewis Kayton, a businessman from Baltimore who settled in Savannah. items.title: Barrièrre Group to open Fouquet’s in Gstaad
items.summary:
Following openings in Paris, New York, Courchevel, St Barth and Mykonos, Fouquet’s continues its global expansion with a new hotel […] 
 The post  Barrièrre Group to open Fouquet’s in Gstaad  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Following openings in Paris, New York, Courchevel, St Barth and Mykonos, Fouquet’s continues its global expansion with a new hotel in Gstaad . Originally built as one of the flagship properties of the Ultima Group in the heart of the Swiss Alps, the hotel is now reborn under the Fouquet’s brand, reimagining the mountain experience through the luxury of space, discretion and time. With 11 suites and six apartments combining 33 rooms, Fouquet’s Gstaad will offer mountain views, fireplaces, contemporary artworks and light-filled balconies. Interiors blend the inviting warmth of a traditional Alpine refuge with contemporary sophistication. For an even more exclusive experience, a nine-bedroom private chalet spanning 1,500m 2 completes the offering. Spanning 800m 2 , the spa will feature a 15-metre indoor swimming pool, sauna, hammam, indoor and outdoor Jacuzzis, snow shower and five treatment rooms, including one double treatment suite. “With Gstaad, Fouquet’s continues its expansion into the world’s most iconic destinations,” says Grégory Rabuel, CEO, Group Barriere. “This sixth property reflects our ambition to establish a truly distinctive brand on the international stage, driven by the excellence of French hospitality and a resolutely contemporary vision of luxury. More than hotels, our ambition is to create places that inspire connection and emotion, where every experience leaves a lasting impression.” Barriere Group europe fouquet's Gstaad switzerland Related Posts 19 May 2026 First Look: Fouquet’s Mykonos 13 December 2024 Miiro announces opening of The Mansard in Gstaad 2 May 2012 The Alpina Gstaad launches December 2012

items.title: Starhotels Collezione unveils refreshed interiors at Rosa Grand Milano
items.summary:
Rosa Grand Milano – Starhotels Collezione has unveils newly refurbished public spaces, combining contemporary interiors with a deeply Italian culture […] 
 The post  Starhotels Collezione unveils refreshed interiors at Rosa Grand Milano  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Starhotels Collezione unveils refreshed interiors at Rosa Grand Milano 18 November 2026 | In Projects | By Eleanor Howard Rosa Grand Milano – Starhotels Collezione has unveils newly refurbished public spaces, combining contemporary interiors with a deeply Italian culture of hospitality. The refurbishment goes beyond aesthetics, expressing an approach to hospitality in which spaces, services and people come together to shape the experience. The lobby and reception now offer a brighter, more contemporary atmosphere. Warm tones and carefully selected materials are complemented by gold, a longstanding feature of Rosa Grand’s decorative identity, now reinterpreted through contemporary details and reflections. Light plays a central role in the redesigned interiors, defining architectural forms, bringing out the qualities of the materials and creating an atmosphere that shifts throughout the day. The new layout balances elegance with informality, offering a more open, relaxed and comfortable welcome. The concierge desk is also an integral part of this new experience, serving as both a point of reference for guests and a gateway to the city. Drawing on the expertise of the hotel’s concierges – all members of Les Clefs d’Or, the prestigious international association of hotel concierges – guests can discover a more authentic side of Milan through tailored recommendations, itineraries and a carefully curated selection of places to visit. At the centre of the refurbishment, the Grand Lounge & Bar has been reimagined as a gathering place that deepens the hotel’s connection with the city. With its clean lines, warm finishes and gold detailing, the new bar counter is a focal point of the interior, reshaping the space and enhancing its welcoming atmosphere. From aperitivo to informal get-togethers, the bar embraces one of Milan’s most cherished rituals, offering a setting in which to meet, converse and spend time together in the heart of the city. The design and atmosphere adapt to the changing pace of the day, from a break during the working day to a casual meeting or a moment of relaxation. The Grand Lounge & Bar is a destination in its own right, welcoming visitors as well as hotel guests and reflecting Milan’s rhythm and sociable spirit. Among the bespoke features, the decorative oval ceiling feature in the Grand Lounge & Bar, designed by Marta Cortese and created by Jannelli & Volpi, brings distinctive colour and texture to the interior. Its contemporary character highlights the craftsmanship at the heart of the project. Next to the bar, the library completes the refurbishment of the hotel’s social spaces, providing a versatile setting for reading, conversation and gathering. Balancing practicality with comfort, it is equally suited to a quiet pause, a casual meeting or an informal working session. While the refreshed interiors provide a new setting, it is people who give the experience meaning. At Rosa Grand Milano, the warmth of the welcome is shaped by the daily dedication of a team that places guest relationships, attention to detail and thoughtful, personalised service at the heart of its work. The refurbishment of its public spaces further reinforces Rosa Grand’s position as a city destination where hospitality, design and urban life come together, evolving alongside Milan through a contemporary aesthetic and a deeply Italian culture of hospitality. europe italy milan refurbishment renovation starhotels collezione Related Posts 14 August 2025 Hotel Kämp reveals refreshed interiors 30 August 2023 Wyndham Grand debuts in Poland 1 September 2015 Starwood launches Sheraton Grand

items.title: Uncommon Hospitality unveils Nordic-inspired spa lodge
items.summary:
Maine-based Uncommon Hospitality has announced Fara Lodge & Nordic Spa, an intimate mountain getaway coming to Rangeley in Late 2027. […] 
 The post  Uncommon Hospitality unveils Nordic-inspired spa lodge  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Uncommon Hospitality unveils Nordic-inspired spa lodge 16 November 2026 | In Projects | By Eleanor Howard Maine-based Uncommon Hospitality has announced Fara Lodge & Nordic Spa, an intimate mountain getaway coming to Rangeley in Late 2027. Designed in partnership with Maine -based architecture firm Jocelyn O Dickson Architecture (JODA), the property will reimagine a historic escape through a contemporary lens, preserving its architectural character while introducing elevated accommodations and an expansive Nordic spa experience developed with MCD Spa Consulting. Inspired by the communal culture of Nordic saunas and the distinctive charm of the Rangeley Lakes Region, known as the “Jewel of the Maine Mountains,” Fara Lodge will offer a design-forward hospitality experience built around the natural rhythm of adventure and restoration. The property will feature a collection of guest rooms and private cottages, comprehensive spa facilities with multiple sauna and thermal experiences, a nourishing café and communal spaces, and a restored historic bar that has welcomed mountain-worn Rangeley adventurers for decades. Fara Lodge is designed to honour the landscape from every vantage point, offering guests a deeply tranquil experience through a contemporary lens. Interiors draw from Western Maine’s rugged character while introducing a more refined approach to mountain design. Original stone fireplaces and pine panelling will sit alongside oversized lanterns, vintage Swedish sofas, and a palette of oxblood, dusty blue, and deep rust, a quietly Scandinavian sensibility that feels entirely at home among the lakes and peaks of this corner of the state. The lodge will feature 10 guestrooms and two private cottages, with simple yet beautiful touches including wrap-around pine banquettes; a considered mix of fabrics by Schumacher, McLaurin & Piercy and Commune for Kufri; integrated boot warmers and built-in storage millwork; and rich teal tilework that offers an unexpected moment of colour in the otherwise neutral, relaxing rooms. “My family has been coming to Rangeley for generations, so this project carries a particular meaning. The design had to honour what longtime visitors already love about this place, its history, its character, its quietness, while creating something that feels genuinely new for those discovering it for the first time,” comments Jocelyn O Dickson, Principal of JODA. “Every material decision, from the Maine-made furniture to the art program, tells the story of this region and the people who have shaped it.” The Great Hall will function as the natural gathering place of the property: a warm, unhurried space anchored by two stone fireplaces. The all-day cafe will offer counter-service breakfast, lunch, and dinner alongside grab-and-go offerings, all inspired by Scandinavian cuisine’s emphasis on seasonality and simplicity. A bar tucked in one of the property’s most historic spaces remains as a humble nod to the lodge’s long history of well-adventured guests, its original wood floors still marked by the spikes of generations of golfers. The heart of Fara Lodge will be its destination-worthy wellness centre overlooking Saddleback Mountain, offering a range of thermal and relaxation experiences derived from the shared humanity of bathing culture. The sprawling wellness campus will feature Maine-built cedar tubs, outdoor wood-fired saunas, an indoor Finnish dry sauna, fireside lounging, a relaxation yurt, and outdoor hot and cold plunge pools. With additional communal areas including a welcoming reception area, outdoor spa deck with hot tubs and showers, and calming relaxation rooms, the experience is built to encourage exploration, both of the facilities’ restorative benefits, and of oneself. “The inspiration for this project is Rangeley itself. We fell for the property and the area years ago, enchanted by the natural beauty and endless things to do. My family now enjoys Rangeley year-round and that personal connection is a big part of why this project means so much to us,” says Nate DeLois, Co-Principal of Uncommon Hospitality. “We’ve learned that the most meaningful hospitality experiences are the ones rooted in genuine place and community, and we’re approaching Rangeley with the same spirit. We can’t wait to welcome a new generation of travellers to experience it for themselves.” Americas Lodge maine spa uncommon hospitality Related Posts 25 January 2024 Das Central welcomes new Summit Spa 24 October 2023 Envi Lodges to debut in Oman 12 October 2020 The Rusty Parrot Lodge & Spa announces details of rebuild

items.title: The Postcard Hotel to debut in Nepal with riverfront retreat
items.summary:
The Postcard Hotel is set to make its debut in Nepal with The Postcard on the Rapti River, Chitwan. Set […] 
 The post  The Postcard Hotel to debut in Nepal with riverfront retreat  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: The Postcard Hotel is set to make its debut in Nepal with The Postcard on the Rapti River, Chitwan. Set along the Rapti River, with uninterrupted views of the surrounding forests and hills, the 22-key luxury retreat adjoins the buffer zone of Chitwan National Park, one of South Asia’s most significant wildlife destinations. The opening marks the brand’s expansion into its fourth country, following India, Bhutan and Sri Lanka. The Postcard on the Rapti River has been conceived to make the surrounding landscape an integral part of the stay. Guests arrive through a Temple Court built around a stupa, an architectural introduction to a hotel thoughtfully designed to reflect its setting. The 22 generously proportioned rooms and suites, starting at 1,300ft 2 , feature private sit-outs overlooking the river or forest. On fortunate days, guests may experience the thrill of watching wildlife from the privacy of their rooms. The two-bedroom Presidential Suite, extending across 5,000ft 2 , offers space and privacy, complete with its own private pool. Dining and leisure are equally connected to the destination. Tree Tops, the hotel’s indoor-outdoor restaurant and bar, occupies an elevated deck overlooking the forest, with The Postcard’s signature anytime breakfast allowing guests to dine entirely at their own pace. As evening falls, Tribal Circle brings guests together around a bonfire for an open-air barbecue inspired by the culinary traditions of the Tharu community, indigenous to the Terai. The hotel also features a swimming pool, spa treatment rooms, a steam room and sauna, while a spacious elevated viewing deck by the pool offers sweeping views of the surrounding wilderness and opportunities for wildlife sightings. Beyond the hotel, programming includes naturalist-led jeep safaris, guided forest walks, canoe excursions along the Rapti River and birdwatching experiences. Visits to nearby Tharu villages offer an introduction to the region’s distinctive cultural heritage and the communities that have lived alongside these forests and rivers for generations. “At The Postcard, we have always believed that some of the world’s most remarkable destinations are those that remain beyond the usual travel map,” says said Kapil Chopra, Founder and CEO, The Postcard Hotel. “Our ambition is to bring these places to life through hotels that are deeply rooted in their surroundings, while allowing the destination itself to take centre stage. “What drew us to The Postcard on the Rapti River was the conviction Savanna and her father, Suraj, brought to the project. Their desire to showcase Nepal beyond its mountains, and to create something that respects the landscape, its wildlife and its people, resonated deeply with our own philosophy. This is precisely the kind of destination we want to introduce to the world – one that offers not just a beautiful place to stay, but a meaningful connection with a part of the world that deserves to be discovered.” Savanna Vaidya Basnyat, owner of The Postcard on the Rapti River, adds: “Chitwan is one of the most precious parts of that world, and sharing its beauty with the world is something I feel deeply passionate about. From the moment we discovered this beautiful bend in the river, overlooking the forest and the hills beyond, we knew we had found something truly special. We wanted to create a place that belonged to its surroundings, rather than one that simply occupied the landscape. My father has been central to bringing this vision to life, and building something so meaningful together has been an incredibly special journey.” Basnyat concludes: “For me, this project is about more than hospitality. It is about conservation tourism and finding a way for tourism and nature to coexist in harmony.” Nepal rapti river the postcard hotel Related Posts 27 September 2024 Trailborn set to debut latest hotel in Arizona 14 April 2015 Delano Hotel to debut in Dubai 19 April 2012 Firmdale to re-open their debut hotel

items.title: Gottfried Gruber and Lains Architects unveil vision for Hotel AUI
items.summary:
Gottfried Gruber and Lains Architects have reimagined the former Lärchenhof Hotel as Hotel AUI in Maranza, South Tyrol. The project […] 
 The post  Gottfried Gruber and Lains Architects unveil vision for Hotel AUI  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Gottfried Gruber and Lains Architects unveil vision for Hotel AUI 13 November 2026 | In Projects | By Eleanor Howard Gottfried Gruber and Lains Architects have reimagined the former Lärchenhof Hotel as Hotel AUI in Maranza, South Tyrol. The project involved a redesign of the building’s exterior, communal areas, part of the spa and most of its 26 rooms. While the original load-bearing structures were retained, the architects reworked the hotel’s identity and interiors to introduce a more flexible approach to hospitality. The hotel takes its new name from the South Tyrolean dialect word for ‘up’. South Tyrol-based studio Lains Architects was responsible for the interior design, collaborating with architect Gottfried Gruber on the building’s exterior and pool. “One of the central ideas behind the design of AUI was the interplay between opposites: social interaction and privacy, activity and relaxation, openness and a sense of comfort, digital and analogue,” explains Sabrina Negri, Lains Architects. “The spaces are designed to accommodate these contrasts naturally.” Green is the defining colour of the redesigned building, extending from its exterior into the interiors. The new façade unifies the previously fragmented structure, with individual balconies connected to form a continuous outer plane. Inspired by the silhouette of traditional pitched-roof houses, the design features coarsely brushed spruce wood finished with a two-layer colour glaze. Its textured surface references traditional South Tyrolean timber construction, including relief structures and coffered elements. “The façade takes its cue from the silhouette of a traditional pitched-roof house, repeated across the building,” notes Gottfried Gruber. “This reference connects the hotel to the Alpine landscape and suggests the idea that each guest can, in a sense, have their own private chalet. At the same time, each individual space remains part of a larger whole, reflecting the idea at the heart of the AUI community: Gruber also designed the new pool, positioned following an analysis of the sun’s path. Light simulations informed its placement, while the indoor-outdoor configuration creates a visual connection with the surrounding mountains. Mirrored surfaces reflect the water, sky and landscape. “The position of the new pool was determined through a careful analysis of the sun’s path,” says Gottfried Gruber. “Using light simulations throughout the day, we identified the point where the experience of the water would be at its best.” Inside, the surrounding forests inform the material palette, particularly the use of larch-inspired greens and copper tones. The ground floor has been reconfigured as an open communal space rather than a conventional hotel lobby. At its centre is a boomerang-shaped table incorporating self- check-in facilities, a traditional stube, a communal dining area and the breakfast buffet. “The first element guests encounter when entering the hotel is a long, boomerang-shaped table,” reveals Sabrina Negri, Lains Architects. “It brings together the self-check-in, the small stube, the community table and the breakfast buffet. In doing so, the traditional separation of hotel functions is dissolved: there is no dominant reception desk, nor a rigid hierarchy between host and guest.” The surrounding areas accommodate a range of functions, including a trust shop and community kitchen. Material changes help distinguish different zones, with larch flooring used in areas intended for longer stays and ceramic surfaces marking circulation routes. Green furniture accents provide further visual continuity throughout the communal spaces. The first and second floors house the redesigned rooms and apartments. Custom-made furniture maximises the available space, while the apartments incorporate compact kitchens and sofa areas that can be converted into additional sleeping accommodation. Spruce is used extensively in the interiors, complemented by fabrics and wallpapers in the hotel’s wider colour palette. “The characteristic green of AUI continues throughout these floors,” explains Michaela Greifenegg, Lains Architects. “Spruce remains the defining material, used extensively in solid wood, and its natural fragrance adds a particular sense of warmth. Carefully selected fabrics and wallpapers complete the material concept, creating comfortable spaces that invite guests to linger.” gottfried guber lains architects refurbishment renovation South Tyrol Related Posts 6 February 2024 Marin Architects designs new addition to New York’s skyline 17 October 2023 First Look: Trunk(Hotel) Sapporo 19 August 2022 GM Architects transforms Lebanese heritage house into boutique hotel

items.title: Q&A: Paragon Studio brings wellness into the guestroom
items.summary:
Having made its name in superyacht and prime residential gyms, Paragon Studio is now working with hotel operators and designers […] 
 The post  Q&A: Paragon Studio brings wellness into the guestroom  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Q&A: Paragon Studio brings wellness into the guestroom 12 November 2026 | In Products | By Hannah Wintle Having made its name in superyacht and prime residential gyms, Paragon Studio is now working with hotel operators and designers to bring wellness into the hotel guestroom. Ahead of the launch of In-Suite at HIX, Founder Edward Thomas talks craftsmanship, carbon and why a hotel’s wellness offering shouldn’t stop in the gym. Paragon Studio began in superyachts and prime residential. What did that world teach you about luxury hospitality? Nobody puts up with an ugly object in a beautiful room for very long. On a yacht or in a luxury home, the gym is often the last space to be designed and the first one the owner judges. So, we work function first and build the form around it. Every hand-made piece has to survive a hard session, and then it has to be a feature that a designer is proud to see on the wall. Yachts also teach you control within a limited space, which is why so much of our range is storage: tree racks, wall units and the Credenza we originally built for a yacht and that now lives in homes on dry land. How does that carry over into hospitality? Hotels have the same problem, multiplied. An operator will specify stone, timber and bespoke joinery throughout, and then fill the gym with black rubber from a catalogue. Inside The Manchester Hotel in Lexington we laser-engraved the hotel’s logo into the end plates of our Diabolo Dumbbells, debossed it into the boxing pads, and matched the racks and cork yoga kit to the finishes upstairs. At the Golden Goose Arena in Milan, a curtain in the members’ lounge draws back on a wall installation we designed around the brand’s star. The brief is always the same: the gym should look as though it belongs to the building and the brand. Wellness now sits on almost every brand’s list of guest experience priorities Where is the industry getting it right? Spas, sleep programmes and personalisation. Luxury hotel groups have invested properly there. The gap is the guest who wants to train at six in the morning and finds the gym is in the basement, shared, and possibly still locked. A lot of people now travel with a routine and don’t want to drop it for four nights. Our research showed that plenty of others would simply rather not exercise in front of strangers. Hotels build wellness offerings around four disciplines (movement, recovery, nutrition, and sleep) but movement gets treated as a single, undifferentiated category (the gym) when it actually splits into three: the gym, activities and in-room wellbeing. Why have you launched In-Suite, your in-room fitness solution? One guest kept coming up in our research, and almost nobody was designing the modern traveller who doesn’t want to use the gym, but still values exercise, movement and routine. This guest profile is more likely to enjoy practicing mindful movement, such as yoga, Pilates and light mobility. These guests value privacy, space and quality and hotels have been slow to notice them while prioritising more and more upgrades in the main gym. That’s why we built an ecosystem around the product: the kit, the content and the service, so the room becomes personalised to the guest. What exactly is In-Suite? The collection is our bespoke offering: a series of kits that hotels can specify around movement, recovery and strength. Each can be supplied as a drawer insert to fit the existing joinery in the room, housed in a wooden tray, or delivered to the room to order by concierge. Recovery and movement kits are the core options, and every element of the look and feel can be specified to match the hotel’s design. Hotels can provide each room with a set. Guests choose what they’d like to do from the menu on the digital platform, which offers workouts for strength and conditioning, Pilates or recovery, each using different equipment from the kit. The platform also lets guests order specialist equipment to their room, if the hotel wants to offer that. Each kit carries a laser-etched plaque with a QR code, which links guests to their workout through the hotel’s software. For our launch at HIX Europe, we have partnered with Naturalmat to display In-Suite within the bed frame itself to show the versatility of the product, and how it can be designed within the room at concept stages of projects. Why a drawer? Because the room is already full. A drawer insert takes up no additional footprint, so it can be retrofitted into rooms that are open and trading, with no change to the layout – and no joinery modifications are required. It’s also easy to manage. Every piece has its own cut-out, so housekeeping can see, at a glance, whether anything has walked. How far can a hotel make it its own? As far as it likes. The starting point is our own web app with the full video library. The next step is light-touch branding: the app in the hotel’s colours and logo, branded intros and outros, subtitles in the languages its guests speak. Beyond that, we’ll film a bespoke library on site, in the hotel’s own rooms. Our software includes an ever-growing library of workout videos that are monitored for performance, and use the data to keep the content fresh, relevant and engaging. The hardware follows the same logic. Equipment can carry the hotel’s logo, and the trays, inserts and kit can be made in finishes outside our standard range to suit the interior. What’s the commercial case for an operator? In-Suite is a room feature a hotel can charge for, and a clear way to separate one room category from another. The video library runs on a subscription, and we look after the hardware through a servicing and maintenance package: an emergency allowance to replace anything stolen or damaged, an ongoing refurbishment programme for well-used pieces, and an annual on-site inspection. Kettlebells do occasionally leave hotels. We’d rather the operator didn’t have to think about it. Sustainability is the question every specifier now asks. What’s
