items.title: Groupe GM brings personalised scent experience to hospitality
items.summary:
Groupe GM has announced an exclusive partnership with Compoz Paris, a French fragrance and wellbeing brand combining patented diffusion technology […] 
 The post  Groupe GM brings personalised scent experience to hospitality  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Groupe GM brings personalised scent experience to hospitality 10 November 2026 | In Products | By Hannah Wintle Groupe GM has announced an exclusive partnership with Compoz Paris, a French fragrance and wellbeing brand combining patented diffusion technology with refined design. Together, the two companies are set to bring a new olfactory dimension to the hotel guest experience through an intuitive and refined approach to personalised scent. Through this partnership, Groupe GM will make Compoz Paris’ technology available to its international hospitality network across more than 80 countries, extending access to a distinctive in-room fragrance experience that moves beyond the traditional hotel signature scent and allows each guest to choose an atmosphere that suits their mood or moment. As travellers increasingly look for stays that feel more personal, immersive and attuned to their wellbeing, hotels are embracing new ways to further personalise and enrich the guest experience. By allowing guests to choose the scent atmosphere around them, Compoz Paris adds a more sensory dimension to the stay, creating moments of comfort, relaxation and escape that can be tailored to each individual. Founded by fragrance and innovation enthusiasts Aymeric Wuidart, David Lopez Bonet and Xavier Pourcines, Compoz Paris was launched in response to five years of research and development around how fragrance can be created, personalised and experienced. The brand developed patented technology enabling the real-time blending and diffusion of fragrance composition in one click, bringing together olfactory expertise, digital innovation and intuitive use. Inspired by the natural movement of scent through the air, Compoz Paris technology releases fragrance molecules without heat, water, alcohol or combustion, creating a clean and refined olfactory experience with no lingering scent once diffusion has stopped. Compoz Paris built its original olfactory repertoire around natural-origin essential oils sourced from renowned producing regions around the world, including ylang-ylang from the Comoros, jasmine from Egypt, patchouli from Indonesia, lavender from Provence or bergamot from Calabria. The brand’s collaboration with Groupe GM centres around Le Compositeur, Compoz Paris’ connected fragrance diffuser powered by patented real-time blending technology. The system works with a curated set of five fragrance capsules: Verbena & Musk, Fig & Sandalwood, Jasmine & Neroli, Incense & Spices and Amber & Chai. The experience is designed to be effortless for both guests and hotel teams. Once the set of five capsules is inserted, Le Compositeur is ready to use. Guests simply browse the available scent experiences on the integrated touchscreen and select the atmosphere they prefer. The system automatically blends the capsules to recreate and diffuse one of ten distinctive scent ambiances, from the fresh and uplifting Mist of Sun to the woody warmth and comfort of By the Fireplace or the aromatic escape of Nature Detox. Unlike conventional room fragrance systems that can leave a lingering scent in the air, Le Compositeur is designed for fragrance diffusion without remanence. Guests can enjoy the atmosphere they choose during their stay without imposing the same fragrance on the next guest, making scent a more personal and flexible part of the experience. Its plug-and-play format requires no complex set-up, making it straightforward for hotel teams to introduce into the guest room and intuitive for guests to use throughout their stay. Le Compositeur has been conceived not only as a fragrance diffusion device, but also as an interior object. Elegant, sculptural and carefully designed, it blends naturally into refined hotel interiors rather than appearing as a technical device. Designed by Alnoor Mitha de Bharat, it is available in lacquered, natural wood and leather finishes to complement different interior styles, with bespoke finishes also available for more customised projects. Le Compositeur can be used across hotel rooms and suites, spas, and meeting rooms, with optimal fragrance diffusion indicated for enclosed spaces from approximately 5 m² to 70 m². The exclusive partnership also brings together Groupe GM and Compoz Paris’ shared consideration for product design, sourcing and resource use. Groupe GM’s long-standing commitment to responsible hospitality through its Care About Earth programme aligns closely with Compoz’s sustainability-focused approach. The brand exclusively uses essential oils of natural origin and supports responsible sourcing practices designed to protect both communities and ecosystems. In addition, used Compoz capsules are recovered and processed through the company’s Natucare programme, allowing approximately 80% of materials to be reused in manufacturing while ensuring the remainder is fully recycled. “Our partnership with Compoz Paris opens a new olfactory dimension within the hotel guest experience,” says Laurent Marchand, President of Groupe GM. “By combining Compoz’s patented fragrance technology and refined French design with Groupe GM’s hospitality expertise and international network, we can offer hotels a genuinely distinctive way to personalise the in-room experience. Guests can choose the scent atmosphere that suits their mood or moment, while hotels benefit from a solution designed to integrate naturally into their guest offering.” Aymeric Wuidart, CEO of Compoz Paris, adds: “When we created Compoz Paris, our ambition was to provide each client with the scents they love, in a fully personalised and natural way. We soon understood that hospitality specialists were looking into enhancing the guest experience and wellness. Today, Groupe GM’s hospitality expertise and international reach gives us a unique opportunity to bring that vision to life providing all hotels around the world with a scent solution that is intuitive for both guests and hotel teams.” www.groupegm.com bespoke scent compoz pari

items.title: Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings
items.summary:
As rising temperatures and energy costs place greater pressure on hospitality operators, Magnovent CEO Jonathan Jover explores how intelligent airflow […] 
 The post  Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings  appeared first on  Sleeper .
items.text: Q&A: Magnovent explores bioclimatic design in hospitality settings 5 November 2026 | In Products | By Hannah Wintle As rising temperatures and energy costs place greater pressure on hospitality operators, Magnovent CEO Jonathan Jover explores how intelligent airflow and bioclimatic design can improve guest comfort while reducing energy consumption. How are changing guest expectations reshaping environmental comfort in hospitality? Rising temperatures and increasingly demanding guest expectations are making thermal comfort a strategic priority for hospitality operators. At the same time, rising energy costs are putting pressure on operating margins. The challenge is to create consistently comfortable environments without allowing energy consumption to escalate. This requires a more intelligent approach to managing temperature, airflow and insulation. What is bioclimatic architecture, and why is it so important for hotels and residences? Bioclimatic architecture considers the relationship between a building, its local climate and the people who use it. In hospitality, this means combining effective insulation, natural or mechanical ventilation and efficient heating and cooling systems to reduce reliance on air conditioning. By designing for climate from the outset, hotels can improve thermal comfort, reduce energy demand and create spaces that feel naturally comfortable while preserving their architectural identity. How can climate and airflow enhance the guest experience? Comfort is not determined by air temperature alone. Air movement influences how the body perceives heat, allowing guests to feel comfortable at higher thermostat settings. By combining air conditioning with well-designed ventilation, hotels can create a more balanced and pleasant indoor climate, while reducing energy consumption. The result is an environment that feels better, operates more efficiently and supports a more enjoyable guest experience. How do your solutions help hotels reduce energy use without compromising comfort? The key is to move beyond the assumption that lower temperatures automatically mean greater comfort. Setting air conditioning to 20°C, for example, can significantly increase energy consumption without necessarily delivering a better guest experience. By combining efficient ceiling fans with air conditioning, hotels can maintain comfort at higher thermostat settings and reduce cooling energy consumption. Based on results reported by our clients, this approach can deliver energy savings of 30–45%, depending on the building, climate and operating conditions. Our objective is to make comfort measurable, efficient and easier to manage. Can you share a hospitality project that demonstrates the impact of your approach? One Ibiza Suites is a good example of how a considered combination of building performance and airflow can transform the guest experience. By improving roof insulation and introducing ceiling fans in the lobby and restaurant, the hotel enhanced thermal comfort in key shared spaces. The combined intervention achieved a reduction in perceived temperature of approximately 4°C, demonstrating that comfort can be improved without relying exclusively on more intensive air conditioning. What’s next for Magnovent? Our next step is to help hospitality operators reduce their reliance on air conditioning, in both summer and winter, with a target of reducing energy consumption by an average of 30%. Through increasingly sophisticated control systems, we aim to manage airflow, heating and cooling as an integrated solution, helping operators maintain their desired level of perceived comfort while optimising energy use. Ultimately, we want to move the industry towards a more intelligent understanding of temperature: one in which buildings are designed and operated around how people actually experience comfort, rather than simply the number displayed on a thermostat. www.magnovent.eu air conditioning bioclimatic design climate change guest comfort magnovent Related Posts 19 September 2023 Inside FOH’s luxury hospitality solutions 22 June 2023 Madera talks timber, bespoke design and hospitality interiors 5 December 2019 Cameron Design House’s Inari chandelier designed for hospitality settings

Hyatt has announced the opening of Thompson Rome, a 69-room hotel owned and operated by AG Group and Rossifin Group, […]

items.text: Hyatt has announced the opening of Thompson Rome, a 69-room hotel owned and operated by AG Group and Rossifin Group, marking the brand’s debut in Italy . Set within a reimagined iconic landmark on Via delle Botteghe Oscure, Thompson Rome draws on the architectural character of its 1940s home and the layered history of Via delle Botteghe Oscure, one of Rome’s most significant streets and a landmark in post-war Italian political history. Original elements, including a sweeping marble staircase, have been carefully restored, while a sculptural wall and inlaid floor by celebrated Italian artist Gio Pomodoro, rediscovered during the renovation after decades hidden from view – have been preserved and given new prominence within the hotel. Bespoke furnishings, refined detailing and layered natural materials bring a contemporary expression to the building’s history. Thompson Rome’s 69 guestrooms and suites take cues from the character of a contemporary Roman residence, pairing warm natural materials with custom furnishings and understated details. With 19 suites, nearly one-third of the hotel’s accommodation offering, guests can choose from Junior Suites, Suites with patios or terraces, and the 104-square-metre Thompson Suite with 80-square-metre private terrace. Designed as a counterpoint to the energy of the city outside, the rooms feel residential and refined, with select accommodations offering views across Rome’s historic rooftops and landmarks. Several rooms feature balconies overlooking Via delle Botteghe Oscure, while select rooms offer private patios facing Rome’s historic buildings. Thompson Rome’s art programme, creates a dialogue between the history of the site and contemporary art. The collection brings together works by artists associated with the Scuola Romana and the Scuola di Piazza del Popolo, alongside contemporary artists whose practices reflect Rome’s longstanding cultural openness and international influences including Francesco Del Drago, Giangaetano Patanè, and Guido Strazza. Presented throughout the hotel’s public spaces and guestrooms, the artworks are an integral part of the guest experience, connecting the memory of the site with the creativity of Rome today. A rotating artist-in-residence programme will further extend Thompson Rome’s connection to the city’s creative community through exhibitions, conversations and other cultural programming. Three distinct food and beverage venues carry Thompson Rome from morning espresso and leisurely lunches through aperitivo, dinner and drinks above the city. At Lyve Restaurant, Executive Chef Fabio Fioravanti brings a contemporary Mediterranean approach to ingredients and traditions from the Italian coast and across the region. Seafood is central to the menu, with Mediterranean fish and shellfish alongside dishes that draw on bouillabaisse, rockfish broths, wild coastal herbs and rouille, reworked with a lighter touch while preserving the depth and character of the originals. The same attention extends to the pastry kitchen, where precise technique and contrasting flavours and textures shape the dessert menu. A native of Ostia, Fioravanti brings more than two decades of international experience, including time with the Alain Ducasse group and at the three-Michelin-starred Le Louis XV – Alain Ducasse at the Hôtel de Paris Monte-Carlo. At Lyve, that technical precision carries through a dining experience that is refined yet relaxed, with the quality of the ingredients and clarity of the cooking taking centre stage. Above the hotel, Lyve Rooftop pairs views across Rome with cocktails, Italian aperitivi and a menu designed for sharing. The Lobby Lounge offers the hotel’s most casual gathering place throughout the day, from coffee and light fare to aperitivo and cocktails. The hotel will extend the guest experience through a year-round programme shaped by Rome’s culinary, artistic and creative communities. Experiences will range from culinary workshops and guided tastings to Empire of Light, a photography-led experience from the hotel’s seventh floor that invites guests to discover Rome from above. “Rome has such a strong identity, so we wanted Thompson Rome to start with the city itself,” says Amar Lalvani, Chief Creative Officer, Hyatt Corporation and President & Creative Director, The Lifestyle Group, Hyatt . “The building, the neighbourhood, the food, the people and the way Romans live all shaped the hotel. The goal was to create a Thompson hotel that feels at home in Rome, a hotel travellers want to discover and Romans want to come back to.” architecture europe hotel design hyatt interior design italy rome thompson hotels Related Posts 14 June 2023 Thompson Hotels heading to Rome 21 February 2022 Design Hotels welcomes four new members 9 August 2021 Thompson Hotels arrives in Savannah

items.title: gerhard richter’s pavilion opens in doha, wrapped in patterns inspired by islamic geometry
items.summary:
six patterned walls, mirrored interiors, and a sculptural tower bring the german artist’s decades-long investigation of abstraction into a spatial experience, drawing connections with the geometric traditions of islamic art. 
 The post  gerhard richter’s pavilion opens in doha, wrapped in patterns inspired by islamic geometry  appeared first on  designboom | architecture & design magazine .
items.text: [FEATURED] gerhard richter unveils permanent pavilion in doha Gerhard Richter ‘s permanent pavilion in Doha, Qatar is now open, conceived as a freestanding work of art and architecture in MIA Park, outside the Museum of Islamic Art. Realized in collaboration with Selldorf Architects , Doha Pavilion: Gerhard Richter houses a collection of the artist’s paintings and sculptures , including works created specifically for the project. The hexagonal structure translates Richter’s exploration of abstraction, repetition, and perception into space, while its patterned exterior draws connections with the geometric traditions of Islamic art (find designboom’s previous coverage here ). The six exterior walls of the pavilion feature decorative patterns derived from Richter’s Abstract Painting (724-4), created in 1990. The artist developed the compositions through a mathematical process that began in 2010, digitally dividing the original painting into progressively smaller vertical strips, eventually reaching 8,192 sections. Each strip is mirrored and repeated to produce a symmetrical horizontal pattern, applied to the pavilion’s exterior. The intricate patterns recall the repeating geometries and interlaced arabesques found in Islamic visual culture, establishing a connection between Richter’s experimental approach to abstraction and the artistic traditions of the region. exterior waterfront view of Doha Pavilion: Gerhard Richter in MIA Park, Doha. Artwork © Gerhard Richter 2026 | image by Iwan Baan , courtesy of Qatar Museums new strip paintings and mirrored interiors define the pavilion Τhree new large-scale works from Richter’s Strip series, which began in 2011, are displayed throughout the pavilion. They translate the original abstract painting into thin horizontal slices, each measuring 0.08 millimeters wide, creating compositions built from fragmented color and repetition. At the center of the space stands STRIP-TOWER (2026), a tripartite freestanding sculpture designed by Richter specifically for the pavilion. Two large, floor-to-ceiling Mirrors, belonging to a body of work the artist began in the 1980s, occupy the narrower walls. Their reflective surfaces capture the artworks and visitors, producing shifting visual relationships and an evolving sense of space. Outside the structure, a stone sculpture titled Brunnen (Well) extends the installation into the surrounding park. Richter’s idea for the pavilion dates back to a visit to Doha in 2013, when the artist was developing his Strip paintings. The architecture and history of the city prompted him to consider how different strands of his artistic practice could come together in a permanent structure. ‘My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work,’ the visual artist explains. ‘ Doha is the right place and the only place for my Pavilion.’ north entry facade view of Doha Pavilion: Gerhard Richter, featuring the artist’s Patterns. Artwork © Gerhard Richter 2026 | image by Iwan Baan , courtesy of Qatar Museums a permanent addition to doha’s public art landscape The project was realized in collaboration with Selldorf Architects and forms part of the legacy of the Qatar-Germany 2017 Year of Culture. Its location in MIA Park places it among a growing collection of public artworks by international artists, including Richard Serra, Nairy Baghramian, and Peter Fischli and David Weiss. According to Qatar Museums Chairperson Sheikha Al Mayassa bint Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, the pavilion aims to connect contemporary artistic practices with the geometric traditions of Islamic visual culture while making art accessible as part of everyday public life. The unveiling coincides with the Qatar Creates Fall/Winter 2026–27 program and the inaugural edition of Rubaiya Qatar 2026, an international visual arts quadrennial running from November 21, 2026, through April 30, 2027. Rather than functioning solely as a space to exhibit Richter’s work, the permanent pavilion extends his investigation of abstraction into the surrounding environment. Visitors encounter the artist’s visual language through the building’s exterior, interior installations, and reflective surfaces, experiencing painting not only as an image but also as a space to move through. looking southeast to Doha Pavilion: Gerhard Richter featuring the artist’s Patterns. items.title: perkins&will and estúdio campana wrap são paulo airport lounge in amazon river-inspired timber installation
items.summary:
inside terminal 3 of são paulo’s guarulhos international airport, perkins&will and estúdio campana design the 1,400-sqm pedra preta lounge, anchored by a curved timber entrance installation modeled on the amazon’s juruá river and espírito santo stone interiors. 
 The post  perkins&will and estúdio campana wrap são paulo airport lounge in amazon river-inspired timber installation  appeared first on  designboom | architecture & design magazine .
items.text: [FEATURED] PERKINS&WILL AND ESTÚDIO CAMPANA’s AIRPORT LOUNGE IN SÃO PAULO Located within Terminal 3 of São Paulo’s Guarulhos International Airport, Latin America’s busiest transit hub, Pedra Preta Lounge (Sala Pedra Preta) is a 1,400-sqm interior designed by Perkins&Will São Paulo in collaboration with Estúdio Campana for Itaú Personnalité and Itaú Private. Rather than organizing the lounge as a single open waiting hall, the layout divides the floor plan into a sequence of interconnected zones calibrated for varying levels of privacy and activity, distributing dedicated areas for dining, work, rest, meetings, entertainment, and wellbeing across the footprint. art gallery | all images ©Fran Parente BESPOKE FURNITURE AND BRAZILIAN ART ORGANIZE MULTI-ZONE PLAN The spatial progression begins at the entrance, where a sculptural timber installation by Brazilian practice Estúdio Campana, modeled on the meandering curves of the Amazon’s Juruá River, wraps the reception area to form a physical and acoustic threshold from the surrounding terminal. Inside, Perkins&Will studio employs curved transitions, layered lighting, and framed sightlines to delineate zones while maintaining orientation toward departure gates. The material palette pairs natural stone quarried in Espírito Santo with warm timber, textured wall finishes, and custom-designed furnishings that integrate built-in architecture with furniture. A curated selection of Brazilian modern and contemporary artworks is embedded throughout the circulation path rather than isolated in gallery displays, complemented by a hospitality program featuring menus by chef Luiz Filipe Souza and wine pairings curated by sommelier Juliana Carani. sculptural natural-wood facade sculptural facade entering the lounge reception and installation bar bar quiet lounge bar quiet lounge ultra premium room 1/4 mezzanine staircase Pedra Preta icon on the entrance restaurant project info: name: Pedra Preta Lounge architect: Perkins&Will | @perkinswill_br , Estudio Campana | @estudiocampana location: Terminal 3, Guarulhos International Airport (GRU), São Paulo, Brazil photographer: Fran Parente | @franparente designboom has received this project from our DIY submissions feature, where we welcome our readers to submit their own work for publication. items.text: Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects. Image © Vinay Panjwani Written by Reyyan Dogan Published on November 23, 2026 The Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects in Indore , India , has been declared the World Building of the Year at the 2026 World Architecture Festival (WAF) . The ultimate accolades of World Building of the Year, World Interior of the Year, and Future Project of the Year were announced as hundreds of architects from across the world convened at a grand finale Gala Dinner at the Broward County Convention Center in Florida . A host of Special Prizes, including the American Beauty Prize sponsored by RFACT, were also announced at the closing event to celebrate the nineteenth edition of the festival. The announcement follows the final day of WAF, in which prize winners across all 42 categories have been competing for the winning titles. + 23 World Building of the Year, supported by GROHE World Building of the Year went to The Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects in Indore, India. Related Article World Architecture Festival 2026: Day Two Winners Announced Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects. Image © Vinay Panjwani Situated within a 32-acre university campus, the main administration offices, along with an open-air auditorium, seminar halls, library, and cafeteria, form the functions of Prestige University. The building gradually steps up from the approach, becoming a multifunctional stage for large-scale events, seating 9000 students at a time. Inside, spaces are interspersed with naturally lit landscaped courtyards, allowing indirect light to infuse the internal volumes at each level, creating an energy-efficient, sustainable building with minimal dependence on artificial lighting and air conditioning - responding to a climate that varies from 30°C to 40°C for 8 months of the year. The built form evokes images of stepped wells in India which have existed since 1100 years; spaces not just built to store water but also social interactions bringing the community together. Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects. Image © Vinay Panjwani The winner was selected by a Super Jury chaired by Grace La, Co-Founder of LA DALLMAN , and Professor and Chair of Architecture at Harvard Graduate School of Design. The Jury also included: Adrien Gardère, Founder and CEO, Studio Adrien Gardère ; Fernando Menis , Architect-Director, Fernando Menis SLPU; and Kai-Uwe Bergmann, Partner, BIG – Bjarke Ingels Group . World Interior of the Year, supported by Deltalight World Interior of the Year, supported by Deltalight, went to &Matcha Three Yards by MLA at Home in the Philippines. &Matcha Three Yards by MLA at Home. Image © Janius Lee At just 100 square meters, &Matcha Three Yards demonstrates how void spaces can become civic infrastructure, where architecture works with the natural elements to set the conditions of the space. The tea shop offers neighbourhood belonging and ecological repair to the site. Gaps have been intentionally designed into the structure as instruments for change, allowing weather, light, shadow, sound, and air to shift so that no two visits are the same. At the centre of these changing sceneries is a floating tea chamber, surrounded by water and tree planes which catch shadows that move through the hours, days, and seasons. Movable tables and chairs also allow each visitor to form their own spatial relationship: alone or gathered, still or conversational, working or simply present. Future Project of the Year Future Project of the Year went to Coding Kelp: Artificial Reef and Data Archive by Terreform ONE , in Vancouver Island, Canada. Coding Kelp - Artificial Reef and Data Archive by Terreform ONE. Image © Terreform ONE This neo-natural ocean kelp reef transforms architectural knowledge into botanical DNA. The structure is 3D-printed from calcium carbonate and engineered with porous zones that support kelp attachment and cold-water growth. Within geo-fenced, airtight vitrines, suspended specimens of dried ocean microalgae demonstrate a transgenic process in which texts, images, and drawings are encoded directly into the genetic material of engineered vegetation. The reef operates as a living, photosynthetic library. At planetary scale, the system merges two powerful sinks: carbon sequestration and long-term cold data storage. Landscape of the Year Landscape of the Year went to Doca Linear Park by Natureza Urbana in Brazil. Doca Linear Park by Natureza Urbana. items.title: Casa Amigó / Estudio Travertino
items.summary: Some renovations update spaces; others reorganize how they are lived in. Casa Amigó belongs to the second group. The project turns the flat into an interior landscape where color, material, and light reorganize the relationships between rooms.

items.title: The Best Coffee Table Books for Design Enthusiasts
items.summary: Beautifully produced books that invite a closer look at art, architecture, design, and the creative minds behind them
items.text: Art The Best Coffee Table Books for Design Enthusiasts 11.20.26 | By Design Milk Staff Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email A great coffee table book does more than look good sitting on a stack. It invites you to pick it up, lose yourself in its pages, and discover something you didn’t know before. Whether it’s an intimate look at a designer’s creative process, an architectural survey, or a collection of extraordinary photographs, the best examples offer plenty to explore beyond their covers. Of course, presentation matters, too. Beautiful printing, thoughtful layouts, and striking imagery can turn a book into a design object in its own right. For this year’s selection, we’ve gathered titles that balance visual appeal with compelling content, spanning architecture, interiors, art, photography, and creative culture. They’re books worth giving, displaying, and returning to long after the holidays. Photography courtesy of Assouline Achille by Glenn Adamson Italian designer Achille Salvagni has a way of making furniture feel like sculpture. Written by design historian Glenn Adamson, this richly illustrated monograph explores Salvagni’s distinctive approach to furniture, lighting, and decorative objects, where classical references meet contemporary forms. Across 336 pages and 246 illustrations, readers get a closer look at his extraordinary use of materials, from bronze and onyx to marble and rare woods. Achille is available at assouline.com for $120. Photography courtesy of Assouline Villa Treville Positano by Nicky Swallow and Govind Friedland Perched above the Amalfi Coast, Villa Treville was once the private retreat of legendary Italian director Franco Zeffirelli, whose theatrical sensibility shaped the property’s richly layered interiors. Assouline’s Villa Treville Positano takes readers inside the historic estate, exploring its architecture, lush gardens, and eclectic collection of antiques and decorative objects. With more than 200 illustrations and a textured cover inspired by the villa’s patterned ceramic tiles, the book captures the property’s distinctive character inside and out. Villa Treville Positano is available at shopbop.com for $120. Photography courtesy of Phaidon Mid-Century Modern Designers by Dominic Bradbury From Charles and Ray Eames to Florence Knoll, the designers who shaped the midcentury movement continue to influence how we live today. Published by Phaidon, this richly illustrated hardcover profiles 300 influential figures, including lesser-known talents whose work deserves a closer look. Spanning furniture, ceramics, glassware, and textiles, it’s an absorbing gift for anyone curious about the history of modern design. Mid-Century Modern Designers is available at hawkinsnewyork.com for $90. Photography courtesy of Artisan Books Après Ski by Erin Isakov From cozy mountain chalets to the rituals that follow a day on the slopes, Après Ski captures the atmosphere of alpine living. Blending interiors, travel, food, and ski culture, the book celebrates a lifestyle that’s as much about gathering around the fire as it is about skiing. A fitting gift for anyone drawn to mountain retreats, whether or not they ever hit the slopes. Après Ski is available at twowebster.com for $40. Baime in collaboration with Porsche, the 224-page volume explores 100 defining moments in the brand’s history, from the original 356 to its racing triumphs, design innovations, and collaborations with artists like Daniel Arsham. Archival photography, design sketches, and vintage advertisements reveal Porsche’s influence beyond the automotive world. Handcrafted in Italy, the book comes housed in a padded clamshell featuring a recessed metal image of the iconic Porsche 917K. Porsche: The Impossible Collection is available at assouline.com for $1,400. Photography courtesy of Prestel Publishing Wild Flowers of North America by Pamela Henson with Illustrations by Mary Vaux Walcott Long before botanical photography became commonplace, artist and naturalist Mary Vaux Walcott spent countless hours outdoors capturing the delicate details of North America’s wildflowers in watercolor. Originally published in 1925, her remarkable illustrations are brought together in this oversized volume featuring more than 250 botanical studies. From the subtle variations in petal color to the intricate shapes of leaves and stems, each painting reveals Walcott’s extraordinary eye for detail. Published in association with the Smithsonian Institution, it’s a beautiful intersection of art, science, and nature that deserves a place on the coffee table. Wild Flowers of North America is available at mcgeeandco.com for $72. MORE GIFT INSPIRATION Still shopping? items.title: How Klafs Is Rethinking the Sauna Through Design
items.summary: From retractable saunas to immersive ice rooms, the German company is exploring how engineering, materials, and technology can reshape traditional wellness rituals
items.text: Home Furnishings How Klafs Is Rethinking the Sauna Through Design 11.19.26 | By Bianca Weeko Martin Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email View Slideshow Klafs’s retractable S1 sauna integrates into a contemporary bedroom, bringing the traditional sauna experience into a residential setting without requiring a dedicated wellness room. Photography courtesy of Klafs. How Klafs Is Rethinking the Sauna Through Design Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email 1/7 Photos Klafs brings the experience of winter indoors with a snow room featuring ice-covered surfaces, dramatic lighting, and a rocky landscape. Photography courtesy of Klafs. 2/7 Photos Blue lighting, textured surfaces, and a sculptural ice fountain transform Klafs’s Frimas ice steam room into an immersive cooling environment. Photography courtesy of Klafs. 3/7 Photos Warm wood surfaces, tiered seating, and integrated lighting define a Klafs sauna at Hotel Sonne-Post, a spa hotel in Waldau, Germany. Photography courtesy of Klafs. 4/7 Photos Inside the S11, continuous horizontal slats, curved corners, and concealed lighting create a sculptural interior that emphasizes materiality and form. Photography courtesy of Klafs. 5/7 Photos The S11 sauna, designed with Studio F.A. Porsche, is a limited edition of 999 units. Photography courtesy of Klafs. 6/7 Photos Klafs’s retractable S1 sauna integrates into a contemporary bedroom, bringing the traditional sauna experience into a residential setting without requiring a dedicated wellness room. Photography courtesy of Klafs. 7/7 Photos Designed in collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, Klafs’s S11 sauna incorporates horizontal wood slats and integrated lighting into a contemporary residential interior. Photography courtesy of Klafs. The sauna is Finnish. The company reimagining it for contemporary homes and spas is German. Klafs , based in Schwäbisch Hall, Germany, sees no contradiction. Its designers approach the centuries-old ritual through engineering, experimenting with heat, air, and materials. As wellness culture expands, the language surrounding its rituals has become increasingly fluid. In my own friend group, “banya” has become nearly shorthand for any spa visit, though it refers specifically to the Russian-style bathhouse. Klafs, by contrast, brings a distinctly German engineering sensibility to these traditions, asking how far the experience can be pushed. At Klafs headquarters, where the company’s newest ideas are developed and tested, the tour begins in a two-tiered, glass-enclosed sauna. Our guide, an experienced training manager named Heinrich, speaks to the heater in the corner. “Hey, Klafs,” he says, with the intonation we’ve learned from Alexa and other voice-activated devices. I hadn’t considered the possibility of a smart aufguss guide. In German, aufguss means “infusion,” or literally “pouring over.” In a wellness context, it refers to a guided sauna ritual, typically involving water poured over hot stones, aromatic infusions, and the circulation of heated air. The practice has helped make sauna-going a communal experience in many North American spas. Klafs’s Vitality Boost, which the company describes as the world’s first personalized heat-waving system, brings elements of that ritual into an automated setting: no towel-spinning guide required, and no need to leave the wooden bench. Blue lighting, textured surfaces, and a sculptural ice fountain transform Klafs’s Frimas ice steam room into an immersive cooling environment. Photography courtesy of Klafs. From the heat of the sauna, the tour moves into an altogether different climate. I retreat into the cool blue light of a Frimas ice steam room, where a glowing central ice fountain grows delicate, flower-like formations. Around the corner, a button labeled “snow” summons flurries from the ceiling of the ice steam shower. The cooling phase of a hot-and-cold bathing ritual isn’t where most people want to linger, but these spaces make a compelling case for slowing down. Rather than treating cold exposure as something to endure, KLAFS creates immersive environments that make it part of the experience. Klafs brings the experience of winter indoors with a snow room featuring ice-covered surfaces, dramatic lighting, and a rocky landscape. Photography courtesy of Klafs. Then there’s the foam. I also discovered foam steam baths, which replace the intensity of a traditional aufguss with a more playful, tactile experience. Steam rooms equipped for foam treatments can be integrated into hotel and spa programming as scheduled group experiences. The suds, reminiscent of childhood bubble baths and the elaborate foam sculptures they inspired, bring out a part of my inner child I had long since stowed away. Espuro, Klafs’s proprietary foam essence, is formulated with plant-based ingredients, including coconut-derived compounds, which the company says help care for skin exposed to heat. Designed in collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, Klafs’s S11 sauna incorporates horizontal wood slats and integrated lighting into a contemporary residential interior. Photography courtesy of Klafs. Beyond these sensory experiments, Klafs has also reconsidered the sauna itself as an architectural object. The retractable S1 sauna expands from a compact enclosure into a full-size sauna, addressing the spatial constraints that often keep one out of the home. The design-led S11, a collaboration with Studio F.A. Porsche, pairs delicate washi paper and multicolor light panels with smooth, sinuous lines. Inside the S11, continuous horizontal slats, curved corners, and concealed lighting create a sculptural interior that emphasizes materiality and form. Photography courtesy of Klafs. Long established in Germany, Klafs has been expanding into the American market since its acquisition by Kohler in 2024. The premium Altea fitness club in my city, for instance, features Klafs installations, including the Sana

items.title: Lindye Galloway Brings Intimacy to a 10,000-Square-Foot Home
items.summary: In Orange County, the interior designer uses natural materials, layered textures, and sculptural furnishings to create a warm, inviting family residence
items.text: Interior Design Lindye Galloway Brings Intimacy to a 10,000-Square-Foot Home 11.17.26 | By Leo Lei Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email View Slideshow For a 10,000-square-foot family residence in Orange County, California, interior designer Lindye Galloway balances modern refinement with everyday comfort, using natural materials, layered textures, and sculptural furnishings to create a warm, inviting home. Photography by Grace Combs Lindye Galloway Brings Intimacy to a 10,000-Square-Foot Home Share on Facebook Share on Pinterest Share on Twitter Share via Email 1/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 2/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 3/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 4/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 5/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 6/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 7/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 8/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 9/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 10/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 11/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 12/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 13/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 14/30 Photos For a 10,000-square-foot family residence in Orange County, California, interior designer Lindye Galloway balances modern refinement with everyday comfort, using natural materials, layered textures, and sculptural furnishings to create a warm, inviting home. Photography by Grace Combs 15/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 16/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 17/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 18/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 19/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 20/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 21/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 22/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 23/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 24/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 25/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 26/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 27/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 28/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 29/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs 30/30 Photos Photography by Grace Combs At 10,000 square feet, a home can easily feel more expansive than inviting. For a new residence in Orange County, California, interior designer Lindye Galloway approached that challenge through a careful balance of natural materials, layered textures, and sculptural furnishings. The goal was to create a home that felt as warm and comfortable as it was refined, with a relaxed atmosphere suited to everyday family life. Photography by Grace Combs Galloway drew inspiration from the architecture and natural surroundings, aiming to create a timeless home. The interiors are organized around texture and natural materials in a soft, understated palette. Warm woods, soft neutrals, and natural stone run through the rooms alongside linen, wool, and mohair. Photography by Grace Combs Tactile upholstery and darker accents contrast with the lighter woods and stone, adding depth and dimension to each room. Furniture was selected for comfort and sculptural appeal, with clean lines and soft, organic forms, giving rooms a relaxed, lived-in quality. Photography by Grace Combs The attention to detail extends to the home’s fixtures and finishes. Hardware from Rocky Mountain Hardware and Nanz is complemented by mirrors from Claude Home and Croft House , while lighting comes from Ravenhill , Atelier de Troupe , and Roll & Hill . Photography by Grace Combs The kitchen, primary bathroom, and living room carry the same combination of wood, stone, and natural fibers. Beyond the main rooms, the property includes a separate guest house with its own bedroom and an indoor-outdoor living area. Galloway extended the same material palette to these spaces, creating continuity throughout the property. Photography by Grace Combs Rather than relying on dramatic gestures, Galloway lets the interplay of materials, textures, and forms define the interiors. It’s an approach that brings warmth and intimacy to a home of considerable scale. Photography by Grace Combs Leo Lei is the founder and editor of Leibal , a publication dedicated to minimalist design, architecture, and interiors. Through his writing and curatorial eye, he highlights thoughtful contemporary work from around the world. You can follow Leo Lei on Facebook , Pinterest , and Instagram . items.text: Product watch: Xuniva Evo from hansgrohe sets the tone in the bathroom • Hotel Designs Product watch: Xuniva Evo from hansgrohe sets the tone in the bathroom WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 23, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Product watch: Xuniva Evo from hansgrohe sets the tone in the bathroom Like an infinity pool at the washbasin – with Xuniva Evo, hansgrohe is further developing washbasin design and creating an aesthetic illusion of infinity… For the first time, hansgrohe is presenting these high-quality sanitary ceramics in four eye-catching surface designs. Xuniva Evo washbasins capture the natural movement of water and, with their natural colour design, create moments that transform ordinary bathroom routines into a relaxed, good ritual. This experience is made possible by the precisely crafted, concealed drain. A slight incline of the inner basin gently catches the flow of water and allows it to flow seemingly limitlessly into the depths. The even and natural movement with which the water finds its way through the pool has a meditative effect. The calming atmosphere is underlined by the different surface colours of Xuniva Evo. In addition to classic white with gloss, Xuniva Evo in matt black, matt slate grey, matt white and matt sand beige is a real eye-catcher in the bathroom. Image credit: hansgrohe Colour Meets Function Thanks to the freedom of colour design, Xuniva Evo can be perfectly combined with the FinishPlus surface range of hansgrohe basin mixers. But it’s not just the colours of the new product that leave a lasting positive impression: the innovative drain design of the new product directs the water invisibly back into the trap without the need for additional components, such as a PushOpen. Thanks to an integrated shadow gap, Xuniva Evo almost appears to float. The delicate ceramic walls and clear, linear edges round off the aesthetic work of art. Xuniva Evo is available in four shapes for countertop washbasins (two square versions, round, and RaceTrack). Image credit: hansgrohe Minimised Cleaning Effort With Xuniva Evo, the water is returned under the basin in the centre. This not only makes the siphon easy to install, but also minimises cleaning effort. In addition, the glaze is designed to repel dirt. The drain channel is also glazed to minimise dirt deposits. In addition, the specially developed combined glaze of SmartClean and HygieneEffect* makes cleaning the white basins child’s play and ensures maximum hygiene with minimum maintenance. The handmade, hard-wearing sanitary ceramic combines the highest level of craftsmanship with modern technology and offers impressive durability. The long service life of the ceramic – underpinned by a 20-year guarantee – makes it a sustainable choice. hansgrohe is one of our Recommended Suppliers and regularly features in our Supplier News section of the website. items.text: Minor Hotels appoints Karin Kopano as Managing Director of The Wolseley Hotel New York • Hotel Designs Minor Hotels appoints Karin Kopano as Managing Director of The Wolseley Hotel New York WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 23, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Minor Hotels appoints Karin Kopano as Managing Director of The Wolseley Hotel New York Minor Hotels has appointed Karin Kopano as Managing Director of The Wolseley Hotel New York, leading the property’s pre-opening strategy and operational planning ahead of its opening in Q2 2027… In her role as Managing Director, Karin Kopano is responsible for the opening and operation of the 77-room hotel at 130 West 44th Street in Midtown Manhattan. The property will bring together guest accommodation, destination dining at The Wolseley New York, the brand’s first United States location and the culinary flagship for North America, wellness facilities and private membership at The Wolseley New York Members Club. Image credit: Minor Hotels Kopano brings extensive experience across hotel openings, operations, asset management, project delivery and talent development. Most recently, Kopano served as Managing Director of The Ned NoMad , where she oversaw strategy and operations across the members’ club, guest rooms and food and beverage businesses. Prior to that, Kopano was Managing Director of Hard Rock Hotel New York, where she led the opening and commercial strategy of the flagship property, including the development of its food and beverage programme. Her earlier career included pre-opening leadership roles for several hotel launches, including Proper Santa Monica, 50 Bowery, and Gansevoort Hotels. In 2018, Kopano was named General Manager of the Year by the American Hotel & Lodging Association. “The opportunity to introduce The Wolseley to New York through a property with such a rich cultural history is enormously exciting,” said Karin Kopano, Managing Director of The Wolseley Hotel New York. “130 West 44th Street has long been a gathering place for the city’s creative community. Our focus is on honouring that legacy while creating a contemporary hospitality experience that combines hotel accommodation, dining, wellness and private membership in a way that feels authentic to both The Wolseley and New York.” Kopano joins the project at a pivotal stage as Minor Hotels prepares to launch The Wolseley Hotels brand globally, extending The Wolseley’s celebrated restaurant heritage into a fully realised hotel experience. items.text: Mama Shelter Mexico City – a vibrant collision of design • Hotel Designs Mama Shelter Mexico City – a vibrant collision of design WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 20, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Mama Shelter Mexico City – a vibrant collision of design Mama Shelter’s first Latin American icon is arriving soon, and she’s already making waves as a major player in the brand’s global expansion, as Mama Shelter Mexico City prepares for its December opening… We Kept the Façade But Didn’t Follow the Rules: Set behind the grand, preserved façades of two historic 19th-century casonas on Avenida Álvaro Obregón, Mama Shelter Mexico City brings the brand’s signature mischief and irreverent spirit to Roma Norte, the capital’s coolest artistic playground. Here, Mama’s in-house design team teamed up with two local Mexican studios to turn traditional craftsmanship on its head, creating unconventional, eye-catching artefactos. The result? A vibrant collision of French-influenced historic architecture and bold contemporary design. Image credit: Mama Shelter At the hotel’s core, a lush, open-air courtyard acts as the ultimate social hub, where the building’s historic soul meets Mama’s festive energy. Across her 100 keys, details draw inspiration from Mexico’s mestizaje soul, pairing Mama’s playful touches and local street-art influences with warm colors and thoughtful references to everyday Mexican life. Walls are painted in a peach hue reminiscent of the shades found in traditional Mexican homes, bringing a familiar sense of warmth and character. Mirrors are adorned with the phrase “Mama te apapachó” – a take on the Mexican expression apapachar – to pamper, cuddle or shower someone with affection, as any good Mama does. Image credit: Mama Shelter Roma Norte Is About to Get a Whole Lot Saucier: At the heart of the hotel is Mama’s Trattoria & Bar, where Italian comfort food gets the full Mama treatment, with generous, large-format dishes designed for sharing. The open-air courtyard will be the heart of the hotel, with a calendar of events spanning DJ sets, live bands and stand-up shows by emerging local comedians. Think of Mama as Roma Norte’s living room – a place for locals and hotel guests to gather, connect and feel at ease, with programming ranging from artist showcases to local run club meetups. Image credit: Mama Shelter Looking ahead, a spectacular rooftop is set to debut in spring 2027, while flexible ateliers for creative workshops, epic celebrations, and a Wellness Studio on the first floor round out Mama’s new Mexican home. Furry Friends Are Always on the Guest List: Embracing Mama’s typical dog-friendly approach and Mexico’s beloved perrhijo culture, Mama Shelter Mexico City welcomes canine companions. Guests can expect considered touches, including water bowls and a welcoming atmosphere where pups are just as much a part of the party as their humans. items.text: When wellness becomes experience: LEMI’s Vibro-Acoustic Vision • Hotel Designs When wellness becomes experience: LEMI’s Vibro-Acoustic Vision WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 20, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio When wellness becomes experience: LEMI’s Vibro-Acoustic Vision Wellness has evolved beyond the concept of a simple treatment, becoming a complete experience that engages the body, mind, and senses. From this understanding comes LEMI’s vision – transforming professional comfort into a profound sensory ritual, where technology and human sensitivity coexist in perfect harmony… At the heart of this philosophy lies vibro-acoustic technology, a system that allows music to be perceived not only through hearing, but also through the body. Thanks to Vibro-Music technology , sound frequencies are transformed into vibrations that travel through the contact surface, creating sensory stimulation that accompanies the listening experience. Sound takes on a new dimension: it is no longer simply something to hear, but becomes a physical sensation capable of promoting relaxation, releasing tension, and guiding the mind toward a state of deep calm. The innovation behind Vibro-Music lies in its ability to create a direct connection between sound and bodily perception, transforming the mattress into a multisensory wellness experience. Harmonic vibrations are gently transmitted throughout the body, accompanying the melodies and enhancing their emotional dimension. Unlike traditional massage, which relies on mechanical action, the vibro-acoustic experience engages the individual through physically perceptible sound frequencies, creating a unique sensation of immersion and continuity between listening and tactile stimulation. Image credit: LEMI LEMI technology also offers five different vibration programs, featuring specific frequencies ranging from 40 to 86 Hz, allowing users to explore different bodily sensations and relaxation experiences. Through the dedicated Vibro-Music app, available for iOS and Android devices, users can select their preferred program and adjust the vibration intensity, personalizing the experience according to individual preferences. This flexibility allows the technology to be integrated into a variety of wellness rituals, from deeply relaxing treatments to experiences designed to restore energy and promote sensory balance. The possibility of combining music, vibrations, and other sensory stimuli opens up new perspectives for the spa industry, where every treatment can become a personalized journey, engaging guests on a deeper and more memorable level. This vision takes shape in two iconic products: Milano EVO and Harmony Lounge, distinct yet complementary interpretations of immersive wellness. Image credit: LEMI Milano EVO embodies the perfect balance between technology, ergonomics, and design. Its Memory Foam mattress adapts to the body’s contours, providing a sensation of support and softness, while Vibro-Music technology transforms music into gentle vibrations that can be felt throughout the treatment. Chromotherapy and the integrated heating system, available in specific configurations, further enhance the experience, combining light, sound, and warmth in a multisensory journey. Minimalist lines, customizable finishes, and the excellence of Italian craftsmanship make Milano EVO a distinctive centerpiece in the most exclusive wellness environments. Image credit: LEMI Harmony Lounge, on the other hand, embodies the art of taking a mindful pause. Designed to provide a prolonged relaxation experience, it embraces the body through ergonomic shapes and an electric tilting movement that gently guides the individual into a position of maximum comfort. In the Premium version, vibro-acoustic technology is combined with integrated heating, adding an immersive dimension that transforms music listening into a physical experience, inviting the body to slow down, let go, and rediscover its natural balance. In both products, technology is not simply an additional feature, but becomes an integral part of the experience, creating a harmonious dialogue between technological innovation and human sensitivity. This is LEMI’s interpretation of contemporary luxury: not excess, but care, precision, and attention to the individual. Because true wellness is not simply about feeling welcomed, but about rediscovering the pleasure of being fully present. LEMI is one of our Recommended Suppliers and regularly features in our Supplier News section of the website. If you are interested in becoming one of our Recommended Suppliers, please email Katy Phillips. items.text: Hotel bathroom wall renovation for operational value • Hotel Designs Hotel bathroom wall renovation for operational value WORDS BY Sienna Shipton November 20, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Hotel bathroom wall renovation for operational value In 2026, hotel renovations remain a priority to boost profitability worldwide. Operators want projects completed quickly. At the same time, they want the outcome to be beautiful and functional… And the wall, as the largest surface in a hotel bathroom, plays a critical role. When a renovation is executed right, it can elevate guest satisfaction while reducing operational costs. There are several factors to be considered to make the renovation successful. Reducing Room Downtime Tiling and waterproofing traditional bathroom walls is one of the most time-consuming parts of a hotel renovation project. Traditional tiling can take up to a week per room. This process requires intensive skilled labor and project costs while locking away booking revenue. To eliminate this bottleneck, hotels are switching to modern material that can achieve design goals without the time spent on tiling and grouting . Using large format waterproof bathroom panels reduces the number of individual pieces installers handle. This can significantly cut installation timeline and improve project turnaround. For example, in a recent hotel renovation project with FastPanel SPC wall panel, contractors renovated 59 bathrooms in only two weeks, averaging 30 rooms per week. Image credit: STEP GUARD Floors & Walls Withstanding Daily Use Hotel bathrooms experience much harsher daily wear than residential bathrooms. Housekeeping carts and guest use frequently cause surface impact. Wall materials that chip, scratch, or crack easily mean hotel management will spend time and money on repairs or replacement. Selecting a rigid, waterproof wall surface protects the property investment long term. Durable wall materials will protect the underlying structure while maintaining a fresh finish after years of use, keeping guest satisfaction high. Easy Cleaning Clean bathrooms protect your guest experience, but the wrong wall material drains your cleaning budget. Traditional tiled walls trap grime and moisture inside grout lines. Natural stone, which is a more luxury choice, needs constant resealing to stay fresh. Grout-free wall surfaces offer a smarter alternative. Housekeeping staff can wipe down large surfaces quickly using standard mild cleaners. This streamlined cleaning process cuts down room turnaround times while ensuring a hygienic environment that protects brand reputation. Image credit: STEP GUARD Floors & Walls Creating Strong Brand Identity with Bathroom Walls In 2026, hotel bathrooms play a major role in how guests feel about a property. A beautiful, well-designed bathroom makes guests feel cared for and confirms they chose the right place to stay. Choosing a wall finish that matches your brand personality leaves a lasting, positive impression. Across different hotel styles, nature-inspired looks lead this shift toward a calm, spa-like atmosphere. Stone-inspired surfaces bring warm, organic beauty into the room, while surface tactility makes the space feel unique and inviting. FastPanel SPC Wall Panel for Hotel Bathroom Renovations STEP GUARD Flooring provides an effective solution for hotel remodel projects seeking speed, performance, and style. The system combines rapid click installation, 100% waterproof protection, and low-maintenance durability with thoughtful designs. Beyond hospitality, FastPanel SPC wall panels offer beautifully designed waterproof interior walls for bathrooms, kitchens, residential renovations, modular housing, real estate projects, and other commercial projects. To solve the conflict between project deadlines and labor shortages, FastPanel SPC panels are designed for fast renovation. Large-format FastPanel SPC wall cladding is up to 2800 x 1200mm, covering entire bathroom walls in just a few pieces. Contractor teams can install FastPanel SPC panel directly over old tiles without demolition. This eliminates noise, keeps neighbouring rooms functional, and cuts installation downtime. Image credit: STEP GUARD Floors & Walls Beyond speed, FastPanel SPC wall panels feature a rigid core that withstands heavy impacts and moisture penetration. Its grout-free tongue-and-groove joints prevent water penetration and mould growth, letting housekeeping wipe down surfaces quickly with only mild cleaners. To support hospitality branding, FastPanel SPC panel offers wood, stone, marble, and tile looks with matte, gloss, slate, and linear textures. Hotel operators can also pair FastPanel SPC panels with matching STEP GUARD SPC flooring for a cohesive, high-end guest experience. Modern hotel renovations require speed, durability, and low maintenance. Adopting STEP GUARD FastPanel SPC wall panel shortens project timelines, simplifies daily operations, and improves the guest experience. STEP GUARD is one of our Recommended Suppliers and regularly features in our Supplier News section of the website. If you are interested in becoming one of our Recommended Suppliers, please email Katy Phillips. items.text: Treehouse puts down roots in Adelaide • Hotel Designs Treehouse puts down roots in Adelaide WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 20, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Treehouse puts down roots in Adelaide Treehouse Hotels is branching out to Adelaide as the brand’s first hotel in Australia and the Asia-Pacific region – set above the new Market Square development, the property brings Treehouse’s playful, easygoing spirit to the heart of this lush city… Treehouse is made for guests who like to feel at home while following their curiosity. In Adelaide, that spirit takes shape in a shared living-room arrival, rooms rich with local character and nostalgia, nooks made for intimate hideaways, and a restaurant celebrating the flavors of South Australia’s farms and wine regions. With the Adelaide Central Market right next door, the hotel has one of the city’s great food destinations on its doorstep and the rest of Adelaide within easy reach. “Treehouse has lived in my imagination for years as a place that feels more like a home than a hotel: comfortable, welcoming, and just a little unexpected. Treehouse Hotels are a happy place for every child—a place of imagination, friendship, and endless fun. That’s our Treehouse vision,” commented Treehouse Creator, Barry Sternlicht. “Adelaide gives us a wonderful setting to bring that feeling to life. The gardens, local artisans, and rich food scene give the city an energy and generosity where Treehouse feels very much at home.” Image credit: Treehouse Adelaide Designed by Woods Bagot, the global architecture and design firm founded in Adelaide, in partnership with the Starwood Hotels design team, the hotel takes cues from the energy and history of the Adelaide Central Market, as well as the city’s Park Lands and Botanic Gardens. Leafy terraces bring Adelaide’s green spaces into the hotel, while handcrafted finishes, market-crate details, and collected objects nod to local makers and traders. “We never want a Treehouse Hotel to feel as though it could have been picked up and placed in any other city,” said Raul Leal, CEO of Starwood Hotels. “In Adelaide, the gardens and the incredible produce have shaped the hotel from the inside out. This may be our first Treehouse in Australia, but when the doors open, we want it to feel as though it has always belonged here.” The hotel’s arrival experience is conceived as a shared living room rather than a formal hotel lobby, with a communal check-in lounge and plenty of soul, inviting guests to settle in from the start. The creative vibe carries into the 248 guest rooms, where Australian wool plaids, textured timber, checkerboard tables, and collected furnishings create spaces loaded with personality. A cuckoo clock offers a playful nod to Hahndorf, a village in the Adelaide Hills known for its German heritage. Oversized windows frame views of the city skyline, hills, or distant coastline. Image credit: Treehouse Adelaide Nearly one in five rooms is configured as a twin, with two beds—giving friends, family members, and colleagues more flexibility when traveling together. Accessible rooms, including options for guests with vision or hearing impairments, are also available. The hotel’s 10 suites offer even more room to spread out and stay awhile. The sprawling Hideaway Suite—the hotel’s signature suite—features a balcony, retro botanical wallpaper, and a powder room. At the top of the hotel, the Canopy Suite is a generous retreat with its own balcony, dining space, a discreet butler’s pantry, and a powder room. An oversized, cushioned daybed takes the place of a sofa, adding a relaxed, playful note to the expansive living area. Patterned wallpaper and furnishings with botanical motifs inspired by local flora complete the look. The food and beverage experience will draw on the abundance of Adelaide Central Market and South Australia’s local produce. Leading the culinary program is Executive Chef Nick Tadija, who brings more than 20 years of experience to the role, including time in Michelin-starred kitchens in London. His approach is shaped by Italian culinary traditions, the seasons, and his connection to South Australia’s Slow Food movement. Image credit: Treehouse Adelaide The hotel’s signature restaurant, Little Lemon, will pair the warmth of Italian hospitality with the daily rhythms of Adelaide Central Market next door. The restaurant’s greenhouse-inspired interiors draw inspiration from Adelaide’s Victorian-era glasshouses and the charm of a working potting shed. Vintage accents and abundant greenery bring a garden-like quality to the room, while an open kitchen gives guests a view of the chefs at work. A private dining room takes its cues from farmhouse gatherings, with a long table made for sharing food and conversation. Four flexible event spaces offer more than 500 square metres for meetings, weddings, and all kinds of celebrations. Natural light, adaptable layouts, and state-of-the-art audiovisual technology allow the rooms to shift with the occasion, whether that means a boardroom session, a banquet, or a cocktail gathering. Wellness at Treehouse is about making room for what feels good to each guest: keeping up a familiar routine, trying something different, or taking a pause between city adventures. The property’s expansive, 205-square-metre gym features the latest-generation Technogym cardio and strength equipment, Technogym Visio for interactive workouts, and Peloton bikes. The hotel will also be the first in Australia to feature Technogym Pilates Reform beds. With a generous, light-filled layout framed by views across the city and toward the coast and ample room to train, guests have plenty of space to move at their own pace. items.text: Hyde & Seek – blending Victorian grandeur with a distinctly bohemian spirit • Hotel Designs Hyde & Seek – blending Victorian grandeur with a distinctly bohemian spirit WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 19, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Hyde & Seek – blending Victorian grandeur with a distinctly bohemian spirit Hyde & Seek, London Hyde Park, a Tribute Portfolio Hotel, has recently opened, following a £42 million transformation, bringing 309 guestrooms, design-led interiors and two new dining destinations to London… Located at 1 Lancaster Gate, the 309-room Hyde & Seek is a blend of bold design , modern comfort with interiors inspired by the natural beauty of one of London’s most iconic green spaces. Image credit: Hyde & Seek Situated on the doorstep of Hyde Park and within easy reach of Paddington, Mayfair and Oxford Street, Hyde & Seek has been designed as a tranquil urban escape, balancing the buzz of the city with the calm of its park side setting. The hotel is within walking distance of some of London’s best-known attractions, such as Kensington Palace, Marble Arch, Little Venice, Oxford Street and the West End. The hotel’s interiors have been curated by acclaimed interior designer Goddard Littlefair , alongside architect Unwin Jones Partnership, drawing inspiration from the bohemian culture of the neighbourhood during the 1960s and 70s. Influences from creatives including Zandra Rhodes, Ossie Clark, David Hockney and David Hicks can be seen throughout the property, with bold colour pairings, rich textures and abstract patterns sitting alongside heritage detailing and Victorian architectural references. Image credit: Hyde & Seek A distinctive palette of reclaimed oak, honed white marble, antique brass and handcrafted Moroccan tiles adds warmth and character throughout the hotel. The design also reflects the hotel’s prime location, drawing inspiration from Hyde Park’s natural beauty with greens and blues used throughout to bring the outside in. Guests can choose from 309 guestrooms and suites, each with its own distinctive design, combining vibrant interiors with modern furnishings. Every room features smart TVs, coffee machines, complimentary Grown Alchemist toiletries and stylish seating nooks, while suites offer more spacious layouts, providing enhanced comfort for guests. Family Hydeaway and Townhouse Suites also include Toto Washlet smart toilets , inspired by Japanese bathroom technology, offering heated seats, integrated bidet functionality and personalised wash settings. Image credit: Hyde & Seek Led by Executive Head Chef Ranjitkumar Sukumaran, the hotel also debuts two distinctive food and beverage concepts, designed to serve both hotel guests and the local community. Seekers Restaurant & Bar offers a contemporary British dining experience overlooking Hyde Park, serving breakfast, lunch, dinner and afternoon tea. The restaurant also features a spacious bar focused on inventive cocktails and relaxed social occasions. HydeOut, the hotel’s all-day café lounge and co-working space, provides a relaxed setting for morning coffee, casual dining, meetings and evening drinks beneath a striking glass-roof. Guests can also enjoy a fully equipped, state-of-the-art gym featuring premium Life Fitness equipment, alongside two flexible meeting rooms, available to book separately or together as a duo for those needing more space. The rooms are ideal for small board meetings and private dinner parties and events. Image credit: Hyde & Seek Andrew Khoo, Chairman of Immersive Hospitality Management, commented: “The opening of Hyde & Seek, London Hyde Park, a Tribute Portfolio Hotel, represents an exciting new chapter for Immersive Hospitality Management and the culmination of an ambitious transformation project. We’re incredibly proud to be bringing new life to such an iconic London building and creating a hotel that celebrates the character, creativity and diversity of this unique neighbourhood” Paul Davies, General Manager of Hyde & Seek, London Hyde Park, a Tribute Portfolio Hotel, added: “We’re looking forward to welcoming our very first guests this September and introducing them to a hotel that’s full of personality. Whether joining us for a weekend in London, afternoon tea overlooking Hyde Park, cocktails with friends or simply somewhere to relax after exploring the city, we want every guest to feel genuinely at home and leave with a memorable experience.” Main image credit: Hyde & Seek You might also like Case study: Alpine architecture and Japanese bathing culture from TOTO Bathrooms / 10.06.2026 Artiq unveils a sensory art journey at Six Senses London Art / 13.04.2026 Hilton London Bankside unveils its multi-million-pound expansion News / 23.12.2025 SPACE: the latest issue In video Latest articles Product watch: Xuniva Evo from hansgrohe sets the tone in the bathroom 23.11.2026 Minor Hotels appoints Karin Kopano as Managing Director of The Wolseley Hotel New York 23.11.2026 Mama Shelter Mexico City – a vibrant collision of design 20.11.2026 When wellness becomes experience: LEMI’s Vibro-Acoustic Vision 20.11.2026 Hotel bathroom wall renovation for operational value 20.11.2026 Receive our newsletter here Recommended suppliers Latest from the DESIGN POD Episode 50: Grant Woodrow – into the Wilderness 03.06.2025 Episode 49: Fettle, the transatlantic design studio with Andy Goodwin and Tom Parker 14.03.2025 Episode 48: Redesigning Historic Buildings with Tom Thorogood 10.01.2025 Episode 47: Form and Function with Nick Hickson 20.12.2024 Episode 46: 40 Years in the Making – David Collins Studio with Lewis Taylor 22.11.2024 Recommended suppliers Upcoming events The Brit List Awards 5th November, 2026 Hotel Summit 22nd April, 2027 This website uses cookies to improve your experience. items.text: Marriott unpacks its Branded Residential pipeline • Hotel Designs Marriott unpacks its Branded Residential pipeline WORDS BY Pauline Brettell November 19, 2026 Atkinson Phillip Jeffries Sanderson ADA Grohe Balsan Harrison Spinks Hypnos Lemi Schulter Soho Lighting WISA Zennio Marriott unpacks its Branded Residential pipeline Marriott International, has announced that the company’s branded residential open and pipeline portfolio across Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA) has reached 115 open and pipeline properties… This milestone, fueled by strong growth momentum in 2026, with 25 residential agreements signed across EMEA year-to-date, underscores the continued demand for luxury and premium branded living experiences across the region. Marriott also expanded its branded residential portfolio into new markets this year including Italy, France and Uzbekistan. Jaidev Menezes, Regional Vice President, Mixed-Use Development, EMEA commented, “Achieving 115 open and pipeline branded residential properties across EMEA is a defining milestone for the company’s regional growth, built on the strength of our brands, the trust of our owners and the growing appetite for distinctive branded living. The demand we are seeing for branded living is significant, and we are proud to work with exceptional developers across the region.” Image credit: W Residences Manchester Marriott has grown its open branded residential portfolio in EMEA by nearly 60% in the last three years, and today its total portfolio across the region encompasses 36 open properties and nearly 80 in the pipeline, across 23 countries and territories. The EMEA region currently represents 37 percent of the company’s global residential pipeline. Marriott’s leading luxury brand portfolio continues to be a significant driver of the company’s growth in the residential segment in the region. Approximately 75 percent of the company’s residential agreements signed in EMEA this year have been associated with Marriott’s luxury brands, reflecting continued demand from developers and residential buyers for luxury living experiences. The United Kingdom continues to be an important market for Marriott’s branded residential portfolio, with three open properties in London spanning the company’s luxury and premium brands including The Residences at The Westin London City and The Lucan, Autograph Collection Residences. The company plans to expand its residential portfolio in the market with three luxury projects in the pipeline, including W Residences Manchester which is anticipated to open in 2027. The W Residences Manchester will be co-located to the W Hotel and will feature the brand’s signature spaces – Living Room, Wet Deck, Away Spa and FIT. The residences are located within No. 1 St. Michael’s featuring offices, retail and dining. Nearly 90 per cent of the units within W Residences Manchester have been sold. Image credit: St Regis Hotels & Resorts Signing highlights in the region spanned across the company’s luxury branded residential portfolio in 2026 include The Residences at The St. Regis Limassol (Cyprus), Palacio Residencial Sagasta, a Luxury Collection Residence, Madrid (Spain), The Residences at The St. Regis Marbella Resort (Spain) and JW Marriott Residences Abu Dhabi Yas Island (UAE). Residential growth in the region is also extending across Marriott’s premium portfolio, as consumer interest in branded living expands beyond luxury demographics. Recent agreements include Westin Residences Dubai Creek Gardens (UAE), Renaissance Residences Dubai Creek Gardens (UAE), Autograph Collection Residences, Ras Al Hekma (Egypt) and Sixteen Eighteen, Sheikh Zayed City, Cairo, a Tribute Portfolio Residence (Egypt). Marriott’s residential growth is driving opportunities to introduce branded living to new markets across EMEA. This year, the company expanded its residential pipeline into Italy with an agreement for the W Residences Sardinia – Poltu Quatu, in France with The Residences at Port Marseillan, a Luxury Collection Resort & Spa, Marseillan and into Uzbekistan with JW Marriott Residences in Tashkent. Image credit: The Residences at Port Marseillan In addition to the signed projects this year, the company anticipates opening six branded residences in the region by the end of 2026: • The St. Regis Residences Financial Center Road, Dubai (UAE) – Features breathtaking 360-degree views and located in Downtown Dubai minutes away from Burj Khalifa. • Expansion of Marriott Residences Al Barsha South, Dubai (UAE) – Designed as a serene retreat from city life. • The Residences at The St. Regis Belgrade (Serbia) – Situated inside the iconic Kula Belgrade skyscraper on the Belgrade waterfront. • Phase 1 of Marriott Residences Heliopolis (Egypt) – Offers an elevated lifestyle experience with Cairo’s first rooftop clubhouse. • The Ritz-Carlton Residences, Diriyah (Saudi Arabia) – Marks the Kingdom’s first branded residential community located near the historic At-Turaif UNESCO World Heritage site. • Sabàtic Sitges, Autograph Collection Residences (Spain) – Comprises exclusive residences in Sitges where luxury meets the Mediterranean, just 25 minutes away from Barcelona Airport.
