items.summary: Downtown LA landmark the Original Pantry Cafe, which closed in March 2025 after more than a century of operation, is back. The diner reopens today, November 19, 2026, under new ownership and in partnership with Hope the Mission, a nonprofit that works to reduce poverty, hunger, and housing insecurity.  The Original Pantry Cafe first opened […]
items.text: LA Restaurant Openings Downtown LA Landmark the Original Pantry Cafe Comes Back to Life The historic restaurant reopens with a new Hope the Mission partnership by Rebecca Roland Nov 19, 2026, 7:30 PM UTC Facebook Link Image: French toast. | The Original Pantry Cafe Rebecca Roland is the deputy editor of the Southern California/Southwest region, who covers the evolving landscape of LA’s food scene. Facebook Link Downtown LA landmark the Original Pantry Cafe, which closed in March 2025 after more than a century of operation, is back. The diner reopens today , November 19, 2026, under new ownership and in partnership with Hope the Mission, a nonprofit that works to reduce poverty, hunger, and housing insecurity. The Original Pantry Cafe first opened at Ninth and Francisco Streets in 1924 as a 24-hour diner, before moving to its current location on Figueroa in 1950. In 1981, then- Los Angeles mayor Richard Riordan bought the restaurant and operated it until his death in 2023. Over the decades, it became a beloved destination for its around-the-clock service, retro interior, and breakfast plates like ham and eggs. In March 2025, the restaurant suddenly closed due to a dispute between unionized workers and its owner, the Richard J. Riordan family trust . Pancakes. The Original Pantry Cafe In September 2025, Leo Pustilnikov, a real estate entrepreneur, bought the Original Pantry Cafe ; at a press conference held alongside Unite Here 11 , the union that represents the Pantry’s workers, he announced he would recognize the union as part of the deal . “The pantry is sort of like the story of LA,” Pustilnikov said at the press conference. “It’s had its ups and downs, and hopefully the reopening will boost the rebirth of Downtown with everything coming to it.” Kenneth Small, the Pantry’s new general manager, says it’s been an “honor” to bring back the historic landmark alongside the non-profit. “Hope the Mission is kind of the white knight in this,” he says. “They revived a lost landmark, and we’re reopening with a new purpose.” Over the last six months, Small has worked to inject life back into the restaurant, whether that meant updating the point-of-sale systems or rifling through pictures and artifacts in storage to hang on the walls. “It was rebuilding a shell of a restaurant back into something that works in 2026 or 2027,” Small says. “The highest technology in the building was a landline phone.” The reopening menu straddles old and new with the return of favorites such as the ham, steak and eggs, the Pantry Breakfast platter, and French toast, alongside new dishes including breakfast tacos. “We wanted to let people know the Pantry is back, so we wanted to honor the old menu and have some familiar items on there,” Small says. “People’s comments online [were] all across the board — people love the food nostalgia-wise, but maybe execution- and consistency-wise, people had concerns.” The updated menu will use all fresh produce, plus add items including meatloaf in a gochujang chile glaze and a chicken banh mi. “We’re opening with a tight core menu just to find our footing, and then we plan to introduce more of the traditional items they had on the special board,” Small says. The Pantry’s union staff will also return. “The Pantry is a building, the Pantry is the food, but the core identity of the Pantry is the workers that have served guests, provided hospitality, and amazing food for decades to people,” Small says. “To me, that’s part of the core identity, and having these people return is an intrinsic part of the reopening.” For now, the Original Pantry Cafe will operate from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. Sunday to Thursday, and 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. Friday and Saturday, but Small says the goal is to return to the full 24-hour-a-day, seven-days-a-week operation: “The Pantry is not really back until it’s 24 hours.” Omelet and hash browns. The Original Pantry Cafe Spread of dishes. The Original Pantry Cafe Exterior. The Original Pantry Cafe Cheeseburger. items.text: LA Restaurant Openings Ensenada’s Cult-Favorite La Morocha Lands in the Arts District This Week Chef David Castro Hussong’s Baja-inflected restaurant opens Thursday with the team behind Daisy Margarita Bar by Mona Holmes Photography by Matt Egan Nov 18, 2026, 11:00 PM UTC Facebook Link Image: Almeja clams with seaweed at La Morocha in the Arts District. | Matt Egan Mona Holmes is an editor at Eater Southern California/Southwest, a regular contributor at KCRW radio, and a 2022 James Beard Award nominee. Facebook Link David Castro Hussong, the chef behind Valle de Guadalupe’s acclaimed Fauna , will bring a charismatic newcomer to the Arts District on Thursday, November 19. Hussong and his award-winning pastry chef wife, Maribel Aldaco Silva, partnered with the team behind Daisy Margarita Bar , Gilbert Pérez Bar , and Mírate , to bring his famed Ensenada destination, La Morocha Resta Bar, to Los Angeles. La Morocha will be the first U.S. restaurant from the chef, who also operates La Pantera Asador and El Tigre Silencioso in Mexico City. La Morocha will reside in the brand new multi-use building adjacent to Bavel and Girl & the Goat . Castro Hussong and Aldaco Silva will serve a menu that leans heavily on seafood, tacos, and a whimsical LA-Baja take on pizza, while showcasing Castro Hussong’s childhood favorites. “La Morocha speaks to how we eat now throughout California,” says Castro Hussong. “I believe that Ensenada food is closer to California than the rest of Mexico. Our comfort foods are also Angelenos’ comfort food.” After opening Valle de Guadalupe’s Fauna Restaurant in 2018, Castro Hussong debuted Bruma Wine Garden in 2020, then Mexico City’s El Tigre and El Tigrillo in 2023. His first project in Ensenada was La Morocha in 2023. Castro Hussong tells Eater that he wants to illustrate the closeness between Baja and California at the Los Angeles location, given his childhood, when he ate plenty of pizza and apple pie with ice cream. La Morocha serves Peruvian tiraditos, tostadas, aguachile, clam seaweed salad, Baja oysters with clarified pico de gallo and olive oil, and a chile relleno taco; eggplant Milanesa, and a braised duck leg quesadilla with consomé. La Morocha’s “picza” crust is a slightly puffy blend of tostada and pizza; the picza gets topped with fresh crab in a beurre blanc, chives, and lemon. Wood-fired options include charred sweet potato with pasilla and peanuts, fish in adobo, and two types of carne asada: a 14-ounce New York strip and a 28-ounce porterhouse. “Picza” crab pizza in a beurre blanc, chives, and lemon. Matt Egan La Morocha’s pastry chef, Aldaco Silva, was the 2023 recipient of Latin America’s Best Pastry Chef award. In the Arts District, she will serve a pixtle cheesecake, which uses processed mamey tree seed, native to Central America, for a sweet, custardy dessert, along with a coffee-laced churro and a Mexican cinnamon macaroon with plantain ice cream. An admitted ice cream aficionado, Aldaco Silva put a mango and passion fruit sorbet crowned with coconut granita and coconut flakes on the menu. La Morocha’s cocktail program is led by Marcos Pulido, who trained under Max Reis (Daisy Margarita Bar). The extensive menu combines elements of Baja California and the Mediterranean with produce, herbs, and hints of wood smoke. Drinks include a honeydew melon and mint margarita; the Koko Canela with roasted pineapple, coconut horchata, and a blend of Mexican and Caribbean rums; and a michelada with a shrimp consomé, Clamato, Salsa Marisquera sauce, and Pacifico. Sommelier Felicia Chavez (Surf & Sand Laguna Beach and formerly Gracias Madre ) built the wine menu around Mexican producers, with a heavy emphasis on Valle de Guadalupe; also find bottles from Italy, Spain, France, and California. A highlight of the lineup is a grenache, syrah, and mourvèdre blend prepared just for La Morocha by noted sommelier Lulu Martinez Ojeda of Bruma Winery. Restaurateur Matt Egan brought on Adean Studios’ Alexa Nafisi-Movaghar for the design; the duo previously partnered on Egan’s projects including Daisy Margarita Bar, Gilbert Pérez Bar, and Mírate. La Morocha features a custom open kitchen, built-ins lined with plants, a 165-person dining room, private dining room, and a 39-seat patio. Lighter elements, including reclaimed wood, burlap accents throughout, custom banquettes, and hanging lights, add to the charm. Other familiar faces are at La Morocha with Randy Evans and Brian Kang, whose operations experience at Daisy Margarita Bar, Gilbert Pérez Bar, and Mírate will help bring the restaurant to life. Castro Hussong and Aldaco Silva have been splitting their time between Baja and Los Angeles. The couple have spent years building their skills in Mexican and U.S. restaurants, and have recently been introducing their children to Los Angeles culture. He wants to give back to Los Angeles with La Morocha. “I did my training in fine dining already,” says Castro Hussong. “When we opened Fauna, I wanted a place where I could sit down and eat. This is exactly how I like to sit down and eat, and enjoy time with my family. I hated cooking at places where my mom couldn’t afford to eat. If you’re in flip-flops and shorts, you can feel comfortable.” Starting November 19, La Morocha will open Sunday to Thursday from 5 p.m. to 11 p.m., and until midnight on Friday and Saturday at 532 Mateo Street, Arts District, CA, 90013. Brunch will follow in the coming months. Aguachile rojo. Matt Egan Clam seaweed almeja. Matt Egan Baja-style taco. Matt Egan Costilla macaroni and cheese. Matt Egan Pixtle cheesecake. The once-weekly stand has blossomed into a full restaurant where Jaquez piles his signature birria into tortillas for tacos, mulitas, and more, alongside new vegetable-forward dishes that spotlight Los Angeles’s […]
items.text: Dining Reports Birria Is Just the Beginning at El Sereno’s Birria Pa La Cruda ﻿Carlos Jaquez has found a permanent home for his birria pop-up by Rebecca Roland Nov 18, 2026, 7:30 PM UTC Facebook Link Birria and mushroom tacos at Birria Pa La Cruda. Rebecca Roland Rebecca Roland is the deputy editor of the Southern California/Southwest region, who covers the evolving landscape of LA’s food scene. In our Dining Reports, we share a firsthand perspective of a recent restaurant visit, covering everything from the vibe to must-get dishes. See more in the Eater app. Download the app Carlos Jaquez’s Birria Pa La Cruda has opened a permanent home on the same El Sereno lot where it has operated its pop-up since 2019. The once-weekly stand has blossomed into a full restaurant where Jaquez piles his signature birria into tortillas for tacos, mulitas, and more, alongside new vegetable-forward dishes that spotlight Los Angeles’s produce. The restaurant feels like a living, evolving platform for Los Angeles native Jaquez, who comes from an upscale dining background at restaurants such as Otium and Bestia , to showcase the breadth of his cooking and growth as a chef over the years. What to order Long-simmered birria — the backbone of the restaurant — is served in multiple forms, including tacos and cheese-laced mulitas. The birria braises in a chile-tinged red stock that becomes a rich, concentrated, restorative consomé true to the restaurant’s name: birria “for the hangover.” Jaquez uses masa from the local tortilleria Kernel of Truth to make pliant but still sturdy tortillas that stand up to the mountain of meat mounded on top. Top the birria with a few dollops of spicy and sharp, lacto-fermented habanero vinegar. Birria Pa La Cruda’s vegetarian option, mushrooms en salsa verde , stands out as an unlikely star on the menu. Currently, the dish employs organic maitake mushrooms from specialty producer Hokto, which retain a pleasantly chewy texture even submerged in salsa. The earthy, savory hits from the mushrooms play well with the salsa verde’s smoky-acidic, tomatillo-rich profile. A butternut squash tamal bathes in date mole, with squash blossoms and sage crowning the top. While the tamal’s ingredients change with the seasons, the version on the menu now captures the feeling of a brisk 60-degree California fall and the first crunchy leaves falling to the ground. The tamal is silky and slightly sweet from the squash, while the mole offers caramelly notes from the dates. The weekday-only wild rice bowl beds a choice of birria, mushrooms en salsa verde, or grilled chicken on chewy wild rice with guacamole, beans, pickled vegetables, and sweet tomatoes. The vibe The interior of Birria Pa La Cruda is fairly utilitarian, with an open kitchen where guests can watch Jaquez cook. The outdoor area is the star of the space, with an expansive, backyard-like patio, string lights that emit a warm glow, and sun shades. Insider tip Head to Birria Pa La Cruda on Saturdays and Sundays for the weekend-only mole-topped chilaquiles. Just be aware that the restaurant has earlier hours on weekends; it’s currently open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The takeaway Birria Pa La Cruda feels like the amalgam of Jaquez’s past experiences: Pieces of his pop-up, Bestia, Otium, and the farmers market-focused pop-up Teotl all live on the menu. Just a few months in, the flavors are well-tuned, and Jaquez’s attention to seasonality leaves room for dishes to grow and evolve. items.text: LA Restaurant Openings The Group Behind Santo and Seco Brings a Sleek New Rooftop Bar to Silver Lake The team debuted Saade on November 11 by Mona Holmes Nov 17, 2026, 11:44 PM UTC Facebook Link If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Image: Hollywood Hills view at Saade. | Justin Chung Mona Holmes is an editor at Eater Southern California/Southwest, a regular contributor at KCRW radio, and a 2022 James Beard Award nominee. Facebook Link The team behind Silver Lake hot spots Santo and Seco debuted the rooftop bar and restaurant Saade on November 11. The expansive views are a compelling draw, and so is the Lebanese- and Persian-inspired menu of meze, kebabs, and cocktails served directly above Sunset Boulevard. Over the last two years, Santo Hospitality Group has established itself in Silver Lake with the popular Seco wine bar and an outpost of Mexico City-based sushi spot Santo. Founder and partner Jos Gozain tells Eater that Saade is one of his most personal projects. Lebanese immigrants first began arriving in Mexico in the late 19th century; the Mexico-born restaurateur’s great-aunt, Adela Frangie, opened one of Mexico City’s first Lebanese restaurants, Restaurante Emir, nearly a century ago. “This is special to continue the tradition after almost 100 years of operation,” says Gozain. “To have a century’s worth of family legacy continue in a different country.” The restaurant group worked with chef Dave Potes (Seco and Okonomi in Brooklyn) to develop the menu alongside Persian American influencer Zoya Biglary. Meze options include pita, hummus, pistachio tabbouleh, charred shallot labneh, and the Persian eggplant dip kashk bademjan. A meal might start with tahini-laced shishito peppers, harissa carrots, and Kumamoto oysters with a harissa mignonette and mint oil, before moving onto a chipotle chicken kebab; braised lamb infused with mint, parsley, dill, tomato paste, and saikyo miso; and golden tahdig. For dessert, there’s labneh cheesecake drizzled with date syrup. Saade’s Persian and Lebanese influences come through in the cocktails, too. A caper berry martini gets extra dirty with a Persian pickle brine, while the Souk Spice Margarita blends tequila and mezcal with strawberry, hibiscus, cucumber, sumac, lime, and jalapeño. Apart from a Lebanese pilsner on the menu, Saade has steered mostly local with beer from the likes of Skyduster and Orange County’s woman-owned Phiella. Wines range from French to New Mexican to cava from Penedès. Non-alcoholic options include a chile margarita and a dragon fruit martini. Saade’s 1,800-square-foot space offers 15 bar seats and another 50 on the patio. Santo Hospitality worked with independent artists to bring the intimate space together, complete with moody lighting and handmade tiles. Studio 39:40’s Aysegul Ozar and Basak Atac spent three years on the bar’s design and buildout, while Jorge Maria Studio installed the extensive woodwork with built-ins. Set designer and painter Alexandra Cianciulli is behind the ceiling folk art and the nature mural with a lion and jaguar representing strength and protection. Gozain looks forward to sharing the flavors he grew up with at Saade, and joining Los Angeles’s vast options for Lebanese and Persian cooking. “When you grow up eating these types of foods, you have a very specific palate, and it’s very nostalgic,” says Gozain. “Your grandmother’s is the best food, better than anyone else’s. Saade’s is a contemporary, fun way and the same style of hospitality as Seco. Very casual, very focused on community, mingling, and getting to know people.” Saade is open from 5 p.m. to 11 p.m. Wednesday to Friday, and noon to 11 p.m. Saturday and Sunday at 3828 Sunset Boulevard, Silver Lake, CA, 90026. items.summary: The line between bar and restaurant continues to blur beautifully across Los Angeles. From Vandell in Los Feliz to Silver Lake’s Bar di Bello and Daisy Margarita Bar in the Valley, the latest crop of watering holes pay equal mind to what’s served on the plate and what’s poured in the glass. In Santa Monica, […]
items.text: Dining Reports Bar Fortuna Bets You Can’t Come Up With a Better Combo Than Pasta and Cocktails ﻿At chef Brian Bornemann’s new Santa Monica spot, Italian charm meets coastal ease by Cathy Chaplin Nov 17, 2026, 10:40 PM UTC Facebook Link Spaghetti with clams Cathy Chaplin Cathy Chaplin is a former senior editor at Eater LA, a James Beard Award–nominated journalist, and the author of Food Lovers’ Guide to Los Angeles. In our Dining Reports, we share a firsthand perspective of a recent restaurant visit, covering everything from the vibe to must-get dishes. See more in the Eater app. Download the app The line between bar and restaurant continues to blur beautifully across Los Angeles. From Vandell in Los Feliz to Silver Lake’s Bar di Bello and Daisy Margarita Bar in the Valley , the latest crop of watering holes pay equal mind to what’s served on the plate and what’s poured in the glass. In Santa Monica, chef Brian Bornemann’s Bar Fortuna is the latest to join the fray. Just a few weeks into opening, the dimly lit and narrow room already captures the ease and elegance of a seasoned neighborhood hub, drawing inspiration from the historic bars Bornemann frequented while learning to make pasta throughout Italy. While the heart of the operation is Italian, its soul is very much Californian. The kitchen sources its ingredients from the Golden State, from the vibrant produce on seasonal small plates to the larger-format proteins anchoring the secondi. Gemeli Cathy Chaplin Terracotta. Cathy Chaplin What to order The pleasure of twirling one’s fork into a hot bowl of handmade noodles while buzzing from an expertly made cocktail is unparalleled. Start with one of the five Negronis on offer. The namesake La Fortuna will please purists, while the Terracotta satisfies tequila-loving rebels. For a non-Negroni option that’s strong yet balanced, get the Sophia with gin, Pineau des Charentes, crème de noyaux, and blood orange bitters. Next, order as many pastas as the table can handle; each serving is precisely portioned to 90 grams. Classic spaghetti alle vongole, dotted with barely cooked clams and tasting of the ocean, packs a more-savory-than-anticipated punch. Squid and its ink take center stage in the fettuccine, tossed in a zingy tomato sauce with plenty of rings and tentacles; lemon zest and fennel fronds brighten the bowl. Bar Fortuna’s team makes the pastas with Sonora wheat sourced from Tehachapi Grain Project. The flour’s nutty flavor and texture really come through in the gemelli with Italian sausage, fennel pollen, grapes, and rosemary. For a closer to remember, order the warm sticky toffee pudding inspired by the flavors of tiramisu. Best seat in the house The 14 stools lining the marble-topped bar are the place to be. Whether seated in front of the open kitchen or closer to the bar, going elbow to elbow with fellow diners makes for a lively night and potentially grade A eavesdropping. Entry. Catherine Dzilenski Insider tip Save room for the One Cedar cocktail as a post-dinner digestif. Crafted by bar director Noah Castellanos — who owns the namesake coffee shop just a mile away — this clarified iced latte is an ideal nightcap, layered with autumnal notes of fig, apple, cinnamon, and orange. items.text: Dining Out in Miami Where to Eat at Miami International Airport (MIA) A guide to the croquetas, cafecitos, mojitos, and all the best food at Miami International Airport (MIA) by Alona Martinez , Olee Fowler , and Henna Bakshi Updated Nov 19, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC Facebook Link Grab pastelitos, croquetas, and Cuban sandwiches at La Carreta at D Gate. Photo by: Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images Part Of The Ultimate Visitor’s Guide to Eating in Miami see all Earlier this year, Food & Wine ranked Miami International Airport (MIA) eighth among the country’s best airports for food and drink. How could they not, when the airport’s home to cafecitos from Café Versailles, Cuban sandwiches from La Carreta, croquetas from Estefan Kitchen Express, and cold mojitos from Ku-Va? The airport has made it even easier to order food with MIA2GO, which offers hungry travelers a contactless way to order, pay, and arrange to pick up food through the website and the official mobile app. You can search by food type and airport terminal, and then schedule orders for pickup to skip the line. Whether you’re grabbing a quick bite or settling in for a meal before takeoff, here’s where to eat at MIA. A classic Cuban sandwich from La Carreta La Carreta North Terminal (Concourse D) American Airlines is the king of MIA, and it shows in its splashy terminal. It boasts the most food options of any terminal in the airport, which makes it a good bet for hungry travelers. Notable options: Cafe Versailles — There’s nothing like a shot of Cuban coffee at Versailles after a long haul, or heck, before a long haul if so inclined. Cuban sandwiches and clamor en español are a burst of local culture, even if you’re only passing through. [D5, D20, D44] Icebox Cafe — Although its South Beach restaurant has closed, the longtime brunch and bakery favorite still satisfies the sweet tooth of weary air travelers at MIA. [D8] La Carreta Restaurant — Sit down or grab to go at this Cuban-rooted restaurant with pastelitos, croquetas, and Cuban sandwiches. [D37] Ku-Va — The family-owned restaurant is a modern Cuban spot serving ropa vieja and other Cuban favorites with speedy service. A meal here isn’t complete without a mojito. It’s so Miami there’s barely a need to leave the airport. [D19] Spring Chicken — This Southern comfort food spot from the restaurant group that created Yardbird serves fried chicken, biscuit sandwiches, Cobb salads, and carrot cake. [D22] Shula’s Bar & Grill — Enjoy Don Shula’s steak and other big-player items in a quicker and more casual setting. [D17] Chefs of the Caribbean — An island-inspired menu including Jamaican patties, conch fritters, jerk chicken, and fresh tropical juices offers travelers a taste of the Caribbean without leaving the terminal. [D29] Sambazon Açaí Bowls — This newcomer opened in October 2026, with a menu of customizable organic açaí bowls topped with fresh fruit, granola, nuts, and seeds, along with protein bowls and superfood smoothies. [D29] The rest: Au Bon Pain: [D44 (post-security); Concourse D departures (pre-security)] — French-inspired bites and pastries. 305 Pizza: [D27] — Square-shaped pizza served by the slice with various toppings. Bacardi Mojito Bar: [Across from D53] — Cuban-inspired bites and drinks. Chili’s Bar & Grill: [D15] — Burgers, ribs, fajitas, and margaritas. Clover Irish Pub: [D30] — Irish dishes and strong drinks. Clubhouse One: [D24] — Expect a variety of crowd-pleasing fare like burgers, sliders, and salads, plus a full bar. The Counter: [D33] — Make-your-own burgers with a variety of toppings. Corona Beach House: [D23] — Typical poolside fare, like Palomilla steak and burgers, with the standard cold Corona and lime. Its grab-and-go counterpart, Corona Fresh Express, is located just south of the restaurant. Einstein Bros. Bagels: [D26] — Bagels and schmears. Estefan Kitchen Express: [D27] — Croquetas, Cuban pastries, and sandwiches from Miami royalty. Fig & Fennel: [D28] — Mediterranean-themed sandwiches, salads, and snacks. Halfmoon Empanadas: [D29] — Empanadas in an assortment of flavors. Islander Bar & Grill: [D4, D49] — Caribbean-influenced cuisine. KFC: [Concourse D] — Fried chicken, sandwiches, and sides. Manchu Wok: [D44, D22] — Counter-service Chinese cuisine. Nathan’s Famous Hot Dogs: [D21, D37] — Coney Island-style hot dogs served with classic toppings, plus crinkle-cut fries and other fast-food favorites. New to the map: The Mexican, Seia, and Nuna join the list. Restaurants are listed geographically from north to south. Elcielo Elcielo received a Michelin Star for its 18-course tasting menu by chef Juan Manuel Barrientos. The modern Colombian menu varies, but expect experiential moments like the restaurant’s “Tree of Life,” bread service entangled on a small tree; and the “Chocotherapy” which invites you to literally wash your hands in liquid cocoa. The tasting menu ranges from $245 to $289 per person (excluding beverages, tax, and a 20 percent added gratuity). Elcielo will accommodate people with allergies and offer a vegetarian menu upon request. There’s also a $98 bar experience where guests will experience a selection of cocktails, each paired with snacks. The restaurant is so intimate that it only accepts five guests at each of its seatings (there are two to three per evening). Those lucky enough to snag a coveted spot will experience Cory himself serving up the finest sushi flown in from Japan. The meal costs $280 per person (plus sake, a 20% service charge, and tax) and lasts approximately three hours. The menu is prepared specially each day, so substitutions are not allowed, and people with food allergies cannot be accommodated. Recently, vermouth and sherry-based drinks, along with classic Spanish cocktails and Italian spritzes, are popping up in the local scene, further shaping […]
items.text: Tin Tin Dining Out in Miami The Best New Bars in Miami Where to grab a drink right now in the Magic City by Allison Ramirez Updated Jul 15, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Facebook Link Allison Ramirez is a freelance journalist with over 15 years of experience covering food and drink, travel, art, culture, and more. As a gateway between the U.S., the Caribbean, and Latin America, Miami has long been a champion of diverse flavors — rum and agave spirits mingling with notes of citrus and exotic fruits. Recently, vermouth and sherry-based drinks, along with classic Spanish cocktails and Italian spritzes, are popping up in the local scene, further shaping the city’s evolving cocktail landscape. Miami’s drinking culture really reflects its melting pot history, and this year, some iconic bars and restaurants have reopened with a refreshed look and feel, bringing back old-school favorites alongside international, travel-inspired drinks. From tiki recipes and passion fruit infusions to sparkling concoctions of all sorts, our latest cocktail map highlights the best drinks and the hottest new spots to try them, from Coral Gables to Miami Beach and everywhere in between. As a gateway between the U.S., the Caribbean, and Latin America, Miami has long been a champion of diverse flavors — rum and agave spirits mingling with notes of citrus and exotic fruits. Recently, vermouth and sherry-based drinks, along with classic Spanish cocktails and Italian spritzes, are popping up in the local scene, further shaping the city’s evolving cocktail landscape. Miami’s drinking culture really reflects its melting pot history, and this year, some iconic bars and restaurants have reopened with a refreshed look and feel, bringing back old-school favorites alongside international, travel-inspired drinks. From tiki recipes and passion fruit infusions to sparkling concoctions of all sorts, our latest cocktail map highlights the best drinks and the hottest new spots to try them, from Coral Gables to Miami Beach and everywhere in between. Sunny’s Steakhouse Sunny’s Steakhouse in Miami’s Little River has been the talk of the town (many towns, actually) since opening in October 2024. The massive space and the dishes are worth the hype, but the unspoken star is the bar, featuring cocktails like the refreshing Green Ghoul (tequila, mezcal, poblano, cucumber, lime) and the Monchito, a coconut-washed agricole rhum drink with sherry that evolved from a piña colada to a ti punch of sorts. The menu includes house cocktails, martinis, and “fine & fancy” options — the fino martini service, which comes with a sidecar, is a must. Made with gin, clarified passionfruit, and fino sherry, it’s a steal at $18 per person. items.summary: A new Mexican seafood restaurant, Mi Vecino, is opening in Circle C, courtesy of chef Amir Hajimaleki and his brother Ali Hajimaleki of Roya Hospitality Group. It’s slated to open between now and early 2027, per a release. The restaurant, Mi Vecino, will open at 5701 West Slaughter Lane, replacing another of the group’s restaurants, […]
items.text: Austin Restaurant News Fire-Grilled Mexican Seafood Is Coming to South Austin The team behind Roya and Oasthouse will open Mi Vecino, a coastal restaurant focused on raw and fire-kissed dishes by Erin Russell Oct 28, 2026, 6:47 PM UTC Facebook Link Chef Amir Hajimaleki will oversee the menu, managed by Mi Vecino’s executive chef Jose Alajandro Sanchez. Sarah Natsumi Moore/Eater Erin Russell is a journalist and an Austin native, who has been writing about food for eight years. A new Mexican seafood restaurant, Mi Vecino, is opening in Circle C, courtesy of chef Amir Hajimaleki and his brother Ali Hajimaleki of Roya Hospitality Group. It’s slated to open between now and early 2027, per a release. The restaurant, Mi Vecino, will open at 5701 West Slaughter Lane, replacing another of the group’s restaurants, Keeper’s Coastal Kitchen , which closed Saturday, October 24. Mi Vecino, which means my neighbor in Spanish, will focus on Mexican seafood dishes, both raw and fire-grilled. That means offerings like shrimp enchiladas with white mole, ceviche, oysters, and fajitas served with fresh tortillas. Drinks-wise, there will be a full bar with margaritas, ranch waters, palomas, and other cocktails. Chef Hajimaleki will oversee the menu, which will be executed by chef Jose Alajandro Sanchez. The Hajimalekis’ restaurants are mostly clustered on Slaughter Lane in South Austin. Gastropub Oasthouse Kitchen + Bar , cocktail bar Daisy Lounge , and forthcoming Mi Vecino all share a building, and the group’s first restaurant , American spot District Kitchen + Cocktails , is just down the street. Mi Vecino replaces Keeper’s Coastal Kitchen, a different Roya Hospitality Group restaurant that closed in October. Jasmin Porter Photography This is not the first time Roya Hospitality Group has reimagined one of their restaurants. Roya , Hajimalekis’ highly personal Persian restaurant in North Shoal Creek, opened this year in a space that was previously Shortie’s, the group’s foray into New England Greek-style pizza. Roya is the group’s only North Austin restaurant, and sits above a former second District Kitchen, which closed and became an event space. Given the group’s penchant for reinvention, only time will tell whether it stays an event space. items.summary: Whether you’re planning a milestone birthday, hosting a corporate dinner, or gathering friends for an engagement celebration, Austin has a private dining room to suit your needs. items.text: Fonda San Miguel Dining Out in Austin The Best Restaurants in Austin for Private Dining, Events, and Parties Everywhere to book for all of your small weddings, celebratory dinners, bridal showers, and more by Darcie Duttweiler Updated Oct 22, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC Facebook Link Darcie Duttweiler is an Austin-based freelance writer, who covers food, beverages, travel, and lifestyle. Whether you’re planning a milestone birthday, hosting a corporate dinner, or gathering friends for an engagement celebration, Austin has a private dining room to suit your needs. Some are swanky and tucked into Downtown dining landmarks. Others are cozy, or perched on patios with sweeping views. All of them make an outing feel like an event, while also taking the stress out of group dining — meaning, there’s no awkward table shuffling, no shouting over the crowd, and no fighting for the check. The city’s best private dining spaces are more than just a curtain and a prix fixe menu. Many spots go beyond dinner, offering perks like custom cocktails, floral design, built-in audio and video setups, and after-hours buyouts. From iconic institutions like Fonda San Miguel, Matties, and Jeffrey’s to sleek hotspots like Eberly, La Condessa, and Bar Toti, these venues combine atmosphere with standout service and memorable menus. Here are the city’s most impressive private and semi-private dining options — spaces that strike the right balance between style and function. In this update, the Peacock’s private dining room joins the map, and Prelude, Maie Day, and Bar Peached leave the list. items.text: 82. Bar Bête NEW YORK | Carroll Gardens map Photo by OK McCausland for Resy Our staff has a long-term crush on this pitch-perfect Carroll Gardens neobistro — and for good reason. The quiet Montreal-esque tweaking of French classics remains a joy, from an indulgent leeks vinaigrette (you heard that right) to duck haché with black garlic jus and a chicken-liver parfait with plum jam. And of course there’s Nick Ferrante’s nonpareil wine list, full of delights and free from dogma, which isn’t something you get to say often in Brooklyn these days. Like Lutèce in D.C., L.A.’s Bar Etoile and L’Echelle in Portland, it shows how you can be a French American restaurant these days while taking full latitude to not simply lean on the hoary old roster. items.title: How to Get Into Little Bear in Summerhill
items.summary:
Otherwise known as the little restaurant that could, Summerhill’s Little Bear opened in February 2020 and reverted to a take-out… 
 The post  How to Get Into Little Bear in Summerhill  appeared first on  Resy | Right This Way .
items.text: How to Get Into Little Bear in Summerhill — Resy | Right This Way Little Bear 4.7 · New American · $ Summerhill Book Now Published: Nov. 18, 2026 Otherwise known as the little restaurant that could, Summerhill’s Little Bear opened in February 2020 and reverted to a take-out only model almost immediately, a move that lasted for nearly a year. Today, it’s one of the hottest reservations in the city and maybe the coziest place to dine south of I-20. In the dining room, guests can expect hip-hop pouring through the speakers , a funky crowd, neon-lit bathrooms (check them out, seriously), and thanks to chef-owner Jarrett Steiber’s creative mind, a menu that changes daily based on the availability of whatever’s good nearby. On any given day, you’ll likely find a soup or salad of some sort on offer (like a recent chicory salad or an emerald soup with pork meatballs and kale) in addition to protein-heavy and veggie-forward dishes at this Michelin Bib Gourmand joint. Drinks might include syrups made with locally foraged berries or more unexpected combos like apple and cacao. To finish, folks love the blondies and milk with benne seed flavor and whiskey milk for dipping — a crowd pleaser for nearly six years now. Stieber makes it easy for diners who want to try it all with affordable prix-fixe options and even a booze pack that includes off-menu cocktails and wine. We asked him how to snag a primetime spot at the beloved neighborhood restaurant , and what to expect when you get inside. Photo courtesy of Little Bear Photo courtesy of Little Bear Resy: How many seats are there at Little Bear, including the bar and sidewalk? Jarrett Steiber: Thirty-five including two two-top sidewalk tables. Indoors, there are 21 tabled seats along the dining room banquette, two in our front window nook, and eight at the bar. When do reservations drop, and how far ahead are they released? Reservations are visible for up to 90 days in advance on Resy. How quickly do weekend reservations typically book out? “Prime time” weekend slots (from 7 to 7:30 pm) generally book up three to four weeks in advance, and weeknights a little less competitively. How many seats do you usually hold for walk-ins on any given night? On weeknights, we make every seat in the restaurant, including the bar, available for reservations because we almost never get walk-ins at the bar (people seemed really concerned about having reservations). So, we figure getting butts in seats by reservation is more important than making sure we have a dedicated walk-in space. Since demand isn’t crazy on weeknights, there are usually walk-in seats open at the bar, and sometimes at unbooked tables. For weekends, we keep four of the bar seats open for walk-ins. More From Atlanta Dish By Dish Five Menu Highlights That Tell the Story of Little Bear By Lia Picard The One Who Keeps the Book How to Score a Table at BoccaLupo, Atlanta’s Palace of Pasta By Mike Jordan The One Who Keeps the Book How to Get a Table at Lyla Lila, and What to Order By Mike Jordan The One Who Keeps the Book How to Get a Table at Alpharetta’s Up on the Roof, And What to Order By Ashley Twist Cole What time would you recommend arriving to snag one of those walk-in tables? On weeknights, basically anytime is feasible, but on busy nights, I’d say showing up between 5 and 6 p.m. and then between 8:15 and 10 p.m. to avoid the 6:30 to 7:30 p.m. rush, due to a “we live in Atlanta and refuse to eat outside what we consider normal dining hours” mindset. What’s the typical wait time for walk-ins on a busy night? Forty-five minutes to an hour if we’re full but don’t have a long wait list; an hour-and-a-half to an hour-and-45 minutes if we already have a couple names on the waitlist. Which nights of the week are hardest to get in — and which are most underrated? Fridays, Saturdays, and early Sundays (5 to 7:30 pm) are usually booked up. Tuesdays are by far the quietest night on a weekly basis and super easy to get in whenever. Wednesdays and Thursdays are chill, too. Mondays have been the busiest weeknight for us, maybe because of industry people coming by when they’re off work. How many covers do you usually do on a typical service? On a quiet weeknight, around 15 to 20; on a decent weeknight, maybe 35 to 40; on weekends, we’ll do between 85 and 100 including walk-ins; sometimes over 100 if we’re really busy. Photo courtesy of Little Bear Photo courtesy of Little Bear Is there a difference between reserving the bar versus a table — and do you recommend one over the other for first timers? I prefer bar seating in general because I like seeing the action, which at LB includes drink making and a direct view into the open kitchen. I also like being able to talk to the bartender during my meal. Restaurant people will always assume you’re a better guest if you’re willing to and enjoy sitting at the bar instead of being the sort of person who only wants to dine at a table. I also love our cozy little front window nook. But you’ll get the same experience at a table, the nook, the bar, or the outside tables. Same menus, same service. In your opinion, what’s the best seat in the house and why? The kitchen seats [and] the four bar chairs directly in front of the open kitchen, because you’re in the heart of the action there. Are guests able to have a drink at the bar while waiting for a table? Yes, of course, but that’s assuming there are bar seats open. They can always have a drink and hang out at the standing room area next to the window nook, or kick it outside as long as they stay close to the restaurant. We also love sending folks to our neighbors for a quick drink — Redacted , Southern National , or Halfway Crooks — while waiting for seating. Do you ever accommodate last-minute cancellations or same-day openings? There is a Resy Notify list feature people can sign up for that alerts guests of table cancellations automatically by email. That’s a great way to get in on shorter notice, especially on weekends dur

items.text: Watr map Miami Beach Photo courtesy of Watr at the 1 Picking the best restaurant view in South Beach is kind of like picking the best croissant in Paris — you’re hard pressed to find a bad one. Watr at the 1 Hotel wins our award, a 360-degree poolside panorama stretching from the Miami skyline to the Atlantic. Sunday drinks at the bar here are a low-key pool party, but stop in for dinner and you can watch the sunset behind you while cruise ships sail out in front. The menu is heavily Asian-inspired, with lots of sushi, roasted yuzu snapper, and steaks in Japanese sauces. For visitors, you won’t find a better sense of place in South Beach. items.title: All About Bar Cosme, Enrique Olvera’s Sultry Evening Spot in NoHo
items.summary:
Chef and restaurant owner Enrique Olvera has had a very busy 2026. His group Casamata debuted San Damián and Ditroit… 
 The post  All About Bar Cosme, Enrique Olvera’s Sultry Evening Spot in NoHo  appeared first on  Resy | Right This Way .
items.text: All About Bar Cosme, Enrique Olvera’s Sultry Evening Spot in NoHo — Resy | Right This Way Bar Cosme 4.8 · Modern Mexican · $$$ NoHo Book Now Published: Nov. 18, 2026 Chef and restaurant owner Enrique Olvera has had a very busy 2026. His group Casamata debuted San Damián and Ditroit in Southern California, and Pujol.itto in Mexico City. Their final opening for the year is actually a flip, transforming the NoHo space that housed Atla for nearly a decade into Bar Cosme , which opened on Nov. 10. Despite Bar Cosme’s name, this sibling of his Flatiron spot Cosme , is a restaurant, not a bar. “We want people to come in and have dinner, but in a bar experience [at] a counter,” Olvera says. “As we [get to] know ourselves better, we recognize that this is the kind of dining we want to propose. Where you can see the interaction,” he says. A big, open kitchen takes up a large portion of the room, where chefs press and cook tortillas on a rotating comal to order. The presentation here is pared back. “We want to keep things as simple as possible, but very high quality,” Olvera adds. Dinner can be ordered à la carte, but the menu is designed as a $135 prix fixe, where guests choose one item from four sections. Most of the ​mains,​​​ like lamb belly and Dover sole, come largely unadorned and with tortillas on the side. That simplicity is also reflected in the design, which feels moody, sleek, and in situ. Despite the group’s roots in Mexico, Olvera says: “We don’t want the restaurant to feel like it landed from somewhere else. We want to do a New York restaurant with Mexican food.” Here’s everything you need to know about Bar Cosme. The Resy Rundown Bar Cosme Why We Like It Think of Bar Cosme as Cosme’s younger, downtown sister. All of the seating is at two long bars and everything is accompanied by tortillas pressed to order or tostadas. Essential Dishes While diners can order à la carte, the menu is designed as a $135 prix fixe. Start with the king trumpets with duck sabayon or oysters with jicama, then move on to the lamb belly in xintextle, and soft-serve or Cosme’s signature corn husk meringue for dessert. Must-Order Drinks The cocktail menu from Eleven Madison Park vet Sebastian Tollius and Casamata’s Jorsand Diaz is broken into two parts: “De la Casa” for spins on classics like a martini with mezcal-brined morita smoked olives; and “De la Barra” for inventive creations like the Lestat with Tequila, corn, yellow Chartreuse, and passion fruit. Who and What It’s For There are no tables at Bar Cosme; all of the leather stools line two long black granite counters; bring a date or come solo. Reserve a spot facing the kitchen, if you like a show. How to Get In Reservations drop 30 days in advance at 10 a.m. with limited seatings held for walk-ins from 5 to 9 p.m. After 9 p.m., the restaurant is walk-ins only. Pro Tip Every meal here starts with tostadas and two salsas, which change daily. Expect ones like a Thai-inspired salsa with fish sauce and habanero chiles, and a Japanese riff on salsa borracha or “drunken salsa” made with sake instead of pulque. Bar Cosme is located in the NoHo space that housed Atla for nearly a decade, which was entirely overhauled with a focus on looking inwards. Photo by Evan Sung, courtesy of Bar Cosme Photo by Victoria Martinez, courtesy of Bar Cosme Photo by Victoria Martinez, courtesy of Bar Cosme 1. Corn is served with nearly every dish. “The idea is that you always have some kind of corn preparation,” Olvera explains. Eating here is meant to be a little playful, he adds, with diners using their hands to assemble their perfect bite. The meal kicks off with tostadas and two salsas, which rotate daily, like one that takes inspiration from Thailand with fish sauce blended with habanero chiles, and a Japanese take on salsa borracha, or drunken salsa made with sake instead of pulque. As diners reach the main course, the tostadas are swapped with tortillas that are pressed to order and cooked on a comal in the center of the restaurant that’s so large, it rotates, so the chefs can reach all of the tortillas. “I think tortillas are more and more, for us, the center of the restaurant,” Olvera says. Like the ones at Cosme, the tortillas here are made with heirloom corn varieties from Mexico sourced by suppliers like Masienda. Corn also finds its way onto the dessert. The team is also serving Cosme’s signature dish, the corn husk meringue . The Dover sole. Photo by Victoria Martinez, courtesy of Bar Cosme The Dover sole. Photo by Victoria Martinez, courtesy of Bar Cosme 2. The menu is built as a $135 prix fixe, but you can still order à la carte. “When you have a restaurant that wants you to come often, it’s nice to keep things simple,” Olvera says. Milton Revilla , who has worked with the Casamata team for years, is overseeing the kitchen at Bar Cosme. The menu is divided into four sections including starters to pair with those tostadas like prawn tartare with prawn head mayonnaise and king trumpets with duck sabayone, which is a small nod to the beloved duck carnitas at Cosme. In the 12 years since Olvera opened Cosme, New York’s taco scene has grown exponentially. So there are no assembled tacos on the menu here, by design. The main course offerings focus on proteins adorned primarily with just a sauce like Dover sole al ajillo, with garlic, guajillo chile sliced almost as finely as saffron threads, and olive oil. There’s also lamb belly in xintextle , a sauce traditionally made with dried shrimp, which the team swapped for a variety of toasted and crushed ants that taste like beef jerky. Sides like those at a steakhouse can be mixed and matched with the proteins. There’s roasted onion in salsa matcha, potato puree , and a chicory and radish salad . Diners can order à la carte, but the portions will be more substantial. Instead of a piece of the Dover sole, expect a whole fish. The small dessert selection includes soft-serve and an affogato with espresso made with beans from La

items.text: New On Resy: Portland's Newest Restaurant Openings — Resy | Right This Way Updated: Nov. 17, 2026 Consider this your go-to resource for all things New On Resy . Whether it’s hot new openings , or local favorites new to Resy , we have you covered with this continuously updated list. This is the place to discover and book the latest — and greatest — restaurants in your area. This month … From an excellent place for wine to a beloved favorite for Turkish cuisine, we’ve got you covered with this continuously updated list of hot new debuts and longtime favorites that are now bookable on Resy. New on Resy in Portland 23rd Champagne Poetry Modern Pan-Asian · $$ Nob hill Bistro Alder Bistro · $$ SW Portland Pretty Ugly Burgers · $ Pearl District Wolf Fusion · $$$$ Portland JawFish PDX American · $ Portland Kismet Contemporary American · $$ Downtown Vancouver WA Il Corso Portland Italian · $$ Pearl Arts District See Full Collection › Portland Chef Agir Restaurant Bar It’s got a short but unique-to-Portland menu of Turkish staples, inspired by chef Ertas’ stint at an Italian restaurant in Turkey. Come with a group of friends — all the better to try more of the menu. Book Now Newberg Proteus Wines Head to this boutique winery and vineyard for a tasting of some highly drinkable pours. They’ve been around since 1999, so you’re in good hands. Book Now Sherwood Old Town Mason Fresh, housemade pasta never hurt anyone, especially when it’s prepared as lovingly as it is at Mason. Don’t skip the Italian-leaning wine list, either. Book Now Ladd’s Addition OK Omens This Hawthorne Avenue wine bar is home to one of the city’s best wine lists alongside what are possibly the most creative descriptions we’ve ever seen. Once the never-too-serious little sister to fine dining restaurant Castagna, OK Omens has grown into its own over the past 8 years, landing among the city’s best happy hours with its creative snacks and plates that have a “maniacal devotion to quality sourcing” and frequently pair best with their “deep love of Riesling.” Book Now Sunnyside Old Pal Kitchen + Market Chef Timothy Wastell is fresh off a James Beard win for Best Chef: Northwest and Pacific, and brings joyfully simple vegetable-focused cooking to the menu. The options here have a touch of European flair: herbed frites with preserved lemon mayo, sprouting broccoli with anchovy, and green garlic and ricotta cavatelli with local mushrooms. Book Now New Opening Pearl District Pretty Ugly New from Lulu and Silk Road owners Vijay Kumar and Gilbert Leon comes Pretty Ugly, the duo’s burgers-meets-fancy-cocktail bar in Northwest Portland. The meat-focused menu (though a few vegan options remain) centers on more than half a dozen burgers — made with dry-aged prime beef from local butcher Revel Meat Co. — alongside creative cocktails ranging from “produce-driven, modern signatures” to “vintage desserts” to pair with your burger of the night. Book Now New Opening Pearl Arts District Il Corso Portland Taking over the former home of Champagne-centric Fancy Baby in Northwest Portland, Il Corso is trading hard-to-find bubbles for pasta and Italian wines. Find imported meats and cheeses, snack plates like Calabrian chile-spiked tuna carpaccio, and a short but sweet menu of handmade pastas from chef Brady Stephens (of OK Omens and Scotch Lodge ). In addition to classic Italian varietals, sip aperitifs from the lengthy amaro menu, a low ABV spritz, or a cocktail shaken by Scotch Lodge alum Lisa Talbert. Book Now Dundee The Cellar at Black Walnut Inn & Vineyard While away the dark winter days with a cozy day trip to this luxurious bed and breakfast overlooking the Dundee Hills AVA. By day, this four-star hotel and winery tasting room boasts a casual indoor lounge and outdoor patio seating (make sure to bundle up) at The Cellar. Expect seasonal bites like zhuzhed-up burgers with towering piles of fries, weekly cornhole tournaments and Willa and Hazel, the winery ’s two kunekune pigs, alongside wine pairings. Book Now SW Portland Bistro Alder Anchor your next outing from downtown Portland’s Dossier Hotel, located right in the heart of the city. On the ground floor sits Bistro Alder, the hotel’s casual Pacific Northwest restaurant serving breakfast, lunch, dinner, and happy hour, with a full list of craft cocktails, wine, and beer to pair, all day, every day. Book Now Portland Adelleda Sharing a home with Vtopian Artisan Cheese Shop’s new Northeast Grand Avenue location is this food cart-turned-pasta-pop- up. Find fresh pastas tossed with seasonal and wild-foraged ingredients like fennel, kohlrabi and lobster mushrooms, plus antipasti and small, often fried, plates like honeynut squash fritters. items.text: New On Resy: Los Angeles’ Newest Restaurant Openings — Resy | Right This Way Updated: Nov. 17, 2026 Consider this your go-to resource for all things New On Resy . Whether it’s hot new openings , or local favorites new to Resy , we have you covered with this continuously updated list. This is the place to discover and book the latest — and greatest — restaurants in your area. This month … From a lovely Pan African bistro and wine bar to a new destination for dining at The Music Center, we’ve got you covered with this continuously updated list of hot new debuts and longtime favorites that are now bookable on Resy. New on Resy in Los Angeles Skywalker Grill American · $$ Exposition Park Somni Cocina de Autor · $$$$ West Hollywood Sous Sous French - American · $$$ Los Angeles Savage Seas at Fonda Theatre Cocktail Bar · $$ Hollywood The Tower Bar Californian · $$$ West Hollywood Malka Beverly Hills Israeli · $$ Beverly Hills Gilbert Perez Bar Cocktail Bar · $ Sherman Oaks See Full Collection › Wilshire Montana Wally's Santa Monica The bottle cellar provides a show-stopping backdrop to your meal at Wally’s, where the walls are lined with their many excellent selections, a perfect pairing for their sophisticated take on California-French cuisine. Book Now Hermosa Beach Covinten Chef and owner Mary Roy drives Covinten’s feeling of warm, service-first intimacy. You’re more likely than not to see her around the dining room during your meal, which will likely consist of something European and delicious. Book Now Los Angeles Komal One of the city’s most critically acclaimed restaurants now offers a weekly tasting menu, and we couldn’t be more elated. Here, chef Fátima Juárez assembles a seasonally driven menu that reflects Mexican traditions in more than 22 heirloom corn varieties and counting — a delight for all the senses. Book Now New Opening The Music Center – Downtown Los Angeles Kendall's This is an ideal spot to hit for dinner before catching a show at The Music Center — it sits at the grand entrance of the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion. The fare is of the French brasserie persuasion. Book Now Beverly Hills The Ivy It’s hard to live in Los Angeles without hearing tales of The Ivy. It remains a see-and-be-seen standby for the well-heeled, thanks to its glitzy-casual interior and menu of classic garden-party fare. Book Now Santa Monica Ivy at the Shore This is the shoreside sibling to The Ivy, where you’ll experience all the charm of the original plus ocean breezes and views of the Santa Monica Pier. Book Now New Opening Hollywood Flavors from Afar – Los Angeles What started as a cozy cafe in Little Ethiopia is now this eclectic Pan African bistro and wine bar in East Hollywood that honors the diversity and deliciousness of African cuisine and wine: Think crisp sambusas, Nigerian goat pepper soup, Somali roasted chicken, and wines hailing from Morocco, South Africa, and Zimbabwe. Book Now Long Beach Selva Chef Carlos Surado serves up a menu of Colombian fare inspired by his childhood at this Long Beach hot spot. Know that the fresh sea scallops are a must-order. Book Now Los Angeles Shin – Los Angeles Whether you’re ordering steaming bowls of ramen or freshly plated sushi, Shin has got you covered. No matter what you decide on, know that it’ll be tasty. Book Now Downtown LouLou A restaurant so nice they named it twice. LouLou takes its place on the coastline seriously, making the best of the position with a stunning rattan-filled patio that you’ll never want to leave. Book Now North Alamitos Beach El Barrio Cantina – Long Beach We’d be remiss not to mention the cocktails at El Barrio. Between the frozen piña coladas, margaritas, and aguas frescas, it can be hard to remember what you came for in the first place. Oh, yes, the ceviche. Book Now Downtown Los Angeles Takami Sushi and Robata Is there any better way to enjoy sushi than on a rooftop patio overlooking the City of Angels? If so, we haven’t found it. Book Now New Opening Norma Triangle Christian's Wine Bar & Restaurant Eighty wines by the glass? Caviar service? 24-karat-gold margaritas? Christian’s is made for a night of luxury with its red-walled Sunset Boulevard interior and menu of lofty fare, and we’re here for it. Book Now Granada Hills Odyssey Restaurant This spot’s high elevation means that they boast excellent views of the picturesque San Fernando Valley — views that are only improved by the menu of upscale American comfort food. Book Now Santa Monica Shoreside Maybe it’s the sea breeze, or the view of the coast, but there’s just something about Shoreside that keeps us coming back. Order a spicy margarita and keep an eye out for the live music schedule. Book Now New Opening Little Tokyo Kasa Rin This Little Tokyo izakaya serves up a blend of French, Italian, and Japanese cuisines in a cozy, warm space. Expect stretchy udon and fried chicken that’s criminally crispy. Book Now New Opening Burbank Arya Restaurant and Bar This sprawling spot has room for you and all your most distant acquaintances, with an enormous menu to match. They fuse Indian classics with other favorites here, which means things like penne tikka masala and paneer pizza have made the list. Book Now Los Feliz Tu Madre (Los Feliz) – Los Angeles It’s one of the many Tu Madre locations around our fair city, and its status as one of the local favorites is well-deserved (and hard to come by in a town such as this). Book Now New Opening Miami Beach A Pasta Bar Miami The simplicity of this spot’s name belies what’s going on inside, which is impressively chic. All the pastas are handmade and tasty, just as they are at the New York City original. That means you’ll enjoy golden tostones, empanadas, and arroz con leche in the throwback of an interior. Book Now Miami Ciao Havana Little Havana’s Calle Ocho is the perfect home for this restaurant, where you’ll be served a menu of churrasco and picanha by the pound, plus bold, flavorful starters galore. Book Now Little Havana Old's Havana This Little Havana destination has a rustic-chic interior that harkens back to a lighthearted time in Cuba’s history. Don’t forget to order a mojito (or two). As such, there’s plenty of art deco inspiration inside, from the plush round pink booths to the icy martinis. Book Now New Opening Miami La Sponda Ristorante & Grill Gioia Hospitality Group’s new Italian restaurant pairs one of Miami’s more distinctive waterfront settings with a menu that travels across Italy, while keeping family roots in Puglia front and center. Know that the khao soi gai should absolutely be on your table. Book Now New Opening River North The Lair With its chic, moody, romantic, and smoky interior, you can’t help but be drawn to this subterranean space where you’re sure to have a night to remember. Book Now Warrenville Madurai Kitchen – Warrenville South Indian cuisine takes center stage at this Warrenville spot, where you should plan to order as many of the tandoori specials as you can. Book Now Mid-North District Bacino's This spot has been a Chicago classic since they opened in 1978, serving Italian American fare like the signature stuffed spinach pizza, salads, and pastas. Book Now West Town Elina’s You won’t want to miss this little gem of an Italian place run by chefs Ian Rusnak and Eric Safin, whose résumés include stints at such acclaimed New York establishments as Jean-Georges , Carbone , 4 Charles Prime Rib , and Forgione . Don’t expect the avant-garde here — just old-style classics like clams casino and eggplant Parmesan, done right. Book Now New Opening West Loop Urbanbelly – Fulton Market One of Chicago’s most beloved spots for Korean fried chicken, togarashi fries, coconut curry pho, pork lumpia, and cinnamon-sugar mochi churros is always a good idea. Book Now Forest Park Sendero Cantina & Cocina At Sendero, they serve Oaxacan cuisine in an environment that’s pretty much always what we’d describe as “popping.” Usually, there’s a game on, or a DJ spinning, or lotería to be played. Book Now Rogers Park R Public House Whether you’re people watching on the patio or sipping a draft at the bar inside, you’re likely to run into someone you know at R Public House. It has a convivial, friendly vibe and a menu of standout bar fare that’s hard to resist. Book Now Chicago Loop Venteux Brasserie Café & Oyster Bar – Chicago This gilded, glittering French spot boasts floor-to-ceiling windows, Champagne by the glass, and a seafood tower that’s show-stopping to say the least. Book Now New Opening Evanston Soul & Smoke – Evanston This perpetually crowded Chicago institution is beloved for award-winning slow-smoked meats by the pound, served to anyone who knows what’s good for them. In Evanston, there’s plenty of room to spread out, so bring the whole crew. Book Now West Loop, Chicago Trino Among the array of stellar steakhouses in Chicago, this is one not to miss. Chef Stephen Sandoval (also of Diego) infuses the menu of premium cuts with inspiration from his time cooking in Northern Mexico, Argentina, and Spain. Book Now Humboldt Park Casa Yari The Honduran and Puerto Rican menu at Casa Yari is a showstopper across the board, with a rotating mofongo, pastelitos, and a fan-favorite flan to top it all off. Book Now River North The Franklin Room Descending into the subterranean space at The Franklin Room feels like it should require a password or a skeleton key. Take full advantage of the prohibition-era vibes and order something spirit-forward and classic. Book Now Avondale Eden This is about as local as local can get. Eden has its very own on-site greenhouse from which it sources a lot of its ingredients, then used to make artfully plated dishes. We’re starting to understand the name. Book Now Chicago The Duplex – Chicago Dining here means being in for a good time, whether you choose to indulge in a pitcher of the peach spritz, a creamy pasta, or some questionable dance moves once the DJ starts spinning. Book Now Chicago Rudy's Ramen Escape that bitter Chicago wind with a bowl of steaming, slurpable ramen. Rudy’s makes theirs tonkatsu style. Book Now Wicker Park Dēliz Italian Bec

items.summary: From chic city dwellings to romantic reimagined farmhouses, these are our favorite places to stay across the country.
items.text: 16 Incredible Hotels in Morocco Whether You’re Looking for a Royal Riad or a Kitesurfing Sanctuary | Condé Nast Traveler Skip to main content Africa Chevron Morocco Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story The gateway of Africa is chameleon when it comes to its cultural offering, and thus choosing the best hotels in Morocco is a varied task. Whether you’re looking for a charming riad stay in Marrakech , yearn for serenity and seclusion in the Atlas Mountains or plan to immerse yourself in the Agafay desert, there’s so more to this colorful country than the promise of winter sun . It’s perhaps obvious, then, why Morocco has long since been favored by the fashionable jet set crowd, and has become home to so many notable hotel addresses. Some are so lavish they veer on palaces, others are romantically reimagined farmhouses or bohemian beachside boltholes. Right now the country is witnessing a transformation in tourism as it prepares to host the men's FIFA World Cup 2030. One of the biggest changes is the multi-million dollar rail expansion project, which will connect Kenitra with Marrakech, via Rabat and Casablanca. On the hotel front, Four Seasons is set to open a new address in Tangier, while Virgin Limited Edition plans to open a hotel near Marrakech. For the latest and greatest addresses, here is our pick of the best hotels in Morocco. Top picks: For couples: Kasbah Tamadot, Atlas Mountains For families: Royal Mansour Tamuda Bay, M'diq For by the beach: La Sultana Oualidia Colourful streets in Marrakech Lucy Bruton The pool at El Fenn in Marrakech Lucy Bruton David Dumon Save to wishlist Save to wishlist David Dumon Save to wishlist Save to wishlist David Dumon Save to wishlist Save to wishlist David Dumon Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Chevron Chevron Jnane Rumi, Marrakech Hot List Hot List 2026 Perched at the edge of the desert, Marrakech is improbably a garden city, its medina an intricate jigsaw of riad courtyards that reflect deeply held Islamic beliefs about water, light, and the art of living harmoniously with the natural world. Jnane Rumi—the Garden of Rumi—sits squarely within this tradition in the Palmeraie, Marrakech’s historic palm grove. It was designed by Tunisian-born Charles Boccara as a private home and has just 12 rooms: 7 in the mansion, 4 garden pavilions, and 1 private villa. Boccara grew up in Casablanca and graduated from the Beaux-Arts de Paris, and this mini manor house—with its arches and domes, expressive use of local materials, and elegantly ­mullioned windows that connect the house with a glorious garden of centenarian palms and pistachio trees—embodies his elegant Euro-Maghrebi style. It’s a seductive oasis that ­naturally gathers life, which is why owners Gert-Jan van den Bergh, an art-restitution lawyer, and his somatic-therapist wife, Corinne, felt compelled to transform it into a ­cultural hub, platforming contemporary Moroccan artists and designers, and curating art events and creative retreats. — Paula Hardy Read Full Review Check Availability at Booking.com Check Availability at Priceline Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Chevron Chevron Royal Mansour Tamuda Bay Readers' Choice Readers' Choice Awards 2026 Set between the mountains and the sea, this smart family-friendly resort and discreet spa retreat was conceived and built by King Mohammed VI as a showcase for the artisanal skills and flair that are a cornerstone of Morocco’s cultural heritage. The Royal Mansour Tamuda Bay houses more than 2,000 works of art in an astounding showcase for Moroccan craftsmanship and artisanal skills. Set on a 700-meter private beachfront along the so-called Moroccan Riviera, it sits low within a landscaped garden scented with rosemary, sage lavender, and mint. While there are some big name resorts further along the coastline including Sofitel and Ritz Carlton, this the first home-grown luxury offering and stands head and shoulders above the others for its service (all staff are trained at Royal Mansour’s own hospitality school) and obsessive attention to detail, as well as its sustainable practices. It’s also open year-round for dedicated spa-goers who come for Longevity programs of varying time frames in the largest and most professional med spa in Northern Africa. — Catherine Fairweather Read Full Review Check Availability at Expedia Check Availability at Booking.com Courtesy Four Seasons Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Courtesy Four Seasons Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Courtesy Four Seasons Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Courtesy Four Seasons Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Chevron Chevron Four Seasons Rabat at Kasr Al Bahr A shiny, super-sized proposition from Four Seasons, successfully incorporating beautiful Moroccan touches in the shared areas and sleek luxury in the private spaces. This would be an ideal three- or four-night stop for a spot of sightseeing and a lot of pampering as part of a wider Moroccan tour, with the city itself being a serene introduction to what is a very colorful and frenetic country. The true headliner here is the newly opened spa, which has a thorough menu and high-end treatments for every mood, with the opportunity to relax by the magnificent indoor pool afterwards. There’s an effortless blending of old and new, and a devotion to looking after the guest. Palatial, imposing, luxurious, with an impressive attention to detail, Four Seasons’ newest Moroccan property makes you feel like a modern day sultan. — Matt Charlton Read Full Review Check Availability at Expedia Check Availability at Booking.com Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Chevron Chevron La Sultana Oualidia Readers' Choice Readers' Choice Awards 2026 Three years after opening La Sultana Marrakech in 2004, the owners sought a quieter, more intimate

items.title: The Best Places to Go in Australia, New Zealand, and the South Pacific in 2027
items.summary: For castaway islands, earthy food-and-wine scenes, and underrated cities.
items.text: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story When it comes to the best places to go in Australia , New Zealand , and the South Pacific for 2027, there is a prevailing theme: Familiar destinations are finding new ways to surprise us. In Queensland, old pubs have become home to some of the hottest tables. Just take a look at Noosa’s restored 100-year-old Kin Kin , which has a new lease on life thanks to the arrival of Michelin-trained chef Oscar Holgado. And there’s much more where that came from. Across the country in the East Kimberley , this is the year to dine on native bush foods in the shadow of ancient boabs and red cliffs, and rest your head at the area’s stalwart bush lodges, two of which have just reopened after major renovations. Then there’s Tasmania’s east coast, which is always deserving of a long road trip—and now Tasmanian malt whisky is being made in an oyster hatchery, not far from where little penguins (the world’s smallest penguin species) return to shore after feeding at sea. Across the Tasman, Wellington’s new Michelin guide reminds us that even those stars can’t capture the effortless excellence of this area’s food and wine culture . Plan your visit around a culinary festival, several of which come to life in winter, and you’ll see what we mean. Meanwhile, in the Cook Islands at Highland Paradise on Rarotonga, descendants of the original Tinomana community guide visitors through a 600-year-old ancestral mountain settlement, sharing its history and traditions as they optimistically await UNESCO’s answer on recognition. On our below list of the best places to travel in Oceania for 2027, there is a trip for every type. —Chloe Sachdev This is part of our global guide to the Best Places to Go in 2027 —find more travel inspiration here . The Best Places to Go in Australia, New Zealand, and the South Pacific in 2027 AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Cook Islands East Kimberly, Australia Fremantle, Australia French Polynesia Stewart Island, New Zealand Sunshine Coast, Australia Sydney & Blue Mountains, Australia Tasmania's East Coast, Australia Wellington, New Zealand Whitsundays, Australia Cook Islands Go for: ancient cultural sites, eco-tourism, dazzling island landscapes On the South Pacific, the 15 isles of Cook Islands are scattered across nearly 900,000 square miles. The Cook Islands’ 15 isles stipple roughly 849,000 square miles of the South Pacific, but total less than 100 square miles of land. Most first trips center on a southern pair of islands: Rarotonga and Aitutaki . On the one-hour propeller flight between two, the entire country arrives in flashes: a volcanic ridge inside a white reef, miles of open Pacific, then a blue lagoon with motu gathered along its rim. Rarotonga’s 20-mile coast road threads between reef and pleated peaks, while Aitutaki is defined by its broad lagoon. On the west side of the island Rarotonga, a narrow road climbs from the lagoon into Maungaroa Valley , where a canopy of multi-trunked mato trees covers the remains of a centuries-old settlement. Taken together, the surviving sites form a cultural landscape that will appear before UNESCO’s World Heritage Committee in 2027 as the Cook Islands’ first nomination. At Highland Paradise , a cultural site within the old settlement and managed by descendants of Chief Tinomana, the Tapu’ae Day Tour follows those paths past chiefly house sites and sacred ground as guides explain how the stonework organized life here. On Aitutaki, customary stewardship extends well below the waterline. In 2025 three lagoon zones came under ra’ui, a traditional temporary closure that allows coral and fish populations to recover, with protections scheduled to rotate in 2027. Aitutaki Coral Restoration takes small groups beyond the usual motu-and-sandbar circuit to its underwater nursery and a planting site, where guests clean a dead coral base and secure a naturally broken fragment. Part of each tour fee supports the restoration work. Tourism is growing alongside the conservation push. In March 2027 a new, locally owned hotel, Grand Resort , billing itself as the island’s first five-star hotel, is scheduled to open with 61 adults-only suites on Rarotonga’s west coast. The Destination Stewardship Plan 2026–2030 , meanwhile, shifts the focus from mainly growing tourism to managing its impact with protections for culture and the environment with a greater share flowing to island communities. —Paul Jebara Previous Slide Arrow Next Slide Arrow East Kimberly, Australia Go for: red dirt, remote lodges, and wilderness on an epic scale After a multimillion-dollar transformation, Bullo River Station will reopen in May 2027. Bullo River Station guests will have the opportunity to watch the seasonal mustering of cattle. It’s not just helicopter blades creating a hum in Australia’s East Kimberley. A wave of luxury investment is putting this remote frontier on the global-travel radar—without sanding down the wilderness that makes it so worth the journey. After devastating cyclone damage, Berkeley River Lodge welcomes guests back to a revived 15-villa hideaway, accessible only by private air charter from Darwin. Individual decks overlook a croc-filled coastline, while open-air en suites allow galaxy gazing from the bathtub. Just across the border in the Northern Territory, Bullo River Station sits on the eastern fringe of the East Kimberley. Come May 2027, it will reopen after a multimillion-dollar transformation, pairing a new level of comfort with conservation across its 400,000 acres. The good news is that it remains a dusty working cattle station: Guests can watch seasonal musters, fish for barramundi in the river, or helicopter to watering holes for swims beneath waterfalls or to Aboriginal rock-art sites. There is even more to come. items.text: Europe Chevron France Chevron Ile-de-France Chevron Paris Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story Located just 40 minutes from Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport, Disneyland Paris is the ideal place to begin a Parisian vacation or say au revoir before returning home. Disneyland Paris's two theme parks, Disneyland Park and Disney Adventure World, pair timeless charm with an ease you'll never find stateside. Here, you can sip Champagne in front of Sleeping Beauty's castle—or visit a dragon beneath it—while filling your days with delightful architecture, unprecedented thrills, and the wildest wilderness ride Disney's ever built (Big Thunder Mountain!). There's also never been a better time to visit. Walt Disney Studios Park's March 2026 transformation into the new Disney Adventure World brought a drone-filled nighttime show, Avengers coaster, and even a Frozen -themed land featuring a lifelike Olaf robot to its once-faltering second gate. Now, between Fantasyland classics and futuristic favorites, there's something new and thrilling for the entire family to experience. Of course, you'll need somewhere to rest your head at night, and that's where the best hotels near Disneyland Paris come into play. Staying at a Disney-branded property typically affords guests special amenities including ticket packages, exclusive character meet-and-greets, and Extra Magic Time, which provides bonus time in the parks prior to opening. These hotels are great options, but can also be pricey—luckily, there are also a few non-branded properties in the area that make for great alternatives. There's something here for everyone and every budget. Unsure of whether you want to add something so Américain to your Paris vacation? As a theme park journalist who has visited all Disney parks worldwide , trust me: It's worth the visit. Even with so many cultural monuments in Paris, nothing is more delightfully uncanny than witnessing the United States section of It's a Small World. So, whether you're looking for glamour or simply a good location, read on for the very best hotels near Disneyland Paris. items.text: Central America and the Caribbean Chevron Puerto Rico Chevron San Juan Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story My favorite thing about San Juan ? You can have a morning that feels plucked out of a history book, an afternoon that commits you entirely to the beach , and a night that’s topped off with a frosty Medalla, sweet rum cocktail, and flirty bachata dance. It’s glitzy yet lush, historic yet ever-evolving, a city delightfully full of contrasts, and one I will never run out of reasons to revisit. My father’s side of the family is from Puerto Rico , so I’ve been coming back to the island for years, and I love that there’s always another corner to get to know. There’s Old San Juan, with all its pastel-painted façades, galleries and shops, blue cobblestone streets, and tucked-away restaurants; Condado and Ocean Park for long, sea-salty afternoons by the ocean; and Santurce, where street murals, galleries, haute dining, and a lively bar scene bring a fresh, creative vibe to the city. Of course, there’s no shortage of hotels in San Juan , but sometimes a vacation to the island’s capital calls for a little more room to sprawl, or a front door that opens onto a lush little neighborhood rather than a buzzy hotel lobby. The city’s best Airbnbs offer just that, along with wonderful amenities, whether it’s a private pool hidden behind swaying palms or a breezy courtyard for sipping on some local morning coffee. Consider this your invitation to soak up the sun in Puerto Rico's capital for a few days. Read on for nine of the best Airbnbs in San Juan to consider for your next trip. We've selected these listings based on Superhost status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews. You’ll never be bored at this retro-inspired haven, what with its groovy wallpaper in nearly every room, playful lava lamps, disco ball, and hanging plants. Conveniently, it's situated right in the heart of San Juan’s food and arts district and just a few steps from Ocean Park Beach. If you do decide to stay in for the night, rinse off the sand in your designer rain shower, throw a vinyl on the record player, and cook up some local produce in the fully stocked kitchen. Thanks to the in-unit washer and dryer, you’ll likely depart with no dirty beach laundry. As for the sleeping arrangements? The space can fit up to five guests, but there’s only two bedrooms. So if you’re doubling up, the fifth guest would have to crash on the living room’s sofa bed.
