items.title: Bar Le Trente
items.summary: La entrada  Bar Le Trente  se publicó primero en  Openhouse Magazine .
items.text: Bar Le Trente — Openhouse Magazine Created with Sketch. Subscribe Order Issue 26 Shop Studios My account Search Design , Food Bar Le Trente The Wild Child of Pigalle Written by Patty Castellar Photographed by Tanguy Sergheraert Facebook Twitter Linkedin Share Following Hotel Massé , siblings Corto and Eole Peyron have opened Le Trente. Located next to the hotel, this bar occupies an iconic former loft in Pigalle, transforming it into a place for encounters with both neighbourhood locals and travellers. Like Massé, it draws on the family motto, “make a friend a day”, though its world is slightly different. “Le Trente is a bit like Hotel Massé’s more unruly younger brother. They belong to the same family, but they don’t quite have the same character”, explains Eole. At Massé, calm and intimacy prevail. Step through the doors of Le Trente, however, and the energy shifts: drinks, food , friends and DJs spinning vinyl from Thursday onwards. Close While touches of velvet, wood and beige give the hotel its soft, inviting aesthetic, Le Trente feels sexier and bolder: leather, mirrors and very low lighting in the evening. Once again, Olivier Guyot and studio Gasparetto Parenti worked with the Peyron family to rethink the space and bring Le Trente to life. Outside, the lettering and green marble frontage mark the entrance to this singular place. Inside, a raw, conceptual universe takes shape: a large vintage wooden bar, red-painted floors, high and low seating, small tables and even an outdoor alcove. Close As at Massé, every object has been sourced second-hand or custom-made. “We really didn’t want everything to feel new or perfectly matched”, Eole notes. “There are things we found, contemporary artworks, pieces made specifically for the space and objects and memories from our family”. This is precisely what creates a space that feels both artistic and homely: the walls are covered with personal photographs featuring familiar faces, many of them tracing the expeditions of their father, Stéphane Peyron. Close “Our father has spent his life travelling and meeting people in some of the most remote parts of the world”, Eole comments. “He taught us that it’s the people you meet who make the journey and the memories”. This philosophy, central to both Corto and Eole, runs through Le Trente and is what prompted them to open a bar alongside the hotel. “At Le Trente, Massé guests mix with neighbours and Parisians. You can come for dinner, have a drink, celebrate a birthday, hold an exhibition or a book signing”. Close This same understanding of connections with people from all walks of life extends to their team. Some were friends before the project was born; others have become friends along the way: “The Massé and Le Trente teams are young and very close-knit. It wasn’t something we planned – it just happened naturally”. Close Gabrielle, a young neighbourhood sommelier who knocked on the door during the renovation, curates a minimalist selection of natural wines from France and beyond. Louis, a neighbour of Le Trente and a music enthusiast, is in charge of the music programme. Discovered at listening sessions, on the radio or in the city’s record shops, Le Trente’s DJs share one passion: vinyl. Ambient, house, jazz, downtempo or electro. Corto and his childhood friend Cyril teamed up with Félix to imagine Le Trente’s menu, built around a simple question: what do we want to eat in a bar? The answers became the menu: simple but really good dishes, designed for sharing. Close The menu changes weekly and follows the seasons, so regulars can keep coming back without tiring of the same dishes. The music rotates in a similar way: “We tend to favour artists from the local scene, whether emerging or already established, and we give them a lot of freedom”. Each artist brings their own records, generating a mood that is personal yet lively. “Le Trente never has exactly the same soundtrack two nights in a row, and that’s exactly how we like it”. Close Upstairs, you walk into a huge glass-roofed room: “You can almost feel as though you’re in a New York loft, until you look outside and see the Haussmann façades – you see Paris”. A contrast that sums up the place perfectly. Family, vintage, modernity and intention coexist naturally at Le Trente. The room has an immediate depth and character, and nothing feels forced: instinctively, you feel at home, whether it’s your first visit or you’re a regular. items.title: Badi Restaurant
items.summary: La entrada  Badi Restaurant  se publicó primero en  Openhouse Magazine .
items.text: Badi Restaurant — Openhouse Magazine Created with Sketch. Subscribe Order Issue 26 Shop Studios My account Search Architecture , Design , Food Badi Restaurant A Layered Sense of Taste Written by Patty Castellar Photographed by Adrien Maurice & Benjamin Baltus Facebook Twitter Linkedin Share For Victoria Merret and Maxime Bourdigal, Badi embraces everything: their job, their interests, their tastes, their values, and their personality. In other words, Badi embodies the couple’s vision. Every sphere comes together under the same sensibility: a pursuit of balance between beauty, precision, and flavour. At Badi, located in Saint-Gilles (Brussels), design , materials, and cuisine interact seamlessly. Initially, the idea sparked for a cider bar: “We kept saying to ourselves: ‘We’d love to go to a wine bar that serves a hundred different ciders,’ so we decided to create it.” As a product that hits close to home with their Breton roots, it seemed like an effortless path to take. Close Nevertheless, three years after opening, Badi has now established itself as a fully-fledged restaurant. “We rediscovered ourselves through the world of natural wine,” and the evolution came instinctively. A place where raw products and ingredients are at the centre of everything, and that is guided by honesty, quality and craftsmanship. The menu and the space complement each other, sculpting an experience that is both curated yet welcoming. In the kitchen, Maxime, who has worked for Bertrand Larcher in Paris and Japan, as well as Ötap in Brussels, collaborates with Paul-Antoine Bertin (Rebel, Grain, Raki, Ötap…) to develop product-centred menus. For the interior, the couple worked with Nelly Smets. Close “We immediately connected through a shared vision regarding materials and influences, but the challenge was then to make all the elements work together harmoniously,” they comment. Inspired by Nordic and Japanese style, raw elements were non-negotiable. Wood, natural stone, steel, textured walls… They all come together around the protagonist of the show. Close A large central travertine counter dominates the space, defining a cohesive and immersive experience. And that was the intention from the beginning: “The central counter encourages interaction with our guests because everyone is seated at the same height, forming a closeness.” The environment becomes convivial, light, easygoing, and authentic. “We would probably say that our home is more an extension of the restaurant.” “The design of the space is much more connected to the food and drinks selection than people might think.” Built by craftsmen with honest materials, this philosophy equally translates to the curation of the menu: “It’s just as we do when selecting our natural ciders, wines, and ingredients for the kitchen.” Constantly adapting to the seasons, every menu balances freshness, indulgence, comfort, and elegance, while keeping everything approachable and never overly complex. Close This same ethos translates to Victoria and Maxime’s home: “We would probably say that our home is more an extension of the restaurant.” Separating work and private life, the apartment was also driven by the desire to work with raw resources, with wood playing a very important role, but this time in a more personal way. Close “For the restaurant, we tried to develop the most timeless design possible so it could age beautifully over the years. For the apartment, however, we allowed ourselves to make stronger choices to build something with a more distinctive identity.” Altogether, with the help of Nelly Smets and, for their home, her daughter Iolie Coufo. Close In both spaces, the couple is present in many ways. “We constantly dig into memories, experiences, and travels to shape our inspirations; a mix of different influences and emotions we’ve collected over the years, brought together in a way that feels genuinely ours.” For Victoria and Maxime, interior design is about much more than conceiving beautiful places; it’s about shaping spaces where people come to create meaningful moments. items.title: Jaç HiFI Café
items.summary: La entrada  Jaç HiFI Café  se publicó primero en  Openhouse Magazine .
items.text: Jaç HiFI Café — Openhouse Magazine Created with Sketch. Subscribe Order Issue 26 Shop Studios My account Search Architecture , Design Jaç HiFI Café A 21st century temple of sound Photographed by Salva López Written by Openhouse Studio Facebook Twitter Linkedin Share A new café has taken over Avinguda Diagonal 335, in the heart of Barcelona: JAÇ HiFi Café. Designed by Isern Serra Studio , the space opened in July 2025 with not one, but two missions: to invite guests to drink coffee and to listen. In fact, its name carries multiple meanings: a nod to jazz music itself, a reference to Japan’s jazz kissa and in Catalan, the word “jaç,” which means to recline, rest, and let go. But, what were jazz kissa ? Characterized by compact and dimly lit venues, these spaces were intimate listening bars that flourished from the 1950s onwards and were dedicated entirely to the appreciation of recorded jazz. Its complex nature, designed and conceived as temples of sound, found no similarities elsewhere: they were neither bars in the Western sense nor cafés in the European style. Close Instead, in jazz kissa , conversation was minimal, the record player was sacred, and music was played on high-fidelity equipment at volumes that demanded full attention. Originating after the Second World War, kissa provided a haven for serious listeners who could not afford records or audio systems of their own. Over decades, their interiors developed a distinct aesthetic — wood-panelled walls, warm lighting, and seating arranged to face the speakers rather than each other — creating a sense of intimacy and deep focus. Close JAÇ HiFi Café reinterprets that philosophy for a contemporary Mediterranean city. The design is warm yet refined, with an emphasis on tactile materials and an atmosphere that feels as familiar as one’s own living room. The space, covering 95 square metres, unfolds in a series of distinct zones, each offering a different relationship with music, people, and the city outside. Close In the lounge area, iconic pieces such as Akari E lamp by Isamu Noguchi and artwork by artist Chidy Wayne welcome the visitors. Further into the bar, a monolithic piece of walnut wood that doubles as a giant speaker cabinet plays both parts, as a functional counter and audio sculpture. The most dramatic element of JAÇ, however, lies toward the rear: a large walnut-wood installation that curves across walls and ceiling to form a semi-enclosed listening alcove. The effect is immersive — a space that seems to embrace the listener, pulling them into a cocoon of warm wood and resonant sound. Close Overall, JAÇ conveys a special closeness, brought by its design and enhanced by the music and the people that enjoy it. With contrasting but matching materials, the space is given its own unique personality, bridging Japanese precision with Mediterranean ease. All accompanied by lighting, shaping the atmosphere and framing shared moments. JAÇ HiFi Café ultimately reimagines the jazz kissa experience for 21st-century Barcelona. It offers a place to slow down, to sit alone or with friends, to discover a song or hear an old favourite in new detail, and to inhabit a space where design, music, and human presence are in perfect balance. Subscribe Order Issue 26 Shop Studios My account Search Food YESS Restaurant “A little bit of effort” (and a whole lot of fire) Photographed by Austin Leis Written by Forde Visser Facebook Twitter Linkedin Share On the morning I met with Junya Yamasaki, chef and partner of YESS restaurant , he arrived with armloads of wild fennel—stalky and open, a tangled supernova exuberance of yellow flowers. Because I had already made a cursory tour of Junya’s online presence, I was not surprised; I knew this activity was not unusual. Close YESS, an izakaya style “progressive Japanese restaurant” (website) opened in 2024 in the Arts District of Los Angeles. That’s the simple version of a more detoured (but no time wasted) trajectory. Junya, from the Japanese region of Kansai, began to map his career(s) through Tokyo, London, and Paris, studying (respectively) politics, photography and fine arts . In Tokyo he had also worked in film, but in Paris a restaurant kitchen job pointed him towards the culinary world, and eventually a return to London to help develop the wildly popular Koya noodle bar, which significantly diversified London’s Japanese food scene with traditional udon and inventive daily specials. Close In addition to Junya’s commitment to the local and seasonal present, he also holds a reverence for change, which has been mightily exercised since the restaurant’s beginnings. This year, between the LA Fires and the immigration dynamics, Los Angeles has been a special test. YESS took a breath, a short pause to ensure a safe environment for everyone, and exhaled with a new invitation, the addition of a lunch menu. As welcoming as an exuberance of flowers. items.title: Kissabō: A Contemporary Japanese Tea Bar in Berlin
items.summary: The post  Kissabō: A Contemporary Japanese Tea Bar in Berlin  appeared first on  IGNANT .
items.text: Name Kissabō Images Clemens Poloczek Words Rosie Flanagan On a sunny tree-lined street in Berlin’s Prenzlauer Berg, plum-coloured noren (暖簾) — traditional Japanese split curtains — float gently in the breeze. They mark the doorway to Kissabō , a 16-seat tea bar that its owners, Marcin and Gosia Chelkowski, describe as a space for attention and curiosity. Two years ago, the couple moved to Berlin from Szczecin in Poland to realise an idea that had been brewing across their lives. As Gosia explains, “there wasn’t a specific moment in time that Marcin and I came to tea, it was very gradual.” Marcin continues, “In Poland, we were exposed to a lot of Japanese culture through videos and gaming when we were growing up. My thoughts when I was young were, well, Japanese games are cool, so everything in Japan must be cool! [Laughs] So as soon as we could afford to visit there, we did.” Gosia adds, “Instantly, we felt very at home.” Their first visit to Japan was twelve years ago, and since that fateful trip, they have returned almost every year. “We thought, well, we like it so much here, maybe we shouldn’t waste time visiting or experiencing other things,” Marcin says, Gosia nodding in agreement. It was on these visits that they were first exposed to a culture of tea: from the crisp bottles lining convenience store shelves, to the formal practice of chanoyu (茶の湯) practiced in tea houses. “In Japan, tea is everywhere,” Marcin notes. “But when we began drinking tea, we weren’t really pursuing it with intention. As we continued, we began to develop an understanding of the culture — a curiosity about the practice and the way it is connected to something more meaningful.” They describe their path to opening a tea bar as something like osmosis: every time they visited Japan, they met more and more people related to the world of tea — farmers, teachers, craftspeople — and their interest grew. Neither comes from a hospitality background, but both had reached a point in their careers where they felt the need for change. “We were talking to a friend who has a tea school in Kyoto, and he said something that really vibed with us. He told us that for him, having tea during a tea gathering — what we in the West call a tea ceremony — is like a visit to an onsen, it’s a form of relaxation. You take time out of your day to get there, and you know that it will bring calm and clarity. We found this really interesting and started thinking about tea in this kind of direction.” In The Book of Tea, Okakura Kakuzō wrote that “Tea is more than an idealisation of the form of drinking; it is a religion of the art of life.” Published in 1906, the tea philosopher’s seminal work introduced Western audiences to an understanding of tea as an expression of Japanese aesthetics and spirituality; a practice of attentiveness shaped by its entanglement with Zen Buddhism and Taoist ideas of simplicity, impermanence, and the beauty of the ordinary. The sixteenth-century tea master and cultural reformer Sen no Rikyū refined the developing wabi-cha (侘び茶) tradition, in which tea ceremonies emphasised humility and restraint. "In Japan, there is a culture of kissaten (喫茶店), traditional cafés where you come to relax, be silent, and listen to music." With this rich history in mind, Marcin notes that tea culture itself can be very broad. “It can be very casual, it can be very simple: it is special in different ways. There are many places you might be afraid to step into because you feel you don’t possess the experience required. We want to remove that ‘knowledge’ barrier and make it easy for everyone to share in our curiosity.” The result is a space that draws from the rich culture of tea houses and ceremonies, but renders it slightly anew. “Beyond appreciation for the craft, the culture, and everything that surrounds it was really the desire to create an easy-going atmosphere. In Japan, there is a culture of kissaten (喫茶店), traditional cafés where you come to relax, be silent, and listen to music. We thought this idea was great. Why not present the depth of tea in this way?” "We really believe in creating an atmosphere of attention." The kissaten tradition offers a useful lens: where the formal tea ceremony demands studied preparation and ritual knowledge, the kissaten asks only that you sit and attend. Kissabō’s name draws on this lineage. Written 喫茶房, it shares its first two characters with kissaten — 喫茶, tea-drinking — but swaps 店, shop, for 房, chamber. A quieter word for a quieter place; and in Berlin, where inner-city neighbourhoods are crowded with VC-backed coffee chains serving thousands of three-euro flat whites, a completely unique hospitality offering. As are Kissabō’s guidelines: lowered voices, no photography or filming of those present without their consent, and the expectation of queueing quietly outside during busy times. “We really believe in creating an atmosphere of attention,” Marcin explains. “And since opening, we’ve observed that people really enjoy this — the calming of the space — even if they didn’t have that intention when they arrived.” "Nobody is in a rush when they see how much attention is being put in." When visiting Kissabō, it is easy to see how it elicits such a response. The earthen-toned interior – replete with a custom oakwood tea bar, a communal table, a tatami area, and Noguchi light sculptures – is warm and atmospheric. “Everything kind of blends in, but has a voice of its own,” says Gosia. Their tea offerings – currently matcha, gyokuro, genmaicha, and hōjicha – are sourced from Japan and served alongside non-alcoholic seasonal cocktails and a range of handmade Japanese sweets. “We are very fortunate that people have trusted us with their work, their traditions, their years of culture. It is very humbling, and we are trying to do our best to share it in a proper way: without fuss, without overexplaining, always with proper care. items.title: Strom by Celeste Asfour: A Seasonal Café Where Reverie Meets Play
items.summary: The post  Strom by Celeste Asfour: A Seasonal Café Where Reverie Meets Play  appeared first on  IGNANT .
items.text: Name Celeste Asfour Images Clemens Poloczek Words Rosie Flanagan In the heart of Berlin, a quiet courtyard sits framed by historic properties that once thrummed with the energy of industry. Here, on the ground floor of a 19th-century building, you’ll find Strom —a café where reverie meets play, conceptualised by Berlin-based architectural multihyphenate Celeste Asfour . Celeste’s early life unfolded in an architectural household. “I grew up completely surrounded by it,” she explains. “As a child, my mum was always dragging me to museums and construction sites.” For a time, such proximity made her hesitant about joining the world of design. “That is, until I realised I was lying to myself,” she laughs. While grounded in architecture, her practice finds form in a range of aesthetic expressions—from interior design to objects and photography. “My philosophy now is to take what is there and work with it. That’s why I prefer the scale of interior architecture.” She says that this path emerged while studying: “It was at university that I realised I might not want to be an architect in the classical sense, because I had a problem with the scale required. It was always: Building, building, building. New, new, new. And that’s just not how I enjoy working.” Her approach turned to what already exists, to material research, and a combination of old and new. “My philosophy now is to take what is there and work with it. That’s why I prefer the scale of interior architecture.” In late 2024, she was approached with a proposition that closely aligned with her interests: a to-be-determined café, bar, or bistro set on the ground floor of a historic complex that was once home to Berlin’s earliest and most successful restaurateurs. Today, the 19th-century buildings are populated by a new generation of businesses, start-ups, and studios whose offices overlook a large internal courtyard. “The courtyard is beautiful and so are the buildings,” Celeste notes. “But it is a space that was never really used by the public because it wasn’t activated—you would never walk in and discover it unless you worked there.” "In general, I love creating spaces where people meet and interact, so this gastronomy project was ideal..." This project was determined to change this, and—unusually—Celeste joined at its very inception. “It was quite a different setup,” she recalls, “there was no name, no logo, no website, no branding, no colours.” Working with the founders and Swedish branding and design agency Several, Celeste helped imagine what kind of offering would best serve the location. “In general, I love creating spaces where people meet and interact, so this gastronomy project was ideal,” she adds. “The outcome was really shaped by the process: by the way it began, by the space and its requirements, and by the people that I worked with, and by a desire to have fun with it.” From their early conversations, an idea emerged: a seasonal café for artisanal coffee, small plates, and afternoon drinks. A space that would transform the courtyard from a place of transit to one of gathering and encounter. The courtyard has three entrances through which people stream in and out of each day—this perpetual circulation animates the area and renders it a kind of “safe harbour,” says Celeste. From here came the café’s name: Strom translates from German as “electrical current” or “stream”: a flow of people and energy. “I hate when everything is completely beige or lacquered, when spaces don’t have any sense of texture." The graphic identity embraces these ideas. Playful and minimal, its refined sensibility bounces across the webpage and stacks atop itself in the logo. This concept is given physical form by Celeste’s interior design, which focuses on spatial arrangement and a balance of materials. “In every project, I think you have to create some sort of tension,” she says. “I hate when everything is completely beige or lacquered, when spaces don’t have any sense of texture. You have to balance hard things with soft things. That kind of tension results in balance.” In Strom, this balance emerges through combining traditional techniques and historic elements with contemporary processes and objects. “A lot of thought went into the textures and materials,” Celeste explains. “We spent a long time selecting the marble and the wood, considering how the colours and forms would work together.” The rich darkness of the oiled cherry wood contrasts with the bright weight of the brutalist-edged rose marble counter. The tension between these elements is counterbalanced by the softness of the locally handmade terracotta tiles covering the floor. These organic materials are complemented by a range of modern finishes that lend the space a distinct character. Brushed-steel shelves, produced by Studio Ultimo alongside the wooden panelling, hold magazines and objects that Celeste sourced from local antique markets. One shelf provides a view into the kitchen, giving guests a small insight into the creation of their plates before they arrive at their tables. Another features a mirrored backing that adds further depth to the space. Milky-hued mauve tabletops, made from recycled polycarbonate ‘Karlite’ by Dutch studio Plasticiet, are grounded by wooden chairs from Form&Refine and bench seats upholstered in Kvadrat fabric. The space features concertina windows that open the café to the courtyard during warmer weather. When the sun is high, they bring ample light into the space. During the winter months, the lighting design is used for aesthetic form and atmospheric effect. Hand-textured Murano sconces from Milan-based studio 6 am cast a warm rose-hued glow across the interior. A Noguchi lamp throws papered light from the shelves, and a faceted pendant by Asca Studio draws the line of sight to the coffee bar below it. Though the interior is undoubtedly elevated, it is not without a sense of play. The bathroom has been completed with a bulbous, bubble-gum pink sink, whi

items.title: TRADER HiFi Tunes Hamburg’s Coffee Culture to a New Frequency
items.summary: The post  TRADER HiFi Tunes Hamburg’s Coffee Culture to a New Frequency  appeared first on  IGNANT .
items.text: Name TRADER HiFi Images Clemens Poloczek Words Anna Dorothea Ker Hamburg’s growing TRADER constellation stems from founder Vincent von Thien’s wish to offer his city more than another café. TRADER Gallery in the Schanze set the first tone, uniting specialty coffee with art and design. The latest outpost, TRADER HiFi in the city’s Ottensen district, brings von Thien’s interest in sound into clearer focus. Drawn from the lineage of Japanese kissas and tuned to contemporary life, the space shifts between daytime sociability and evening sessions that invite attentive listening. A considered acoustic architecture, a custom sound system and collaborations with design studios across Europe give the small space its distinctive presence. What emerges is a third place where listening becomes a shared daily pleasure. Origins Vincent von Thien’s route to TRADER began years earlier during long stints in Australia during his modelling career. Sydney in 2011 introduced him to a style of café culture he hadn’t encountered at home—in his words, “my first real encounter with the specialty coffee scene.” It left a mark, even though the tools to build something similar in Germany were out of reach at the time. He began with a mobile version, launching Coffee Bike Hamburg with a friend and serving espresso at festivals. When modelling lost its appeal, he returned to the idea of a fixed space. A small unit in the harbor city’s Schanze district became TRADER Gallery, combining coffee with art and a selection of vintage design. von Thien wanted to offer something civic, not only commercial. “A small fusion of specialty coffee and art,” as he puts it; “to give Hamburg something more than just another café around the corner. I liked the idea of offering emerging artists a fair platform.” TRADER Gallery laid the groundwork for what would follow. Its second iteration, TRADER HiFi—opened in Ottensen in September 2025—extends that vision into the field of sound. Culture of Listening TRADER HiFi’s framework comes from Japan’s jazz kissas—listening cafés—of the 1970s, where, as von Thien puts it, “people could listen to music in high-quality sound because they didn’t have the equipment at home.” He matched this with the atmosphere of today’s listening bars, then rethought the model for Hamburg. The café works in two modes. Days are social, shaped by DJs whose sets provide a spirited backdrop to conversation. Evenings shift to focused sessions where the room falls still. “The idea is that for those sessions we ask people not to talk,” von Thien shares. “They’re dedicated to music.” Performances range from live sets to curated record journeys routed directly through the custom sound system. An accompanying beverage program keeps the mood clear-minded. “We don’t serve alcohol, as I want full focus on specialty coffee and music.” Programming Eclecticism Though still young, TRADER HiFi has already welcomed a wide sweep of genres. “We’ve already had world music, ambient, jazz, disco house,” von Thien shares. Artists such as Coco Maria, Barış Kadem and Dounia hint at the range that threads through the programme, alongside recurring sets by Panama.x and others. “What matters is high-quality music and talented people,” von Thien says. The format attracts those looking for a change in pace or setting, and requests arrive from both Hamburg and abroad. “We’re getting lots of requests from DJs, including international ones. It shows there’s a real need here in Hamburg.” As the first listening café in the city, TRADER HiFi gives artists a venue to explore ideas outside the club context. “Many DJs want to break out of their usual musical setting or play in a different environment, maybe even try another genre,” von Thien notes. The only condition is that the set suits the space. “It’s not a party. It should fit the concept, and artists should have freedom to shape the evening as they imagine.” Room for Sound The interior in Ottensen had to support both hospitality and audio without asserting either too strongly. von Thien pursued his vision for a room that settled the senses. “I wanted to create a timeless, grounding space that suits the music, an atmosphere that invites you to linger and feel calm,” he explains. Cork became central to the acoustic design. Burnt cork lines the ceiling of the main listening room, and a required structural beam was enlarged, packed with acoustic wool and wrapped in cork, acting as a central sound absorber. The custom concept grew in partnership with Antwerp-based Studio Corkinho , whose practice draws on the Alentejo’s long tradition of harvesting oak bark and reworking reclaimed cork into objects and spatial elements with a highly sensorial presence. For the sound system, von Thien worked closely with H.A.N.D. HiFi in Berlin. They developed the layout of the horns, booth and supporting speakers, ensuring the acoustic performance sits naturally within the space. With 70 square meters to work with, every decision counted. To define its configuration, von Thien spent in the emptied space, studying how people would move and where sound would settle. “I moved ideas around, thought things through,” he shares. The footprint is compact, so circulation and bar flow had to work intuitively. Collaborators contributed meaningfully to the final environment. Lisbon-based THER created furniture pieces that lend the room its stripped-back clarity, including wooden tables informed by Japanese woodworking techniques and produced with Portuguese carpentry studio Nó Marceneiros . Brussels-based porcelain studio Frizbee Ceramics produced the tableware used throughout the café, and Vitra supported the project with Akari lamps that bring a soft, diffused light to the interior. Von Thien emphasizes the long view that guided his collaborations: “The idea wasn’t to create hype, but to build a place that still works ten years from now.” A Growing Menu Specialty coffee anchors the beverage program at TRADER HiFi. items.title: Chef Michele Esposito Draws on His Italian Roots for Lido’s Exquisite Mediterranean Flavor
items.summary:
Inside The Surf Club’s original ballroom, the culinary wonder has crafted a menu driven by dishes that create a bridge between the Amalfi Coast and Miami Beach 
 The post  Chef Michele Esposito Draws on His Italian Roots for Lido’s Exquisite Mediterranean Flavor  appeared first on  Galerie Magazine .
items.text: Lido Restaurant at the Surf Club. Photo: Courtesy of Four Seasons Hotel at The Surf Club The Surf Club at the Four Seasons in Miami is famous for many things—its historic past as the winter playground for cultural elites such as Winston Churchill and the Kennedys, an architectural marvel with a reimagined tower by Richard Meier with breathtakingly chic interiors by Joseph Dirand , and a culinary destination with an acclaimed restaurant by culinary legend Thomas Keller . Now, Michele Esposito, the executive chef of Lido , is poised to become one more extraordinary reason to visit. Chef Michele Esposito. Photo: Courtesy of Four Seasons Hotel at The Surf Club Esposito joined Lido, the restaurant located in its original ballroom and oceanfront terrace, this summer—after holding positions at Villa Crespi and Quattro Passi, both three Michelin-starred restaurants in Italy, as well as locally as the executive chef at Casa Tua in Miami. He draws on his Italian roots to create a menu filled with authentic Mediterranean flavors. “I do not believe in making dishes complicated simply to make them appear sophisticated,” says Esposito, whose culinary philosophy fits right in with Miami culture. “To me, true luxury lies in the quality of the ingredients, the precision of execution, and the ability to transform something simple into a memorable experience.” Linguine Nerano. Photo: Courtesy of Four Seasons Hotel at The Surf Club Scallops Crudo. Photo: Courtesy of Four Seasons Hotel at The Surf Club Esposito delivers on that viewpoint with standouts that create a bridge between Miami Beach and the Amalfi Coast. An order of tagliolini al limone with red prawns instantly transports guests to the Amalfi Coast with its delicate presentation of the seafood, heightened by the zing of just enough lemon. The chef shares that one of the most personal dishes is linguine nerano, a zucchini dish, which is a tribute to his mentor Antonino Mellino, chef and owner of the three-Michelin-starred Quattro Passi restaurant in Nerano. There’s also his ravioli filled with a veal ragù, which reminds him of Sundays with his family in Naples. “My cooking is deeply connected to memories, family traditions, and the flavors of Southern Italy, while remaining open to creativity and international influences,” Esposito shares. Lido Restaurant at the Surf Club. Photo: Courtesy of Four Seasons Hotel at The Surf Club Given Esposito’s background, there’s also an exceptional pasta pomodoro, the execution of which is said to the be the true measure of any Italian chef. To create this signature sauce, he blends a variety of tomatoes including San Marzano DOP tomatoes, yellow tomatoes from Mount Vesuvius, and cherry tomatoes from the Agro Nocerino region. Each variety brings its own unique characteristics, creating a sauce that is naturally sweet, rich in flavor, and beautifully balanced. “I believe the true skill of a chef lies in highlighting an ingredient without losing its identity,” he says. In hands, the tomato is beautifully honored. While one might not typically associate Miami’s culinary scene with Italian flavors, Esposito’s skillful and soulful cooking at Lido is bound to change that. Feasting on his fresh and light take on Mediterranean cuisine feels right at home on the breezy Lido terrace overlooking the ocean—even if it is the Atlantic. “I want every guest to discover something about my homeland or reconnect with a special memory of a journey to Italy through a familiar flavor,” says the chef. “For me, that is the true essence of cooking: creating emotions through food.” Tags: Miami Richard Meier Thomas Keller Winston Churchill

items.title: Hotel of the Week: In Provence, Three Artist Brothers Transform a Collection of Romantic Houses and Gardens into an Edenic Retreat
items.summary:
At Toile Blanche near Saint-Paul-de-Vence, an adventurous collection of works animates lush, rambling gardens, bucolic paths, and elegantly reserved suites  
 The post  Hotel of the Week: In Provence, Three Artist Brothers Transform a Collection of Romantic Houses and Gardens into an Edenic Retreat  appeared first on  Galerie Magazine .
items.text: Toile Blanche, Saint-Paul-de-Vence. Photo: Courtesy of Toile Blanche In the wooded hills of Provence, where Chagall imagined floating lovers, Matisse painted pomegranates and palm trees, and the Fondation Maeght has drawn contemporary art lovers for decades, it’s hardly surprising to find a hotel created by three artist brothers. At Toile Blanche , just outside Saint-Paul-de-Vence, the Belgian-born Leroys—Nicolas, Gilles, and Gregory—have turned a collection of houses into an intimate 22-room retreat, filling the rooms, terraces, and gardens with their own work as well as pieces by some artist friends. There are sculptures to discover along the garden paths, a contemporary art gallery hosting changing exhibitions beneath reception, and surprises at almost every turn. Toile Blanche. Photo: Courtesy of Toile Blanche Toile Blanche. Photo: Courtesy of Toile Blanche Toile Blanche. Photo: Courtesy of Toile Blanche The property, open year-round, feels more like a small hamlet than a hotel , with separate Mexican-meets-Moroccan-style houses connected by winding paths through gardens planted with lavender, olive trees, and Mediterranean shrubs. Alongside a restaurant, an open-air guinguette, three swimming pools and a pétanque court, art is everywhere, from monumental sculptures in the gardens to paintings and photographs in the bedrooms. The whimsy is subtle, laced with a streak of irreverence, whether it’s the Leroy Brothers’ Art for Money, Money for Art —featuring a squirrel, a pig, and a gold-digging mole burrowing through a mountain of their own handmade coins —or the cryptic sayings in the bedrooms that leave guests pondering as they hit the pillow: “Nothing big and nothing little, everything is that size.” These plexiglass-encased sayings are drawn from Witness Your World, the Leroys online platform that invites people to submit photographs and phrases. Guest suite at Toile Blanche. Photo: Courtesy of Toile Blanche Guest suite at Toile Blanche. Photo: Courtesy of Toile Blanche The story of the hotel began with the brothers’ father, Dany Leroy, who served as a consultant to Belgian art dealer Guy Pieters at his gallery in Saint-Paul-de-Vence. The family eventually settled in the enclave, where they opened Toile Blanche, initially a modest bed-and-breakfast with just three rooms and a restaurant, that soon attracted a loyal following. Two decades later, the brothers were preparing to expand when COVID brought their plans to a halt. Soon after three neighboring properties came up for sale at once. With banks reluctant to finance a hotel project during the pandemic, they turned to friends for help and found themselves competing with major property developers. “We were fighting the big ones,” Gregory recalls. “We won!” Toile Blanche. Photo: Courtesy of Toile Blanche Inside, the rooms vary in shape and size, but many have the feel of private little haciendas, particularly the spacious duplex suites. With their lofty ceilings, sleek furnishings, and Breccia marble kitchen counters, the interiors are minimalist yet far from austere. Original works by the Leroy brothers hang in every room, adding a jolt of color or humor. Many of these, along with pieces exhibited in the gallery, are available for purchase. Bedrooms have warm plaster-toned walls, linen throws, and tiny glasses of herbs freshly picked from the garden. Tadelakt floors and sculptural basins lend the bathrooms an almost spa-like quality. The most sought-after accommodations: four suites opening onto sun-drenched wooden decks with private heated swimming pools, screened by Mediterranean greenery from the rest of the property. Toile Blanche. Photo: Courtesy of Toile Blanche Toile Blanche. Photo: Courtesy of Toile Blanche Toile Blanche. Photo: Courtesy of Toile Blanche On warm days, the guinguette takes over a corner of the tree-shaded, fragrant garden, with a menu of Provençal dishes designed for sharing, including petits farcis niçois , the region’s traditional stuffed vegetables. After a Provençal Spritz on the cocktail deck overlooking a small carp pond, guests drift toward the open-air restaurant terrace, with the swimming pool below and the silhouette of Saint-Paul-de-Vence against the blue-gray foothills in the distance. French classics get a creative twist, from roasted scallops with hazelnuts, endive and kumquat to beautifully cooked lamb served with glazed carrots, followed by a lemon dessert with contrasting textures. Art makes its way to the table, too, from works by the Leroy brothers in the interior dining room right down to the slightly Alice in Wonderland-ish illustrated menus, including a breakfast scene featuring a formally dressed hare announcing, “A promising start to the day.” Outdoor terrace at Toile Blanche. Photo: Courtesy of Toile Blanche In partnership with Galerie Podgorny, Toile Blanche has created an outdoor sculpture park featuring works by international artists, including Arik Levy and the Gao Brothers. New pieces arrive regularly, and some, especially commissioned for the property, from Ora Ïto’s blue circles on the side of a building to Gregory Orekhov’s arresting gold tree outside reception. The collection is a family affair, too, with more discreet works by the brothers’ grandfather, Raymond Leroy, to be discovered along the garden paths. Their latest initiative, RAD/ART, is a digital guide to appreciating contemporary art in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, which can be reached on foot via a path behind the hotel. A work by Arik Levy installed at Toile Blanche. Photo: Courtesy of Toile Blanche Gregory Orekhov, Magic Bed (202). Photo: Courtesy of Toile Blanche The brothers aren’t finished yet—six more rooms, a spa, and an expanded restaurant are on the horizon. But their most ambitious project is still to come: a center devoted to creativity rather than commerce. “That will be the cherry on the cake, the art center,” Gregory says. And then, almost as an afterthought, he adds: “Always in the end, the art.” Tags: Art

items.title: Editor in Chief Jacqueline Terrebonne Shares Highlights from Galerie’s Winter Issue
items.summary:
This edition features 12 rising stars in the art world, five up-and-coming interior designers you need to know now, and the stunning transformation of Sea Island’s ladies’ lounge into a tranquil haven 
 The post  Editor in Chief Jacqueline Terrebonne Shares Highlights from <i>Galerie’s</i> Winter Issue  appeared first on  Galerie Magazine .
items.text: A living room in Marin County, California, by Chroma. Photo: STEPHEN KENT JOHNSON, STYLED BY YEDDA MORRISON Celebrating the tenth anniversary of Galerie this year has me reflecting on how the magazine has stayed true to the original vision of our founder and editorial director, Lisa Fayne Cohen. It all started with her realization that there was nothing on the market that spoke to both art and design , showcasing homes with dynamic collections that elevate the decor to new heights. Over the past decade, Galerie has brilliantly delivered on her mission—sharing how to Live Artfully. With James Cohen, chairman of Hudson One Media, and Lisa Fayne Cohen. Photo: KELLY TAUB The kitchen dining area in the Paris home of Oscar Lucien Ono. Photo: AMAURY LAPARRA A sketch of the Butterflies bracelets (1956) by Jean Schlumberger from the Musée des Arts Décoratifs’ archives. Photo: © MUSÉE DES ARTS DÉCORATIFS That driving sentiment is wondrously depicted on this issue’s cover, featuring Paris -based designer Oscar Lucien Ono ’s own home. By mixing artworks by Eduardo Chillida and Fernand Léger with design treasures by Willy Rizzo and Pierre Chareau, he achieves a glorious balance resulting in a sultry, transportive atmosphere that’s pure magic. We also look at how our core concept spreads to other métiers, including the way legendary Tiffany & Co. jeweler Jean Schlumberger was at heart an artist. Haejin Park Enough to Shimmer , (2026). Photo: CHRIS GARDNER, COURTESY OF THE ARTIST Another important focus for Lisa has always been shining a light on up-and-coming creatives who are destined for greatness. Every winter, that promise takes shape in Galerie’ s annual list of emerging artists , who are chosen by a group of art-world luminaries. This special portfolio of 12 exhilarating new voices represents a wide range of mediums and styles—from Haejin Park ’s color-soaked paintings to the digitally manipulated photographs of Akari Takenobu . In the Ladies’ Links Lounge, designed by Bill Brockschmidt and Courtney Coleman of Brockschmidt & Coleman, a vibrant abstract artwork from Wendover Art Group reverberates against Sanderson’s large-scale Cantaloupe print wallpaper. And in a first-of-its-kind project for the magazine, Galerie partnered with Sea Island on the reinvention of its Ladies’ Locker Room . We tapped esteemed New Orleans- and New York-based firm Brockschmidt & Coleman for the task of creating a space where women would want to relax and spend time after a round. Verve double diamond ring by Fie Isolde. Photo: COURTESY OF FIE ISOLDE In addition, we profile a host of on-the-rise interior designers , including San Francisco–based studio Chroma, with its fearless mix of art and interiors, as well as select a notable group of jewelry designers who are the names to know now, including Fie Isolde, who envelops diamonds in free-flowing gold forms. It’s exciting to think about how they will hone their craft in the years to come and how they will grow and evolve while honoring their original vision—just as we have at Galerie . A version of this article first appeared in print in our 2026 Winter Issue. Subscribe to the magazine. Tags: Emerging Artists Jean Schlumberger Oscar Lucien Ono Tiffany & Co.

items.title: Oscar Lucien Ono Puts a Dramatic Touch on His Historic Paris Apartment
items.summary:
The Maison Numéro 20 founder known for transforming the world’s most memorable boutique hotels brings his panache and a penchant for chiaroscuro to his home 
 The post  Oscar Lucien Ono Puts a Dramatic Touch on His Historic Paris Apartment  appeared first on  Galerie Magazine .
items.text: n the Marais home Oscar Lucien Ono shares with his husband, Rubén Cuenca Ramos, a custom curved sofa in a Misia mohair velvet faces a vintage Willy Rizzo cocktail table with a built-in bowl. A 1970s chandelier hangs from the lacquered ceiling. When designer Oscar Lucien Ono and his husband, Rubén Cuenca Ramos, bought their Paris apartment, they left it untouched for the first 12 months. “It stood empty,” Ono admits, adding, “I didn’t know where to start.” Since he founded his interiors studio, Maison Numéro 20 , in 2014, his projects have included the restoration of the Paris cabaret Paradis Latin; an apartment in a historic building in Madrid ; and more than 30 hotels , including Le Soleia in Nice, Villa Miraé in Cap d’Antibes, and Hôtel Elysia in Paris. His signature style is rooted in classicism, pairing glamour and fine craftsmanship with a predilection for both 1930s and ’70s design as well as luxurious materials like lacquer and varnished woods. Still, when it came to his own home, he initially toyed with a completely different look. “None of it felt like me,” he recalls. “As soon as I got back to something that reflected my taste, things quickly fit into place.” Several factors attracted him to the apartment, located on the ground floor of a circa-1700 townhouse near Place des Vosges. The exterior was immortalized in the early 20th century by Eugène Atget, the photographer known for his haunting images of a bygone Paris. “I’m very drawn to anything old,” says Ono, who studied art history at the École du Louvre, specializing in ancient Greece and Rome . Ono is joined by a Hamilton Conte side table and a sconce by Pierre Chareau; the fireplace is of Portoro marble with a chimney breast covered in églomisé glass panels. The interior courtyard dates from the historic townhouse’s original construction, circa 1700. Seventeenth-century garden statuary enlivens the courtyard. He was also charmed by the garden in the paved courtyard, as well as by the residence’s lofty proportions. Yet the space came with challenges. The only windows were the ones at the front of the living room, and there were few original architectural details, except for some of the wood beams. With plenty of ceiling height to work with, Ono decided to conceal even those behind a lacquered, lowered ceiling in the living room. “They didn’t fit the mood I was after,” he explains. That space—hushed, intimate, and a touch nocturnal—is more aligned with the atmosphere Ono was hoping to create. Part of his inspiration came from Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé’s rue de Babylone duplex apartment on the city’s Left Bank. “For me, it conjured up a passion for both objects and history,” he says of that celebrated home, which the couple decorated and curated over decades with their interior designer, Jacques Grange . In the living room alcove, custom chairs sit in front of an églomisé screen by Ulgador. The kitchen, which doubles as the dining room, has walls sheathed in Dedar moiré fabric. Vintage Pierre Lottier chairs with seats in a Schumacher textile pull up to a 1970s table. The 18th-century portrait is Spanish. The artworks of Caravaggio were also on Ono’s mind, with their moody contrasts between light and dark and palettes of gold and burnished bronze. “I’ve always been obsessed with Caravaggio’s paintings,” he says. “They have a dramatic tension.” Ono incorporated luxurious materials throughout the apartment, from millwork in Macassar ebony to a mantel of Portoro marble, a stone that was popular in the 1930s. Walls were clad in moiré fabrics, velvet, and microsuede, and the chimney breast and cupboard doors were sheathed in églomisé glass decorated with stylized trees. He even embellished the baseboards with a painted faux-marble motif and coated the teeth of the living room’s dentil cornice in two tones, alternating them irregularly, like the keys of a piano. “I wanted to give them a rhythmic, graphic quality,” he says. As soon as I got back to something that reflected my taste, things quickly fell into place” Oscar Lucien Ono The designer is drawn to objects that span eras and styles. On a living room shelf sits a miniature plaster replica of the pediment of the Folies Bergère, an object that was given to guests at the unveiling of the music hall’s new Art Deco façade in the 1920s. In the fireplace’s hearth, he placed a gargoyle sculpture that is believed to have belonged to a granddaughter of French president Charles de Gaulle. A minotaur sculpture by his friend Rose de Ganay, on a console in the living room, and a classical bust near the bath speak to his love of antiquity. The Willy Rizzo cocktail table is a touchstone of 1970s design, while a Pierre Chareau stool is a beloved Art Deco find. “The shape is simple yet has presence,” he says of the latter. His most recent acquisition is a set of dining chairs by 20th-century French designer Pierre Lottier, who decorated a house for Ava Gardner in Spain. In the bath, 1970s lighting casts a warm glow against walls and floor clad in Emperador marble. Ono leaned into the bedroom’s darkness by covering the walls and ceiling in terra-cotta velvet. The bed, which has a headboard of Macassar ebony, is dressed in fabrics by Dedar, Romo, and Casamance. The artwork is by Keith Haring. The apartment that once sat empty while Ono figured out where to start is now a cabinet of delights. Its heart is the alcove to the left of the fireplace, which he formed by wrapping a pair of L-shaped screens around a trio of fringed armchairs. “It’s there that I talk things through with my husband or make calls,” says Ono. “And when a friend comes round, it’s inevitably there that we end up.” A version of this article first appeared in print in our 2026 Winter Issue under the headline “Holding Court.” Subscribe to the magazine. items.title: Shrine of the Most Blessed Sacrement in Hanceville, Alabama
items.summary:
Extraordinary architecture designed to resemble a 13th-century Italian Franciscan church, particularly the Basilica of Saint Francis of Assisi. Marble floors, gold ornamentation, stained glass, and soaring ceilings. 
 The Spanish religious-art workshop Talleres de Arte Granda, founded in Madrid in 1891, designed and furnished the church's interior. 
 It was founded by Mother Angelica, the founder of EWTN, and opened in 1999. Three donors provided all of the funds needed for construction and completion.

items.text: About Located in Maine's Acadia National Park, along the rocky shoreline of Mount Desert Island, Thunder Hole is a natural geological formation known for producing a booming, thunder-like sound phenomenon that gives it its name, as well as for explosive water sprays reaching up to 40 feet. Resulting from glacial activity over thousands of years ago, what began as a small, natural fissure in the solid granite cliffs, slowly gave way to the 10 foot wide channel seen today. As high tide rolls in, and wave force increases, water rushes into this channel, and into a small underwater cavern contained therein. When an incoming wave forces water into this cavern, trapped air in the cavern is compressed and then escapes, almost as if through the blow hole of a whale, with magnificent water sprays and reverberating claps that sound like thunder. Stand in awe on this rocky outcropping, as you take in the sweeping coastal views and the natural wonders that Mother Nature has provided. Thunder Hole is best viewed approx 2 hours before high tide (check google for tide tables). Know Before You Go Enter Acadia National Park and follow Park Loop Rd, which is a one way street that loops around the section of the park where Thunder Hole is located. Thunder Hole is approx 1-2 miles in from where you enter on Park Loop Road. Parking is available all along the right side of the road. You can park anywhere along here and walk the rest of the way along the pedestrian foot path that snakes along the left side of the road. There are multiple small trails along this path that lead down toward the water for closer viewing of rocky shores and beaches, etc. Take caution as some of these paths are steep and rocky. Not recommended for those with weakness or balance issues. While often steep and potentially treacherous, these little paths are short and the views are breathtaking. As you walk along, there will be plenty of beautiful, awe inspiring sights and you may find yourself exclaiming...this must be it! Or..is this Thunder Hole? What about this spot? The signage for Thunder Hole in not great. But, rest assured, you will know it when you see it. If a longer walk is not for you, that's ok! There is a very small gift shop and parking lot (on the right side of the street) located directly across the street from the main Thunder Hole viewing area. Parking lot does have a couple of handicapped parking spots, and the walk to the viewing area from there is quite short (approx 0.1 mile from parking lot to accessible viewing ramp and walkway). Note that parking lot fills up quickly during peak summer months. Alternately, you can use the free Island Explorer Shuttle bus which makes regular stops right at the entrance to the Thunder Hole parking lot. listed address takes you to the gift shop across the street Community Contributors Added By Toes in the Sand Published November 19, 2026 Edit this listing Make an Edit Add Photos Related Tags Geological Oddities Oceans Water

No traffic, no reservations, no problem. I’m Nora Ritchie, and this is Atlas Obscura, a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. This episode was produced in partnership with Travel Alberta. Explore Canada’s Wild Side. This month, we’re talking with Canadian writers and artists who find inspiration in their home province of Alberta. Today, I’m talking with Andrew Phung. Andrew is a comedian and actor best known for playing Kimchee on Kim’s Convenience , and he’s the creator and star of Run the Burbs . But for this conversation, what matters most is that Andrew is a superfan of Calgary, the medium-sized city where he grew up. This is an edited transcript of the Atlas Obscura Podcast : a celebration of the world’s strange, incredible, and wondrous places. Find the show on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , and all major podcast apps. To Andrew Phung, Calgary is simultaneously a big city and a small town—in all the right ways. Travel Alberta / Sameer Ahmed Calgary is in southern Alberta, where the prairies meet the foothills of the Rocky Mountains. And to be honest, it’s not exactly considered the poster child for Alberta tourism. That honor usually goes to places like Banff and Lake Louise, with their turquoise lakes and mountain views. But Andrew thinks his hometown deserves a little more love. Andrew: I would describe Calgary as a really big city that has all the amenities but feels a bit like a small town at times in regards to its friendliness. The mountains are right behind you. There’s really fresh air, and it is so bright. I think there’s some wild statistic, like Calgary gets the most sunshine in, like, all of the world during the winter or something like that. Nora: I wanna hear about the street you grew up on, your neighborhood. Andrew: I will talk about Northeast Calgary until I die. The northeast of Calgary is a quadrant of the city. It is the most culturally diverse. I grew up in Whitehorn, Temple, Falconridge, Coral Springs. I’ll name the neighborhoods, but Coral Springs was where we ended up last. And what I loved about it was, Coral Springs is full of dreamers. It’s people who this was the first new house they bought. And it was really affordable to new immigrants, families starting out fresh. So literally everyone on my street had kids, and so we were always playing. Like, every day after school, we’d come home, we would get on our bikes, we would go to someone’s house, get the baseball equipment, get the hockey equipment, carry the net, you know, all that stuff. Every day at 5:00, you know, people would come home from work, and then we’d have to go inside and have dinner and do homework. That was our street. It felt a little bit like Pleasantville. Nora: It does sound like Pleasantville. So your parents are Chinese and Vietnamese. How did they end up in Calgary? Andrew: So most people assume your parents come to Canada together. My parents met in Canada. They had different immigration stories. My mom immigrated to Airdrie, Alberta, which is a suburb of Calgary. My dad ended up in Saskatchewan. A church there had sponsored a bunch of Vietnamese refugees into Canada. And then my dad tracked down a friend living in Calgary, and he went to take the bus to Calgary and waited for him at the bus station, and the guy didn’t show up. And then my dad saw another person delivering Chinese food, went and talked to that guy, and that guy took my dad home, and my dad lived with him for two years. The Asian community in Calgary in the ’70s and ’80s was so tight-knit. Like, if they saw one of their own, they would take you in. It was so supportive. And I remember years later, my dad saw an old friend. I’m like, “Yo, who was that guy?” My dad’s like, “Oh, I used to live with him.” And I’m like, “You need to give me the full backstory on that.” But my mom and dad met in Airdrie at a card game. My uncle introduced my mom and dad, and I was born and raised in Calgary. That’s our immigration story, and I really always reflect on how welcoming Canada was in the ’70s and ’80s. Really welcoming in refugees and immigrants to build a better life. And my parents always say, “Andrew, we’re living the Canadian dream. Everything we do is the Canadian dream.” Nora: Related to your work in comedy and growing up, was there a time in your childhood that you were sort of like, “Wait a minute, I’m pretty funny. Like, people think I’m funny. Maybe I should explore this more?” Andrew: Growing up as an Asian person in Calgary, comedy and the arts isn’t really an avenue you pursue. And so even though I was very outgoing, I went to university for a degree in economics, with a focus on oil and gas. I thought I was gonna work in oil and gas. I thought I was gonna become a lawyer, like that was the route I was gonna take. The only person I saw that was Asian in the media was, like, Jackie Chan, Jet Li later on. items.title: Anchorage: A City Within the Wild
items.summary:
In  Anchorage , exploring nature isn’t only for a rare free day or a well-planned vacation; it’s a part of daily life, as integral to the city as its infrastructure and cultural offerings. A day here may start with a morning walk on any of the hundreds of miles of trails, continue with freshly caught salmon for lunch at a restaurant with coastal views, and end with a sunset picnic on a rocky outcropping, where the only sounds are crashing waves and the fleeting glimpses of beluga whales.   
  Located on a coastal plain that shifts into alpine slopes farther east, Anchorage is unique
items.text: ' data-toggle="tooltip" title="Link Copied" class="DDPNavbarItem js-social-action-tracked" data-position="Sticky Header" data-service="Link" data-action="Copied" aria-label="Copy Link"> Copy Link Facebook Twitter Reddit Flipboard Pocket Sponsored By Visit Anchorage, Alaska In Anchorage , exploring nature isn’t only for a rare free day or a well-planned vacation; it’s a part of daily life, as integral to the city as its infrastructure and cultural offerings. A day here may start with a morning walk on any of the hundreds of miles of trails, continue with freshly caught salmon for lunch at a restaurant with coastal views, and end with a sunset picnic on a rocky outcropping, where the only sounds are crashing waves and the fleeting glimpses of beluga whales. Located on a coastal plain that shifts into alpine slopes farther east, Anchorage is unique in how its different ecosystems overlap, creating rich diversity in wildlife, botany, and geology. You can experience the best of nature while still enjoying all the creature comforts of urban life and stumble across breathtaking sights without even looking for them. In this guide, we’ve given you some starting points for exploring the wild from Alaska’s biggest city, with wonders ranging from undisturbed wooded trails to marshes that all kinds of animals call home. Ready to take a walk on the wild side? Fishing season runs roughly from late May to early September. Wayde Carroll for Visit Anchorage Ship Creek This 25-mile-long river flows from the Chugach Mountains down into the Port of Alaska on Anchorage’s northern side, where it’s become a popular spot for sport fishing and bird watching. Thanks to its mud and sedge flats, and ocean-fed waters, this area is home to a massive annual run of coho and Chinook salmon. In fact, it’s the only urban Chinook fishery in the world. The 5.8-mile Ship Creek Trail is a perfect way to spend time in nature without leaving the city limits, providing views of salmon spawning and swimming upstream during the summer. Stops along the way, like Ship Creek Overlook Park and the pedestrian bridge just off King’s Landing, provide especially great panoramas of the river and the surrounding mountains. It’s not uncommon to see anglers trying their luck for 20- to 30-pound salmon, and you can even visit the statue of Dena’ina matriarch Grandma Olga , fish filets in her hands and a bronze drying rack behind her. The trail’s namesake is a former Anchorage mayor and Alaska governor. Chris Arend for Visit Anchorage Tony Knowles Coastal Trail For a longer walk, try this 11-mile path that stretches from downtown Anchorage all the way to the Kincaid Park Chalet. However, if you’re looking for a shorter trek, have no fear: The trail is accessible from multiple points in the city, meaning you can hop on or off. You don’t have to explore on foot either, as the trail can be traversed easily by bike and, in the winter, cross-country skis. No matter how you travel the trail, you’re guaranteed some incredible views of downtown Anchorage, Mount McKinley (Denali), Mount Susitna, and Fire Island, especially as you reach the hills near Point Woronzof. The trail offers a rare chance to pass through a number of different biomes, as it winds through marsh, muskeg (acidic, waterlogged peatland), and thick spruce forest. There’s also plenty of wildlife nearby, with moose, in particular, enjoying long walks on the path during the winter. Other animals often spotted include sandhill cranes, ermine, bald eagles, and even beluga whales in Cook Inlet, so don’t forget your camera. Trails rising from the sand dunes and following the bluffs provide some of the best views in Kincaid Park. Paxson Woelber via Flickr CC BY 2.0 Kincaid Park For even more great hiking, visit Kincaid Park, a 1,400-acre green space that was once a Cold War missile base. There’s plenty to do in Kincaid: walk down the 40 miles of cleared trails, practice archery on a designated range, paddle through Little Campbell Lake, or play disc golf on an 18-hole course. There are also seven different soccer fields, a motocross course, and a giant sand dune with stunning views of Cook Inlet and the Kenai Peninsula. In the winter, the park becomes a premier destination for sledding and cross-country skiing, with trails for every skill level. The marsh’s many overlapping habitats make it a hub for all kinds of wildlife. Jody O. Photos for Visit Anchorage Potter Marsh Just 15 minutes south of downtown, this part of the Anchorage Coastal Wildlife Refuge is one of the best wildlife viewing spots in all of Alaska, offering sweeping vistas of the Turnagain Arm tidal waterway and half a mile of boardwalk across the channels and sedges. This wetland ecosystem is full of creatures big and small, from muskrats paddling through the water to the occasional moose taking a dip. And birders, rejoice: The marsh is home to more than 130 bird species, including Arctic tern, Canada geese, trumpeter swans, red-necked grebes, and northern pintails. Pro tip: Visit in April for the greatest variety of migrating birds, or in midsummer to see three different species of salmon schooling under the boardwalk. Information panels and telescopes along the path make it easy to enjoy a self-guided tour and take in the sights and sounds of the marsh at your own pace. You can also see the marsh from aboard the Alaska Railroad or while driving down the Seward Highway . Beluga Point is also a significant archaeological site, with artifacts 8,000 to 10,000 years old. Monica Whitt for Visit Anchorage Beluga Point Also along the Seward Highway sits Beluga Point, a rocky promontory named for the population of beluga whales that can be spotted each July and August when they come to catch salmon in the inlet. However, no matter what time of year you visit, 180-degree views of the Chugach Mountains make this a worthwhile place to stop and take in your surroundings. items.title: The Best Haunted Hotels to Book for a Spooky Getaway
items.summary: Nothing beats staying in a hotel whose suites hold some stories — especially if they’re of the spooky variety. The same friends who roll their eyes at mentions of luxury amenities and amazing views will be wide-eyed when you tell them about the ghost you accidentally ate breakfast with, the wailings you heard on your way to the icebox, or your run-in with an uncanny Victorian woman wearing all black. Booking a room at a regular old hotel will give you a few nice photos and a comfy robe; booking a room at a  haunted  one will give you tales of terror to tell for the rest of your life.

Established in 1851 by Mary Magdalene Marshall, the building has played many roles: a makeshift hospital during the mid-19th-century yellow fever epidemic, a Union hospital near the end of the Civil War, and a temporary home to Joel Chandler Harris, creator of Uncle Remus, during the Reconstruction era. It’s no wonder then that guests frequently report odd activity in the hotel’s period-detailed rooms and cozy library. Common occurrences include the sound of children running down the halls at night, strange figures spotted in the foyers, doorknobs rattling, and faucets turning on on their own. Many Savannah ghost tours stop outside the hotel, but nothing beats drinking spirits amongst the spirits during the nightly social hour (sometimes with live entertainment!). items.title: Straker's New York
items.text: Straker's New York Post Company Straker's 2026 New York, NY Food & Beverage Role Interior Design Scope Renovation: Restaurant and Bar Partners Client: Straker's Photogapher: Billal Taright Project Narrative For years, 59 Grand Street was Lucky Strike, one of the rooms that defined downtown dining in SoHo. It is now the first home outside London for Straker’s, chef Thomas Straker’s wood-fired restaurant from Notting Hill, and something of a homecoming for a chef born in the United States. Our renovation keeps the bones of the old institution and treats them as a classic neighborhood restaurant, with a brighter, more natural palette. The room is built around an expansive open kitchen clad in steel and topped in green stone, and its fire and energy reach every corner. At the front, the bar and low banquettes in vegetable-tanned leather look straight into the kitchen. At the back, a dining room set with white tablecloths is more formal, for long dinners and larger gatherings. Work by Keith Haring, Damien Hirst, Brian Clarke and Jake Clark hangs throughout. The same playfulness reaches the bathrooms, which are wrapped floor to ceiling in marble and mirror.

items.title: Fente Collection
items.text: Fente Collection Post Company Fente Collection 2026 New York, NY Furniture & Fixtures Role Furniture & Fixture Design Scope Fente Collection: Single Sconce, Double Sconce, Flush Mount, Single Pendant, Double Pendant, Quad Pendant Partners Production: Roll & Hill Retail: Roll & Hill Photography: Billal Taright Made in Grand Rapids, MI Project Narrative Named for the French word for “slot,” the Fente Collection takes its cue from shutters, louvers and narrow window openings, where light is shaped as much by what holds it back as by what lets it through. Each fixture is a solid metal cylinder ringed at its base with vertical perforations, which release light in narrow, even bands, while hand-blown glass inside softens it into an ambient glow. The collection is the third with Roll & Hill, after Bell and Delta. It comes in six configurations, in bronze anodized aluminum for interiors and black powder coat for outdoor use. We photographed it at the Taconic School House, a 19th-century schoolhouse in Salisbury, Connecticut. Its hand-carved paneled parlors set off the collection’s spare, precise geometry.

items.title: Lakeville Village Residence
items.text: Lakeville Village Residence Post Company Lakeville Village Residence 2026 Lakeville, CT Residential Role Building Design, Interior Design Scope Renovation & Addition: Single-Family Residence (original 1,300 sq ft Cape, roughly doubled) Partners Owner: Private Photography: Chris Mottalini Project Narrative The Lakeville Village Residence began as a rental. It was a 1,300-square-foot Cape in Litchfield County that Jou-Yie Chou and his family found in the summer of 2020, and four years later they asked the owners if they could buy it. Our renovation doubled the house while keeping the original Cape as its emotional center. The new additions borrow from the New England vernacular, with gabled rooflines, corrugated roofs and barn-like forms. Contemporary detailing keeps them from reading as a reproduction. Inside, Shaker-inspired cabinetry, vintage furnishings, family rugs and polished brass hardware make the rooms feel as though they evolved over time. We gave particular care to the things touched every day: door hardware, faucets, bath fittings, lighting and countertops. The idea is that the closer an object is to the body, the more its quality matters. The dining room lighting is scaled to echo an old New England lantern. Here the designer was also the client, and the house is built around family life through all four seasons, as a place to be lived in rather than looked at.

items.title: Pantelleria • Rodolphe Parente
items.text: EN Pantelleria 91017 – un laboratoire créatif au cœur de la Méditerranée. Sur l’île de Pantelleria, un territoire baigné par une lumière unique, entre volcans et terres agricoles, 91017 se veut un projet d’expression et de réflexion, un laboratoire interdisciplinaire qui invite des créateurs et penseurs issus de disciplines variées – artistes, architectes, écrivains, scientifiques, chefs culinaires – à interroger la notion de territoire sous toutes ses formes, en dialogue avec le contexte singulier de l’île. Situé au large du canal de Sicile, Pantelleria, carrefour culturel entre Méditerranée, devient le cadre d’une exploration nouvelle, où le paysage agit comme un catalyseur pour repenser nos pratiques et nourrir des réflexions contemporaines. 91017 est une invitation à réinventer notre rapport au temps, au territoire, à travers une exploration humaine, créative et collaborative au cœur de la Méditerranée. L’ambition de ce projet est de donner carte blanche aux invités pour qu’ils apportent un regard différent sur l’île, explorent ses problématiques et enjeux contemporains, et nourrissent une réflexion collective. Ce dialogue entre les disciplines et le territoire vise à construire des passerelles entre art, science, culture et environnement. Chaque séjour et chaque réflexion sont retranscrits à travers un ouvrage d'art en édition limitée. Sur invitation uniquement. 91017@rodolpheparente.com Instagram

items.title: 53 Interior Design Styles You Need to Know - Parts And Labor Design
items.text: 53 Interior Design Styles You Need to Know - Parts And Labor Design Skip to content 53 Interior Design Styles You Need to Know Interior Design ON September 11, 2026 BY Elaine Gross Written By Elaine Gross Elaine is the lead author at Parts and Labor Design, covering interiors, furniture, and home improvement. She spent twelve years in full-home residential design before turning to writing. About Author Edited By Leslie Royce Leslie is the managing editor at Parts and Labor Design. She studied interior design before moving into editorial work, and reads every piece before it’s published. Table of Content You have a folder of saved photos, and no two of them really match. That’s exactly how most people run into interior design styles, one photo at a time, with no idea what any of it is even called. I see it with almost every client before we open a single paint deck. You don’t need one perfect label to fix that. You need to know which materials, colors, and shapes keep repeating in what you save. That’s what this guide breaks down, style by style, so you can walk into a store or a paint aisle already knowing exactly what you’re looking for. There are dozens of types of interior design out there, and most of them borrow a little from each other. Modern overlaps with Minimalist. Farmhouse can lean Rustic. Scandinavian rooms often share features with Japandi. The label matters less than the details that keep repeating: furniture shape, color, material, pattern, and lighting usually reveal the strongest influence. This guide breaks down all interior design styles I work with regularly, from familiar Modern and Traditional looks to specific regional and period styles, and compares the ones people mix up most What Actually Defines an Interior Design Style A few consistent details do most of the work behind any interior design style. The color palette sets the mood first: soft neutrals read one way, bold contrast another. Materials and textures come next, since wood, metal, stone, and natural fiber all behave differently depending on finish. Texture shapes how a room feels even when the colors stay the same. Furniture shape matters too. Curved, low pieces feel different from sharp, tall ones. Lighting, from a statement fixture to a hidden source, shifts the atmosphere more than most people expect. In my experience, tracking these five things is faster than memorizing style names, and it is what the comparisons below are built on. Style Family Examples What Usually Defines It Modern & Contemporary Modern, Contemporary, Urban Modern, Minimalist Clean lines and controlled decoration Scandinavian & Japanese Scandinavian, Japandi Simplicity, function, craftsmanship Traditional & Classic Traditional, Victorian, Regency Classic shapes and decorative detail Mid-Century & Retro Mid-Century Modern, 70s Revival, Vintage Period-specific furniture and color Glamorous Art Deco, Hollywood Regency Polished finishes, stronger contrast Coastal & Warm Climate Coastal, Mediterranean, Moroccan Light colors, tile, stone, texture Mountain Alpine Chic, Chalet Heavy timber, stone, warm textiles Farmhouse, Rustic & Country Farmhouse, Rustic, Country Practical furniture, natural materials Creative & Mixed Bohemian, Eclectic Layered pattern, personal collection Real rooms usually fall between two or three of these families, so treat the table as a starting point rather than a strict rulebook. How to Use This List Before You Buy Anything A style label does not tell you where the sofa goes, and getting the room’s basic clearances right matters more than matching a photo exactly. A chair that is period-correct for Regency does nothing for you if it blocks the door. Leave at least 36 inches of walkway through any main traffic path, and closer to 42 inches anywhere two people need to pass at once. Keep 14 to 18 inches between a sofa and a coffee table so knees clear it without a shuffle. Budget 24 inches of clearance on each side of a bed so the bed can actually be ma
